A PROCLAMATION,

For dissolving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGER.

WHereas We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to dissolve this present Parliament, which now stands prorogued to *fttefday the Fifteenth Day of November next: We do for that End publish this Our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly: And the Lords-Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and BurgetTes, and the Comtllissioners for Shires and Burghs of the House of Commons, are dif-ch*rged from their Meeting and Attendance on *?*tfday

the said Fifteenth D%y of November next. And We being desirous and resolved, as soon as may be, to meet Our People, and to have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known to all Our loving Subjects Our Royal Will and Pleasure to call a new Parliament; and do hereby further declare, That, with tire Advice of Our Privy Council, We have this Day given Order to Our Chancellor of Great , to issue out

Writs in due Form, for calling a new Parliament; which Writs are to bear Teste on Saturday the First Day of October next, and to be returnable on Yuefday the Twenty-ninth Day of November following.

Given at Our Court at St. James's, the Thirtieth Day of September, One thousand Seven hundred and

Seventy-four, in the Fourteenth Year of Our Reign., GOD favc the King.

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to at* tend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker elett, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty in the House of Peers: Where Mr. Speaker elect was presented to His Majesty for His Royal Approbation: And,

Then the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, after receiving Directions from His Majesty, signified His Majesty’s Approbation of Mr. Speaker elect.

The House being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported. That the House had been in the House of Peers: Where His Majesty had been pleased to approve of the Choice the House had made of him to be their Speaker; and that he had, in their Name, and on their Behalf, by humble Petition to His Majesty, laid Claim to all their antient Rights and Privileges, particularly that their Persons, their Ef-tates, and Servants, might be free from Arrests, and all Molestations; that they may enjoy Liberty of Speech in all their Debates, may have Access to His Majesty’s Royal Person, whenever Occasion Hi all require; and that all their Proceedings may receive from His Majesty the most favourable Construction; which, be said, His Majesty had confirmed to them in as full and ample Manner as they have been heretofore granted or allowed by His Majesty, or any of His Royal Predecessors.

And then Mr. Speaker repeated- his most respectful Acknowledgments to the House for the Honour they had done him.

Mr. Speaker then put the House in Mind, that the first Tiling to be done, was to take the Oaths, and make and subscribe the Declaration, and to take and subscribe the Oaths of Abjuration and Qualification, by Law required.

And thereupon Mr. Speaker first alone, standing upon the upper Step of the Chair, took the said first-mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the said Oath of Abjuration; and also delivered in to the Clerk of the House an Account of his Qualification, and took and subscribed the Oath of Qualification.

And, after him, several other Members took the said first-mentioned Oaths, and made and subscribed the said Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration; and such of the said Members as are by Law required to deliver in to the Clerk of this House an Account of their Qualification, and to take and subscribe the Oath of Qualification, delivered in such Account, and took and subscribed the said Oath accordingly.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

the ensuing Year to be laid before you; and I doubt not but that, in this House of Commons, I shall meet with the same affectionate Confidence, and the same Proofs ot Zeal and Attachment to My Person and Government, which I have always, during the Course of My Reign, received from My faithful Commons.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Let Me particularly recommend to you, at this Time, to proceed with Temper in your Deliberations, and with Unanimity in your Resolutions. Let My People, in every Part of My Dominions, be taught by your Example, to have a due Reverence for the Laws, and a just Sense of the Blessings, of Our excellent Constitution. They may be allured that, on My Part, 1 have nothing (b much at Heart as the real Prosperity and lading Happiness of all My Subjects.

Xkg* Mr. Speaker reported to the House, That when the ffcoe did attend His Majesty upon last, in

the Hscae of Peers, His Majesty was plealed to make a exxt Gracious Speech horn the Throne to both Houses c£ Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mid ikes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It gives Me much Concern, that I am obliged at the Opening of this Parliament, to inform you, that a most daring Spirit of Resistance and Disobedience to the Law dill unhappily prevails in the Province of the Massachu-set’sBay, and has, in divers parts of it, broke forth in ffeQi Violences of a very criminal Nature. These Proceedings have beea countenanced and encouraged in other of My Colonies, and unwarrantable Attempts have been made to obstruct the Commerce of this Kingdom, by unlawful Combinations. I have taken such Measures, and given such Orders, as I judged most proper and effectual for carrying into Execution the Laws which were pasted in the last Session of the late Parliament, for the Protection and Security of the Commerce of My Subjects, and for the restoring and preferring Peace, Order, and good Government, in the Province of the Massachuset'% Bay; and you may depend

upon My firm and (teadfaft Resolution to withstand every Attempt to weaken or impair the supreme Authority of this Legislature over all the Dominions of My Crown; the Maintenance of which I consider as essential to the Dignity, the Safety, and the Welfare of the British Empire; alluring Myself, that, while I aft upon these Principles, I shall never fail to receive your Assistance and Support.

I have the greatest Satisfaction in being able to inform you, that a Treaty of Peace is concluded between and the Porte. By this happy Event, the Troubles which have so long prevailed in one Part of Europe are composed, and the general Tranquillity rendered complete. It shall be My conftarst Aim and Endeavour to prevent the breaking out of fresh Disturbances; and I cannot but flatter Myself, I shall succeed.as I continue to receive the strongest Assurances from other Powers of their being equally disposed to preserve the Peace.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Estimates for the Service of

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro- Addref* o* posed. That an humble Address be presented to His *he king'* Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this ^P*6*1' House, for His most Gracious Speech from the Throne:

To allure His Majesty, that we receive, with the highest Sense of His Majesty’s Goodnef, the early Information which He has been pleased to give us of the State of the Province of the MajjachtBay:

That we feel the most sincere Concern, that a Spirit of Disobedience and Resistance to the Law should still unhappily prevail in that Province, and that ic his broke forth in fresh Violences, of a most criminal Nature; and that we cannot but lament, that such Proceedings should have been countenanced c d encouraged in any other of His Majesty’s Colonies, and that any of His Subjects should have been so far deluded and miffed as to make ra(h and unwarrantable Attempts to obstruct the Commerce of His Majesty’s Kingdoms, by unlawful Combinations:

To present our most dutiful Thanks to His Majesty', for having taken such Measures as He judged most proper and effectual for carrying into Execution the Laws which were passed in the last Session of the late Parliament, for the Protection and Security of the Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects; and for restoring and preserving Peace, Order, and good Government, in the Province of the Massachuset's Bay.

That, animated by His Majesty’s Gracious Assurances, His faithful Commons will use every Means in their Power to assist His Majesty in maintaining entire and inviolate the supreme Authority of this Legislature overall the Dominions of His Crown; being truly fen-fible that we should betray the Trust reposed in us, and be wanting in every Duty which we owe to His Majesty and to our Fellow Subjects, if we fail to give our most zealous Support to those great Constitutional Principles which govern His Majesty’s Conduct in this important Business, and which are so essential to the Dignity, Safety, and Welfare, of the British Empire:

That we learn with great Satisfaction, that a Treaty of Peace is concluded between Russia and the Porte, and that by this happy Event the general Tranquillity is rendered complete; and that we entertain a well-grounded Hope, that His Majesty’s constant Endeavours to prevent the breaking out of fresh Disturbances will be attended with Succels, as His Majesty continues to receive the strongest Assurances from other Powers, of their being equally disposed to preserve the Peace:

To assure His Majesty, that His faithful Commons will, with the utmost Chearfulness, grant to His Majesty every necessary Supply; and that they consider themselves bound by Gratitude as well as Duty', to give every Proof of their most affectionate Attachment to a Prince, who, during the whole Course of His Reign, has made the Happiness of His People the Object of all His Views, and the Rule of all His Actions.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by inferring after the Word " Throne," at the End of the First Paragraph, these Words; " And " to assure His Majesty, that, animated with the warm- eft Zeal for His Service, and for the Glory and Prosperity of His Reign, we shall enter into the Confident* tion of the present Situation of His Colonies in Anterica, with that Care and Attention, which the Delicacy

" and Importance of the Object require.

" And humbly to represent, that our inviolable Duty " and ltespect to His Majesty, as well as our Situation " in an immediate delegated Trust from His People, " will not permit us to form any Opinion upon a Matter, which may not only sensibly and deeply affect the " landed and commercial Interests of our Constituents, " but lead to Consequences of a still more alarming Nature, without the fullest and most satisfactory Information: And to that End, most humbly to request, that His Majesty would be graciously pleased to " give Orders that all the Accounts received from " America may be laid before this House with all con-4‘ venient Dispatch.

" And that when, by such Information we shall be enabled to form a proper Judgment, we will humbly " offer our Advice on this delicate Situation of Affairs, " and endeavour to find the Means effectually to sup- port the Honour of His Majesty’s Crown, and the " true Dignity of Parliament, which shall be best adapted to connect both with the permanent Peace,

Concord, and Prosperity, of all His Majesty’s Dominions.".

Then the main Question being put;

Rejohed, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne.

To assure His Majesty, that we receive, with the highest Sense of His Majesty’s Goodness, the early Information which He has been pleased to give us of the State of the Province of the Bay.

That we feel the most sincere Concern, that a Spirit of Disobedience and Resistance to the Law should still unhappily prevail in that Province, and that it has broke forth in fresh Violences, of a most criminal Nature; and that we cannot but lament, that such Proceedings should have been countenanced and encouraged in any other of His Majesty’s Colonies, and that any of His Subjects should have been so far deluded and milled as to make rash and unwarrantable Attempts to obstruct the Commerce of His Majesty’s Kingdoms, by unlawful Combinations.

To present our most dutiful Thanks to His Majesty, for having taken such Measures as He judged most proper and effectual for carrying into Execution the Laws, which were passed in the last Session of the late Parliament, for the Protection and Security of the Commerce of His Majesty’s Subjects; and* for restoring and pre-l'erving Peace, Order, and good Government, in the Province of the Massachuset’sBay.

That, animated by His Majesty’s gracious Affu-rances. His faithful Commons will use every Means in their Power to assist His Majesty in maintaining entire and inviolate the supreme Authority of this Legislature over all the Dominions of His Crown; being truly fen-fible that we should betray the Trust reposed in us, and be wanting in every Duty which we owe to His Majesty and to our Fellow Subjects, if we fail to give our most zealous Support to those great Constitutional Principles which govern His Majesty’s Conduct in this im-

Vol. 35.

portant Business, and which are so essential to the Dignity, Safety, and Welfare, of the Empire.

That we learn with great Satisfaction, that a Treaty of Peace is concluded between Russia and the Porte, and that by this happy Event the general Tranquillity is rendered complete; and that we entertain a well grounded Hope, that His Majesty’s constant Endeavours to prevent the breaking out of fresh Disturbances will be attended with Success, as His Majesty continues to receive the strongest Assurances from other Powers, of their being equally disposed to preserve the Peace.

To assure His Majesty, that His faithful Commons will, with the utmost Chearfulness, grant to His Majesty every necessary Supply; and that they consider themselves bound by Gratitude, as well as Duty, to give every Proof of their most affectionate Attachment to a Prince, who, during the whole Course of His Reign, has made the Happiness of His People the Objcdt of all His Views, and the Rule of all His Actions.

Byron accordingly, when a Multitude of disorderly Persons, armed with Sticks and other Weapons, assaulted the said Returning Officers in a riotous and outrageous Manner, and, by open Force and Violence, obliged them to return the said Francis Eyre, instead of the said William Byron, along with the said Peter;

whereby the Petitioners are deprived of One of their legal Representatives, and have haul another illegally imposed upon them: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard by their Counsel against the said Return; and that such Relief may be granted to the Petitioners, and such Punishment inflicted upon the Offenders, as to the House shall seem meet.

Memorandum 1 .

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members, to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

fcleftionj. And several other Petitions, complaining of undue Elections and Returns, being offered to be presented to the House at the same Time; and Mr. Speaker having recommended to the House, to consider what was fit to be done upon that and limilar Occasions, and to establish some proper Order relative to the Method of delivering in the said Petitions;

Resolved, That, whenever more than One Petition, complaining of an undue Election or Return for the fame, or for different,. Plages, shall, at the same Time,. be offered to be presented to the House, Mr. Speaker shall direct such Petitions to be all of them delivered in at the Table; and the Names of the Counties, Cities, Boroughs, or Places, to which such Petitions shall relate, shall be written on several Pieces of Paper, of an equal Size; and the same Pieces of Paper shall be then rolled up, and put by the Clerk into a Glass, or Box, and then publicly drawn by the Clerk; and the said several Petitions shall be read in the Order in which the said Names shall be drawn respectively.

And several Petitions being accordingly delivered in at the Table; and the Names of the Counties, Cities, Boroughs, and Places, to which the said Petitions did relate, being accordingly put into a Glass; the same were drawn by the Clerk, in the following Order; viz.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty Yesterday; with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this mod. gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return You My particular Thanks, for this very loyal and dutiful Address. I receive with the highest Satisfaction and Approbation your AflurancdS of Assistance and Support, in maintaining the Supreme Authority of the Legislature over all the Dominions of My Crown. It shall be My Care to justify, by My Con-dud:, the Confidence you so affectionately express, and to shew that I have no Interests separate from those of My People.

Setting forth, That, at the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Peters-field, Sir Abrqham Hume, Baronet, High Sheriff for the County of Hertford, William Jolliffe, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and that the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe, by themselves and their Agents, after the Dissolution of the last Parliament, and the issuing of the Writ for the Election, and previous to and during the Poll, by themselves and their Agents, and by other Ways and Means, on the Behalf, and at the Charge, of the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe, did give, present, and allow, to the Electors of the said Borough, and to several Persons who bad, or claimed, a Right to vote in the Election for the said Borough, Money, Meat, Drink, Reward, Entertainment, and Provision, in order to procure themselves to be elected for the said Borough, in open De-r fiance of the Law; and that the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe previous to and during the Poll, were guilty of Bribery and Corruption, and attempting Voj.. 55.

to bribe and corrupt those who had a Right to vote in the said Election, in order to procure themselves to be returned as Persons duly elected; and that James Show* ell, pretending to be the Mayor of the said Borough, acted partially and unfairly in the Execution of his Office as a Returning Officer, during the said Poll, in rejecting good Votes for the Petitioner, and admitting bad ones for the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jo I-lisse, and in many other Respects; and that, by the said and other undue Means, the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe obtained a Majority of Votes on the Poll, and were returned accordingly to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in Prejudice of the Petitioner (who was duly elected, and ought to have been returned) and the legal Electors of the said Borough, and in open Defiance of the Law, and Freedom of Elections:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant him such Relief therein as shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Friday the a 8 th Day of April next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Ditto, thereunto subscribed, being Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Petersfield, in the County of Southampton, was also read; Setting forth.

That, at the last Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Petersfield, the Honourable John Luttrell, Sir Abraham Hume, Baronet, and William Jolliffe, Esquire, were Candidates; and that James Showell, pretending to be the Mayor of the said Borough, and who was avowedly in the Interest of Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe, acted unjustly, and to the Prejudice of the Petitioners, in as much as he lessened their Privileges, by the Admission of Persons to vote who came from distant Places, many of them with their Conveyances just executed, of which they would give no Account, nor whether they were in Possession, or whether the Grantor had a Right to grant, though it was objected he had nor; and that they claimed under Conveyances, suspicious at lead upon the Face of them, occasional, and fraudulent in their Consequences, contrary, as the Petitioners apprehend, to the Meaning of the Resolution of the House in 1727, which could only extend to permanent Freeholders, claiming, by Purchase for a valuable Consideration, or by Devise or Descent, and not to occasional Votes, usually termed Faggots, and which may be multiplied at the Will of the Grantor, and, if allowed, mud be totally destructive of the Franchises of the real Electors, who are bur-tliened with all the Taxes; and that the Petitioners therefore conceive the Admission of such Persons to vote is illegal, destructive of the Privileges of the Petitioners, and highly dangerous to the Law and Constitution of Parliament; and that, by these and other undue Practices, the said Sir Abraham Hume and William Jolliffe procured themselves to be returned, to the Prejudice of the Petitioners and the legal Electors of the said Borough: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as to them shall appear to be just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration at the same Time that the last preceding Petition i§ ordered to be taken into Consideration.

and Sir James Cockburn* Baronet, declared themselves Candidates; and that, by the Law of Scotland, and the Constitution and immemorial Usage of the said Borough of Linlithgow* no Person can hold the Office of Magistrate or Counsellor, except those who reside within the Borough, and pay Part of the Taxes laid on the Inhabitants; and that, at the last Election of a Commissionef for the said Borough, James Andrew was duly elected Delegate or Commissioner by the Majority of Counsellors resident in the Borough, who alone are legally entitled to vote fora Commissioner; and that the Election for the Member of Parliament was held at Linlithgow, the presiding Borough, on the 31st Day of October last, when the Commissioners for the Three other Boroughs attended, with the said James Andrew* the Commissioner elected by a Majority of the legal Voters for the Borough of Linlithgow, and Sir James Cockburn, the pretended Delegate for the said Borough; and that the Commissioner for the Borough of Lanark, and James Andrew, the Commissioner for the Borough of Linlithgow, voted for the Petitioner; and the Commissioners for the Borough of Selkirk and Peebles voted for the said Sir James Cockburn; and that, the Votes being thus equal, James Andrew, the Commissioner legally chosen for the presiding Borough, gave his calling Vote for the Petitioner, who was then duly elected the Member to serve in Parliament for the said District of Boroughs; but Sir James Cockburn* assuming to himself the Character of Commissioner for the presiding Borough, gave his Vote for himself; and the Sheriff of t lie County of Linlithgow has thought proper to return him; and that, the Election of the said Sir James Cockbuin being also liable to several other Objections, the Return made by the Sheriff is iq manifest Wrong of the Petitioner, anS in open Violation of Law: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant to the Petitioner such Relief as to them shall seem reasonable.

SIR Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whotft it was referred to consider of the Motion made upon Wednesday last, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty; the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time; Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That a Supply be granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morn-

ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Ordinary of the Navy for the Year 1775, with an Estimate of the Half Pay of Officers of the Navy, and such of the Officers of the Marines as were employed in the last War, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Charge of what may be necessary for the Buildings, llebuiTdings, and Repairs, of Ships of War, in His Majesty’s Yards, and other Extra Works, over and above what are proposed to be done upon the Heads of Wear and Tear, and Ordinary, for the Year 1775, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Charge for Guards, Garrisons, and other Land Forces, for the Year 1775, be laid before this House. ' ,

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year 1775, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That a Lilt of the Regimental and Warrant Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces, and of such of the Officers of the Marines as were reduced before the last War, who are to be on Half Pay for the Year 1775, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Charge of Out Pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year 1775, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That an Account of Services incurred, and not provided for by Parliament, be laid before this House.

Ordered, That an Account be laid before this House, shewing the Monies aril'en within the respective Half Years ended at the 5th Day of April 1774, and the

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions to the proper Officers, to lay before this House, the said Estimates, Lift, and Accounts.

and in other Respects the said Hugh Ellis, both before and at the said Election, acted in a very partial and unwarrantable Manner in the Execution of his Office; and that, owing to the above and other undue Means and Influence, and particularly to the partial Conduct of the said Sheriff, the Petitioner was compelled to discontinue the Poll; A Petition of the honourable George Keith Elphinstone, was read; Setting forth, That at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the County of Dumbarton, in North Britain, held upon the 10th Day of November last, the Petitioner, and Sir Archibald Edmonstone, Baronet, were Candidates; and that after the Roll of Freeholders was called over, and the First of the Number had voted for the said Sir Archibald Edmonstone, another Freeholder informed the Meeting, that Sir Archibald was, by the Act 6th Queen Anne* Cap. 7.

Section 25, incapable of being elected, or of fitting or voting as a Member of the House, because he enjoyed Part of the Profits of the Office of Receiver General of the Customs in Scotland, held in the Name of another Person; and that he the said Freeholder gave that early Notice of the said Sir Archibald Edwonf one's Incapacity, to prevent other Freeholders from throwing away their Votes; and that the Election then proceeded; and of 41 Freeholders present, 14 voted for the Petitioner, 26 for the said Sir Archibald EdmonJloney and he h ini felt voted for the honourable William Efphinfcrte, w ho was no Candidate; and that the Votes being over, the Petitioner entered his Protcft, that, in regard of the said Sir Archibald Edmonstone's Incapacity, the Petitioner was the Person duly elected, and ought to be returned; but this Protest was diiregarded, and the said Sir Archibald Fuimondflone is returned by the Sheriff'; and that, the Election of the said Sir Archibald Edmonstone being liable to sundry other Objections, the Return in his Favour is in wrong of the Petitioner, and in open Violation of Law: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give him such Relief as to the House shall appear just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Friday the 2d Day of June next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of Three Shillings tn the Pound, and no more, be raised, within the Space of One Year, from the 25th Day of March 1775, upon Lands, Tenements, Hereditaments, Pensions, Offices, and Personal Estates, in that Part of Great Britain called England, Wales, and the Town of Berwick upon Tweed; and that a proportionable Cel's, according to the Ninth Article of the Treaty of Union, be laid upon that Part of Great Britain called Scotland.

A Petition of John Seton, was presented to the House, arc.’ and read; Setting forth. That at the last Election of

Election, a Member to serve in Parliament for the District of Boroughs of Elgin, Banff, Cullen, Kintore, and in North Britain, Thomas Lockhart, Esquire, and Colonel Morris, were Candidates; and the said Colonel Morris was returned; and that the said Thomas Lockhart, being then very much indisposed and confined to his House in London, was not present at the said Election, and has since gone to Lisbon, in the Kingdom of Portugal, for the Recovery of his Health; and that the Friends of the said Thomas Lockhart, being convinced the Election of the said Colonel Morris was brought about by undue Influence and unlawful Means, did dispatch an Express to London to the Petitioner, with Orders to have a Petition, in the Name of the said Thomas Lockhart, presented to the House j but that Authority not being sufficient, the Petitioner dispatched another Express to Scotland, to inform them thereof; and that the said Boroughs are situated in the Northern Parts of Scotland, at a very great Distance from London; and that last Night, about Nine o’Clock, the Petitioner received another Express, with a Petition, signed by George Ogilvy, Esquire, a Constituent Member of the Borough of Cullen, in Behalf of himself and the other Counsellors of that Borough, complaining of the Election of the said Colonel Morris; which Petition the Petitioner immediately lodged with the Clerk of the House of Commons; and that the Time allowed to Petitioners, by the House, for questioning the Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, expired Yesterday; but the Petitioner hopes, that, when the Absence of the said Thomas Lockhart, the great Distance of the Place of Election, and the Badnels of the Roads at this Season of the Year, are considered, the House will fee Vou 35.

Cause for dispensing, in the present Instance, with their Order of the Fifth of December Instant: and therefore praying the House, that the Petition of the said George Ogilvy may be received.

And a Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That, in Consideration of the particular Circumstances set forth in the said Petition, Leave be given to present the Petition of the said George Ogilvy, as desired by^the said John Seton;

And a Debate arising in the House thereupon;

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the Debate be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " Tomorrow " Morning," and inlerting the Words " the 20th Day of January next," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Tomorrow Morning" Hand Part of the Question.

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

The laid Papers are preferred amongst the other Papers of this Session.

A Petition of John Dewar, Esquire, was presented to Crickhde the Hause, and read; Setting forth. That, at the late £lcftion. Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, in the room of William Earle, Esquire, deceased,. Samuel Peach, Esquire, and the Petitioner were Candidates; and that, at the said Election, which came on the 27th Day of December la ft, before Thomas Carter, Bailiff and Returning Officer for the said Borough, a great Majority of Jegal Votes was given for the Petitioner, who ought to have been returned accordingly; but the said

15 Geo. III. 19° — 200 J67

Returned the said Sairuu'.I Patch and the Petitioner, instead of the Petitioner alone, to the great Injury of the Petitioner, and in Violation of the Rights of the Electors of the said Borough: And therefore praying, That the said Return may be amended, by erating the Name of the said Samuel Peach therefrom, and that the Petitioner only may be declared duly cleded, or have such other Relief as the House shall think meet.

Ditto. A Petition of Samuel Peach, Esquire, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That at the late Election of a Member to represent the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of in this present Parliament, in the room of William , Esquire, jdeceased, the Petitioner and John , Esquire, were

Candidates; and that the said Eiedion came on about Eleven of the Clock in the Forenoon of the 27th Day of December last; and the Returning Officer proceeded to take the Poll in the Church, as the most convenient Place for that Purpose, and continued the Poll to Four of the Clock in the Afternoon of the same Day, when only Forty-one out of near Two hundred Persons having a Right to vote had given their Suffrages; and that the Poll being adjourned to the same Place, and at the Hour of Nine the next Morning, the Petitioner, with his Counsel, Agents, and a very numerous Body of Electors, who meant to vote for the Petitioner, appeared at the Church Porch, pursuant to the said Adjournment; and that, as the Returning Officer and the Candidates, together with the Electors, were entering , the Church, in or^ler to proceed to the Place of Polling, a Riot commenced, which obliged the Returning Officer immediately to close the Poll; and on that Account he returned the said John Dewar and the Petitioner, to represent the said Borough, in the room of the said William Eatle, and that the Petitioner, by reason thereof, was prevented from receiving the Suffrages of a large Majority of the Electors for the said Borough, and of obtaining a legal Right to represent tire said Borough for the Remainder of this present Parliament; and that, from the Time of the Decease of the said William Earle unto the Close of the Poll, the Town of Cricklade, by Means of the Feasts and Entertainments daily and constantly given by, and at the Expence of, the said John Dewar, or his Agents, to the Electors of the said Borough, in order to procure their Votes for the said John Dewar, was kept in continual Riot, Tumult, Idleness, and Dissipation, to the great Injury of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, whereby the Morals of the People were corrupted, and the public Peace much disturbed; and that, by the above and other undue Means made use of by the said John Dewar or his Agents, and by the Conduct of tire Returning Officer, the Sense of the Electors at large has not been taken, and the Petitioner is thereby much aggrieved: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief therein as to the House shall, upon Examination, appear to be just.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be taken into Consideration upon Monday the 6th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11 th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petitions were ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as Vox.. 35.

shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matters of the said Petitions.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners arc all essentially interested in the Trade to North America, either as Exporters and Importers, or as Venders of and

Foreign Goods for Exportation, to that Country; and that the Petitioners have exported, or fold for Exportion to the British Colonies in North , very

large Quantities of the Manufacture of Great Britain and Ireland, and in particular the Staple Articles of Woollen, Iron, and Linen, also those of Cotton, Silk, Leather, Pewter, Tin, Copper, and Brass, with almost every British Manufacture, also large Quantities of

Foreign Linens, and other Articles imported into these Kingdoms, from Flanders, Holland, The East Countries, Portugal, Spain, and Italy, which are generally received from those Countries in Return for British Manufactures; and that the Petitioners have likewise exported, or fold for Exportation, great Quantities of the various Species of Goods imported into this Kingdom from the East Indies, Part of which receive additional Manufacture in Great Britain; and that the Petitioners receive Returns from North America to this Kingdom directly; videlicet. Pig and Bar Iron, Timber, Staves, Naval Stores, Tobacco, Rice, Indigo, Deer and other Skins, Beaver, and Furs, Train Oil, Whale Bone, BeesWax, Pot and Pearl Ashes, Drugs, and Dying Woods, with some Bullion, and also Wheat Flour, dian Corn, and Salted Provisions, when on Account of Scarcity in Great Britain, those Articles are permitted to be imported; and that the Petitioners receive lie-turns circuitously from Ireland (for Flax Seed, ^. exported from North America) by Bills of Exchange on the Merchants of this City trading to Ireland, for the Proceeds of Linens, fAc. imported into these Kingdoms, from the West Indies, in Return for Provisions, Lumber, and Cattle, exported from North America, for the Use and Support of the West India Islands, by Bills of Exchange on the IV'eJlIndia Merchants, for the Proceeds of Sugar, Melasses, Rum, Cotton,' Coffee, or other Produce, imported from those Islands info these Kingdoms; from Italy, Spain, Portugal, France, Flanders, Germany, Holland, and The East Countries, by Bills of Exchange or Bullion, in Return for Wheat, Flour, Rice, Indian Corn, Fish, and Lumber, exported from the Britpi Colonies in North America, for the Use of those Countries; and that the Petitioners have great llcafon to believe, from the bed Information they can obtain, that, on the Balance of this extensive Commerce, there is now due, from the Colonies in America, to the said City only, 2,000,000l. Sterling, and upwards; and that, by the direct Commerce with the Colonies, and the circuitous Trade thereon depending, some Thousands of Ships and Vessels are employed, and many Thousands of Seamen are bred and maintained, thereby increasing the Naval Strength and Power of Great Britain-, and that, in the Year 1765, there was a great Stagnation of

\ ol. 35. (

the Commerce between Great Britain and her Colonies, in consequence of an Act for granting and applying certain Stamp Duties, and other Duties, in the British Colonies and Plantations in America, by which the Merchants trading to North America, and the Artificers employed in the various Manufactures consumed in those Countries, were subjected to many Hardships 1 and that, in the following Year, the said Act was repealed, under an express Declaration of the Legislature, that the Continuance of the said Act would be attended with many Inconveniences, and might be productive of Consequences greatly detrimental to the commercial Interests of these Kingdoms; upon which Repeal, the Trade to the Britipi Colonies immediately resumed its former flourishing State; and that in the Year 1767, an Act passed, for granting certain Duties in the British Colonies and Plantations in America, which imposed certain Duties, to be paid in America, on Tea, Glass, Red and White Lead, Painters Colours, Paper, Paste-board, Millboard, and Sealeboard, when the Commerce with the Colonies was again interrupted; and that, in the Year 1770, such Parts of the said Act as imposed Duties on Glass, Red and White Lead, Painters. Colours, Paper, Pasteboard, Millboard, and Scale-board, were repealed, when the Trade to America soon revived, except in the Article of Tea, on which a Duty was continued, to be demanded on its Importation into America, whereby that Branch of our Commerce was nearly loft; and that, in the Year 1773, an Act passed, to allow a Drawback of the Duties of Customs on the Exportation of Tea to His Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in America, and to empower the Commissioners of the Treasury to grant Licences (o the East India Company, to export Tea, Duty free; and, by the Operation of those and other Laws, the Minds of His Majesty’s Subjects in the British Colonies have been greatly disquieted, a total Stop is now put to the Export Trade with the greatest and most important Part of North America, the public Revenue is threatened with a large and fatal Diminution, the Petitioners with grievous Distress, and Thousands of industrious Artificers and Manufacturers with utter Ruin; under these alarming Circumstances, the Petitioners receive no small Comfort, from a Persuasion that the llepresentatives of the People, newly delegated, to the most important of all Trusts, will take the whole of these weighty Matters into their most serious Consideration: And therefore praying the House, That they will enter into a full and immediate Examination of that System of Commercial Policy, which was formerly adopted, and uniformly maintained, to the Happiness and Advantage of both Countries, and will apply such healing Remedies as can alone restore and establish the Commerce between Great Britain and her Colonies on a permanent Foundation; and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves or Agents, in Support of the said Petition.

A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Society of Merchants Venturers of the City of Bristol, under their Common Seal, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a very beneficial and increasing Trade to the Colonies in America,

has been carried on from the Port of Bristol, highly to the Advantage of the Kingdom in general, and of the said City in particular; and that the Exports from the said Port to America consist of almost every Species of British Manufactures, besides East India Goods, and other Articles of Commerce; and the Returns are made, not only in many valuable and useful Commodities from thence, but also by a circuitous Trade carried on with Ireland and moll Parts of , to the great Emolument of the Merchant, and Improvement of His Majesty’s Revenue; and that the Merchants of the Taid Port are also deeply engaged in the Trade to the West India Islands, which, by the Exchange of their Produce with America, for Provisions, Lumber, and other Stores, are thereby almost wholly maintained, and consequently become dependant upon North America for Support; and that the Trade to , which is carried on from the said Port to a very considerable Extent, is also dependant on the flourishing State of the fVt.fi India Islands and America; and that thel’e different Branches of Commerce give Employment, not only to a very numerous Body of Artists and Manufacturers, but also to a great Number of Ships, and many Thousand Seamen, by which Means a very capital Increase is made to the Naval Strength of Great Britain; and that the Trade to America has of late Years suffered very considerable Checks, the first of which was after the passing of the Act for levying Stamp Duties there, which subjected the Merchants here to many and great Losses and Inconveniences, and threatened them with Ruin, from which the Repeal of that Act in the following Year removed their Apprehensions, and restored the Trade'to its former flourishing State; and that, in this prosperous Situation, the Trade continued till the next Year, when an Act passed for levying Duties on Glass, Paper, and other Articles, in , and it

again received a considerable Check; but the Repeal of a great Part of those Duties revived it, till the passing of certain Acts of Parliament, and other Measures lately adopted, caused such a great Uneasiness in the Minds of the Inhabitants of America, as to make the Merchants apprehensive of the moll alarming Consequences, and which, if not speedily remedied, must involve them in

utter Ruin; and the Petitioners, as Merchants, deeply interested in Measures which will so materially afteft the Commerce of this Kingdom, and not Iefs concerned, as Engfilhmen, in every Thing that relates to the general Welfare, cannot look without Emotion on the many Thousands of miserable Objects, who, by the total Stop put to the Export Trade to America, will be di (charged from their Manufactures for want of Employment, and must be reduced to great Distrers; and the Petitioners look back with Regret to those Times in which their Trade suffered no Interruption; but they presume not to suggest any particular Mode of Relief to the House, in whole Wisdom they place the most unreserved Confidence; they venture, however, to express their Willies, that the former System of commercial Policy may be taken into Consideration; and that the destructive Breaches made in their Trade, by the Alarms to which it has been for many Years subject, may be doled, the Peace of this great Empire restored, and Commerce once more fixed on the most foiid and permanent Foundation.

Piccadilly A Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Pe-Paviifg, tition bf several Gentlemen, and others, Inhabitants of Houses, in that Part of Piccadilly between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Corner, and of that Part of Park Lane between Piccadilly aforesaid, and the North Side of Hertford Street, within the Parish of Saint George, Hanover Square, and Liberty of Westminster, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of King George the First, and in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, Two Acts Were made, for repairing the Road leading from Hyde Park Corner, and several other Roads therein mentioned, in the County of Middlesex, of which so much of Piccadilly as lies between Clarges Street and Hyde Park Corner, and also so much of Park Lane as lies between Piccadilly, and the North Side of Hertford Street, were Part; and the Trustees for the Care of the said Roads were, by the said Acts, required to water so much of Piccadilly as lies between the End of Berkeley Street and

Hyde Park Gate, during the dry Weather, and to defray all Expences attending the several Works aforesaid out of the Tolls arising by virtue of the said Acts; and that by an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, so much of the said former Acts as relate to such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Clarges Street and Hyde Park Corner, and also such Part of Park Lane as lies between Piccadilly and the North Side of Hertford Street, were repealed; and such Parts of the said Street and Lane were, by the said last mentioned Act, put under the foie Management and Direction of the Commissioners for paving the several Streets and other Places within the City and Liberty of Westminstery and, in Consideration of the Expences attending the fame, the Annual Sum of £. i,oooo is by the said Act directed to be paid, by the Trustees of the said Roads, out of the Tolls collected at the Turnpike at Hyde Park Corner, to the said Commissioners; which Sum has ever since been regularly paid, according to the Directions of the said Act; and that the said Commissioners have caused such Parts of Piccadilly and Park Lane to be paved, cleansed, and lighted, and did also, for some Time after passing the said Act, cause such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Corner to be watered, as was formerly done by the said Trustees; but the said Commissioners have of late discontinued to water the said Street; and, upon Application being made to them by the Inhabitants to water the fame, they alledge, that the Annual Sum of800 (Part of the said £.1,000) had been mortgaged, in order to raise Money* to enable them to carry the Purposes of the said Act into Execution; and that the remaining Annual Sum of £.200, together with the Annual Rates now levied on the Inhabitants, is not sufficient to defray the Expence of repairing, cleansing, lighting, and watering, the said Street, in a proper Manner; and the Inhabitants of the said Street, being desirous to have the same watered as heretofore, are of Opinion, that, if the several Works aforesaid were put under the Management of Trustees to be appointed amongst the Inhabitants, the Annual Rates winch they now pay, with the Assistance of the said Annual Sum of £. 200, would be sufficient to defray all the Expences of repairing, cleansing, and lighting, the same for the future, and likewise of watering such Parts of Piccadilly as was formerly done by the said Trustees: And therefore praying,

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, and for repealing the several Laws now in being, so far as the same relate to such Parts of Piccadilly and Park Lane as aforesaid; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.’

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Sehvyn, Mr. Curzon, &c.:

And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

on the Account of North American Merchants and Traders, to the several Provinces of that extensive Continent; but, since the unhappy Differences which have arilen between Great Brit and the Colonies, a Stop hath been put to the Exportation of the said Manufactures to North America; and that the Inhabitants of the said City, liable to the public Taxes, are already greatly burther.cd with a numerous Poor; and, if the Demand of Norwich Stuffs to any of the several Parts of Europe (of late plentifully supplied) should by any Means be lessened, the Petitioners are fearful of the Consequences which must inevitably happen to the said City from the Stoppage of the American Trade; and that, on any further Reduction of the Manufactures of the said City, the Number of poor Artificers and thfir Families, which will be thrown on the public Expence, will be inlupportable , and that the industrious Artificers and labouring Men, and their Families, will be reduced, by Poverty and Want of Employment, to be without the necessary Succours of Food and Raiment: And therefore, for the Revival of the Petitioners Trade and Commerce to America, and to prevent the Continuance or Growth of the above Evils, praying the House will take the Premises into their immediate and most serious Consideration, and grant them such effectual and permanent R.liei as they shall think proper.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of Londotiy concerned in the Commerce of North America, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting a Petition presented to the House by the Petitioners upon Monday last; and Setting forth. That the Petitioners have ever conceived that the Connection be-Great Britain and America originally was, and ought to be, of a commercial Kind, and that the Benefits derived therefrom, to the Mother Country, are of the same Nature; and observing the constant Attention which the British Legislature had, for more than a Century, given to those valuable Objects, they have been taught to admire the Regulations by which that Connexion had been preservd, and those Benefits secured, as the most effectual Institution which human Wisdom could have framed for those salutary Pur poles; presuming the refore on this Opinion, and supported by this Observation, the Petitioners represent to the House, that the fundamental Policy of those Laws of which they complain, and the Propriety of enforcing, relaxing, or amending, the fame, are Questions infieparabiy united with the Commerce between Great Britain and America; and consequently that the Consideration of the one cannot be entered on, without a full Discussion of the other j and that the Petitioners observe by the Votes,

that a Committee hath been appointed, to take into their Consideration certain Papers presented to the House by Lord North on 2Ir.rrfday tl:e 19th Instant; and, by the Titles and Dates of the said Papers, and in particular N° 148 and 149 of the lame, the Petitioners are warranted in preluming that the said Papers contain Matters reflecting the prefect Situation of America, and essentially concerning the mutual Interests of the Petitioners and that Country; and that, under all these Circumstances, the Petitioners find Realbn sincerely to lament that the House has thought fit to refer the Consideration of their laid Petition to any other Committee, than that to which the said Papers had previously been referred, and the Petitioners conceive that, by the Rdolution to which the House hath come, respecting the Reference of their laid Petition, they are absolutely precluded from the Bern fit or such a Hearing, in Support of their laid Petition, as can alone procure them that Relief, which the Importance and present deplorable State of their Trade require: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their immediate Consideration, and to direct that the Petitioners may be heard, by ihemselves or their Agents, in Support of their laid former Petition; and that no Resolutioa respecting America may be taken by the House, or any Committee thereof, until the Petitioners shall have been fully heard in Support of their said Petition.

A Petition of sundry Merchants, Factors,- and Ma- American* nufacturers, of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, Colonki. on Behalf of themselves and others in that Neighbourhood, who are interested in the Trade from thence to North America, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth, That the Demand from North America, for the Manufactures of the said Town and Neighbourhood, has of late Years very eonfiderably increased, and many Thousands of People have usually found a regular Employment in making various Kinds of Goods, which have been exported thither 5 and that the present Stagnation of their Commerce with that Country r\s already very materially felt; and although it is with the greatest Reluctance that they thus trouble the House with then* Complaints, yet they might stand accused of a Want of Duty to the House, did they neglect to express their Fears, that, in a short Space of Time, a very numerous Body of working People will be deprived of the Means of Subsistence, which becomes the more alarming on account of the high Price of those’ Provisions which their Industry has heretofore enabled them to procure; and that these their Difficulties are also much increased, by the uneasy Apprehensions of their Traders to North America, for the large Property which they have intruded there: And therefore beseech the

House to take their same into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as by the House shall be judged necessary.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Directions of Two several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 146 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioners, James Calthorpe and Richard Beckford, Esquires, with their Counsel and Agents, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Richard Smith, Esquire, And the Counsel and Agents for the said Thomas Brand Hollis, Esquire, who attended at the Door; were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee attending also at the Bar; and the said Counsel for the said Sitting Members having severally informed the House; that the said Sitting Members being complained of by the said Petition now taken into Consideration, upon the Ground of Bribery at the said Election (which Charge would affect them separately, the said Members not having been joint Candidates, but having stood on distinct Interests at the said Election) desired to separate in their Defence; and no Objection being made thereto by the Counsel for the Petitioners, and the said Petition having been read, the same was agreed to by the House.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed by Mr. Speaker to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

American A Petition of the Manufacturers of Felt Hats, and Colonies. £)eajers therein, as also of the Shoemakers, in the Town of Nemcafile, in the County of Stafford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Town has for many Years pall been the principal Place in the Kingdom for Felt Hats; and that large Quantities of Shoes have been made there; the Bulk of which have from Time to Time been exported to different Parts of America, until the Differences unhappily arose betwixt this Kingdom and the Colonies; since then a total Stop to their Trade thither has taken place; and that their manufactured Goods lie dead upon their Hands, Payments are suspended, and their Works flopped, so that great Numbers of their People are quite destitute of Employment, whereby the Petitioners are involved in the general Distress, and the lower Class of People and their Families are reduced to very great Extremity; and what enhances their Unhappiness is, the very high Price of most of the Necessaries of Life at this Sealon of the Year: And therefore praying, That the House would take the same into their serious Consideration, and concert such Measures as they shall dictate for alleviating their Miseries, and that may operate in opening their Trade again, and thereby enabling them to afford an Opportunity to their working People of procuring a Subsistence for themselves and their Families.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

A Petition of the Manufacturers and Traders in Ditto* Earthen Ware, residing in Burslem, Tunstall, Cobridge,

Shelton, Hanley, Stoke Lane, Delf Lane End, and Places adjacent, in the County of Stafford, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in Burslem, and the several Places abovementioned, there are near 200 separate Potteries* for the making of various Kinds of Earthen Wares, which together have found constant Employment and Support for near Ten thousand People; and that a considerable Part of the Goods manufactured by the Petitioners were exported into the different Parts of America, until the late Differences unhappily arose between this Kingdom and her Colonies; and that the Petitioners have great Quantities of Goods now lying upon their Hands; and instead of receiving from America the Orders usually given at this Season of the Year, those few Orders they had received have since been countermanded, and a total Stop is now-put to that Trade, and the Payments for Goods already sold to them rendered very precarious; in consequence of which, the Petitioners have been obliged to reduce their Wotks, and discharge Numbers of their Servants, and, unless some speedy Alteration in Affairs takes place, they must discharge many more, whereby a greater Number still will be destitute of Employment, and reduced, with their Families, to the utmost Necessity:

And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their serious Consideration, and concert such Mca-sures as to them may seem expedient for opening again the Commercial Intercourse between this Kingdom and her American Colonies.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro posed, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North Ant eric a, is referred.

A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and American Assistants, of the Borough of Leeds, in the County of Colonies York, and of the several other Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, principal Inhabitants, Merchants,

Traders, and Manufacturers, in the Borough of Leeds aforesaid, and in Wakefield, Halifax, Bradford, and other Places, within the West Riding of the said County, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That the Petitioners, convinced that the Preservation of the Commerce of this County and its Colonies depends upon a due Obedience to the Laws of England, are greatly alarmed at the unwarrantable Proceedings now carrying on, by the Inhabitants of Bofion and some other Colonies in North America, in open Defiance of the Supreme Legislative Power of this Kingdom, manifestly* obstruefting Commerce, and subverting all legal Government; and that the Petitioners have great Reason to believe. Attempts are now making, to excite groundless Fears and Apprehensions in the Minds of many of His Majesty's faithful Subjects in this Kingdom, receding the present Situation of American Affairs; and, by false Represen tations, and other undue Means, to prevail upon them to sign Petitions to the House, for a Repeal of several Acts of Parliament; and that the Petitioners, on the contrary, apprehend the maintaining the Authority of the British Legislature is the best Security for all interested in the.Trade to America: And therefore praying the House to take such Measures as may seem to them most expedient, for enforcing a due Obedience to the British Legislature, and restoring Order and good Government in America.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred;

American Petition of the Merchants of Leeds, trading to the Colonies. North American Colonies, or having Property there, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by Means of the North American Commerce carried on directly from the Town of Leeds to the North American Colonies, as also by the very great Quantities of the Manufactures of the said Town and Neighbourhood, passing to the said Colonies, through the Hands of the Merchants of London, Liverpool, &c.

the Petitioners have been enabled greatly to extend the Manufactures of the said Town and Country, and given thereby a large Employ to a great Number of Mailer Manufacturers, and to many Thousands of their industrious poor Labourers; and that the North American Commerce from the said Town and Neighbourhood, taken collectively in its full Extent, is an Object of great Concern to the West Riding of Yorkshire in general, to the Petitioners in particular, and worthy the Attention of Parliament; and that, by the unhappy Differences lately broke forth between and

her American Colonies, the Petitioners labour under the present Stagnation of that Branch of Trade, which in Years pall has been too considerable not to be sensibly felt by themselves, and in Time will be much more so by the industrious Manufacturers of the said Town and Neighbourhood; and that the Petitioners having very considerable Property in the Hands of the North Americans, they cannot, in the present critical Situation of Affairs, but be anxious for the Safety thereof, although in ever so honest Hands the same may be deposited; the Petitipners, therefore, alarmed for themselves and Families, at the same Time feeling for the Distressesof those to "whom in Times pall they have been enabled to give Support, confiding in the Wisdom, the Justice, and the Moderation of Parliament, pray such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Planters of His Majesty’s Sugar Colonies residing in Great Britain, and of the Merchants of London trading to the said Colonies, was presented to the House, and read Setting forth. That the Pe-tioners are exceedingly alarmed at an Agreement and Affjciation entered into, by the Congress held at Philadelphia, in North America, on the 5th Day of September 1774, whereby the Members thereof agreed and also ci-ated, for themselves and the Inhabitants of the several Provinces, lying between Nova Scotia and Georgia, that, from and after the First Day of December X774,they would not import into British America any Me.ifies, Syrups, Paneles, Coffee, or Piementu, from the British Plantations; and that, after the joth Day of September 1775, if the Acts and the Parts of Acts of the British Parliament therein mentioned, are not repealed, they would not directly, orindireftiy, export any Merchandize or Commodity whatsoever to the West Indies-, and representing to the House, that the British Property in the West India Islands amounts to upwards of Thirty Millions Sterling; and that a further Property of many Millions is employed in the Commerce created by the said Islands, a Commerce comprehending Africa, the East Indies, and Europe; and that the whole Profits and Produce of those Capita's ultimately centre in Great Britain, and add to the National Wealth, while the Navigation necessary to all its Branches, establishes a Strength which Wealth can neither purchase nor balance; and that the Sugar Plantations in the West Indies are subject to a greater Variety ol Contingencies than many other Species of Property, from their necessary Dependence on external Support; and that therefore, should any Interruption

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Orders of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and sealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table; and the Seals being inspected by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Out-side of the said Box, signed by Mr. Speaker, purporting, <c That the said Box was, on the ad Day of " February 1775, made up in his Presence, in the Manner directed by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of " the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An " Ad to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, " or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament;" was read.

And the said Names, written on distinct Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be of an equal Size,

I and rolled up in the same Manner, were, by the Clerk, taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers into Six Glasses, placed on the Table for that Purpose, and were there shaken together; and then the Clerk publicly drew out of the said Six Glasses, alternately, the said Pieces of Paper, and delivered them, to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House.

And the Names of Thirty-eight Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the Honourable William Byron was then drawn, but the House having, on the 27th Day of January last, ordered, that Francis Eyre, Esquire, and the Freemen and Eledors of the Borough or Morpeth, should be at Liberty to petition this House, to question the Election of the said Member, within Fourteen Days then next, if they should think fit, his Name was set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House.

And the Names of Eleven other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Eleven other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside with the Names of those who were absent from the House, on Account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Proprietors of Uninclosed and Commonable Lands, within the Hamlet of otherwise Cuttefden, in the Parish of Eredon, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That there are, within the said Hamlet, several Open and Common Fields, Hills, Sleights, and other Commonable Lands, belonging to the Petitioners and others, which, in their present State, are incapable of any considerable Improvement; and that the same would be greatly increased in Value, if divided , and inclosed: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for dividing and inclosing the said Open and Common Fields, Hills, Sleights, and other Commonable Lands, under such Regulations as the House shall think proper.

Mr. Selzvytt reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, and the humble Petition of several Gentlemen and others. Inhabitants of Houses, in that Part of Piccadilly between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Corner, and of that Part of Park Lane between Piccadilly aforesaid, and the North Side of Hertford Street, within the Parish of George Hanover Square, and Liberty of Westminster, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Two Acts, made in the 12th Year of King George the First, and the 14th Year of King George the Second, for repairing the Road from Hyde Park Corner, and other Roads therein mentioned, in the County of Middlesex, were read; whereby it appeared, that the Trustees for repairing the said Roads were directed to repair such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Clarges Street and Hyde Park Gate, and such Part of Park Lane as lies between Piccadilly and the North End of Hertford Street, and to water such Part of Piccadilly as lies between the End of Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Gate aforesaid, in all dry Seasons when the Dull was troublesome to Passengers.

Then an Act, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, was also read; whereby it appeared, that the said former Acts, so far as relates to such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Gate, and to so much of Park Lane aforesaid as lies between Piccadilly and the North End of Hertford Street were repealed, and the same were put under the Care and Management of the Commissioners for paving the several Streets, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster; and a clear annual Sum of £.1,000 is directed to be paid out of the Tolls to be collected upon the said Roads to the Commissioners for Paving, to enable them to pave, cleanse, and light, and regulate, such Parts of the said Street and Lane aforesaid, and for such other Purposes as are therein mentioned. Then,

Vor.. 35.

97

Sampson Wright, Esquire, informed your Committee, That the Commissioners have caused such Part of the Street, called Piccadilly, as lies between Berke'ey Street and Hyde Park Corner, and also f.ich Part of Lane as lies between Piccadilly aforesaid and the North Side of Hertford Street, to be paved, cleansed, and lighted; and did, for several Years after pasting the said Act, cause such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Corner to be watered; but that of late they have discontinued to water the said Street because they have not a sufficient Fund for that Purpose.

General Cho/mondeley, one of the Inhabitants of Pic-

cadilly, being examined, said. That he, with several other of the Inhabitants, had applied to the Commissioners of Paving to have Piccadilly watered as formerly, and the Anl'wer they received from the Commissioners was, That they had not a luflicient Fund at that Time to do it; that one of the Commissioners then present said. That they had then a small Balance in their Hands, which they promised should be applied in watering the said Street.

Mr. Thomas Forfyth, Agent for the Petitioners, informed your Committee, That he attended the Commissioners, together with several of the principal Inhabitants of Piccadilly, sometime in the Summer of 1772, with a Representation of the Acts relative to Piccadilly, and those Gentlemen desired to know of the Commissioners, why they discontinued to water Piccadilly, as was formerly done; that they had a great deal of Converlation with the Commissioners relative to that Matter; and the Commissioners then alleged, that £.800, Part of £.1,000 a Year, paid by the Trustees for the Care of the Roads, to the Commissioners, as aforesaid, had been mortgaged; and that they apprehended the remaining £. 200 a Year, together with the Rates levied upon the Inhabitants of such Part of Piccadilly as aforesaid, was not sufficient for watering the Street, and executing the several other Purposes of the Act; but upon considering the Matter, the Commissioners agreed, that there was a small Balance remaining in the Hands of their Treasurer, and that they would direct the Street to be watered as far as the Money would go, which was accordingly done during the Remainder of that Summer; that the Witness attended the Board again last Spring, with several erf" the Inhabitants of Piccadilly, and the Commissioners then said, They were willing to apply the £. 200 a Year, before-mentioned, together with the Balance then remaining in the Treasurer’s Hands, in Aid of the Rates raised upon the Inhabitants for the Purposes of that Part of the Street.-

And Mr. Forfyth further informed your Committee, That the Inhabitants of Piccadilly arc desirous of taking the Management of that Part of Piccadilly between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Corner, and of that Part of Park Lane between Piccadilly and the North Side of Hertford Street into their own Hands, to be managed by Trustees to be appointed amongst themselves, provided the said £. 200 per Annum, together with the Balance in the Treasurer’s Hands, shall be applied in Aid of the Rates levied on the Inhabitants for that Purpose.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Inhabitants of such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park Gate, and of such Part of Park Lane as lies between Piccadilly and the North Side-of Hertford Street, to pave, cleanse, and light, the fame; and also to water such Part of Piccadilly as aforesaid; and for repealing the several Laws now in being for those Purposes: And that Mr. Selwyn, Mr. Storer, Lord George , and Lord

entered into by Your Majesty’s Subjects in several of the other Colonies, to the Injury and Oppression of many of their innocent Fellow Subjects resident within the Kingdom of Great Britain, and the rest of Your Majesty’s Dominions: This Conduit, on their Part, appears to us the tnore inexcuiable, when we consider with how much Temper Your Majesty and the Two Houses of Parliament have ailed, in Support of the Laws and Constitution of Great Britain. We can never so far desert the Trust reposed in us, as to relinquish any Part of the Sovereign Authority over all Your Majesty’s Dominions, which, by Law, is veiled in Your Majesty, and the Two Houses of Parliament; and the Conduit of many Persons in several of the Colonies, during the late Disturbances, is alone sufficient to convince us hoj|t necessary this Power is, for the Proteilion of the Livflp and Fortunes of all Your Majesty’s Subjects.

We ever have been, and always shall be, ready to pay Attention and Regard to any real Grievances of any of Your Majesty’s Subjects, which shall, in a dutiful and constitutional Manner.be laid before us; and whenever any of the Colonies shall make a proper Application to us, we shall be ready to afford them every just and reasonable Indulgence: At the same Time, we consider it as our indiipenlable Duty, humbly to beseech Your Majesty, that You will take the moll effectual Measures to enforce due Obedience to the Laws and Authority of the Supreme Legislature; and we beg Leave, in the most solemn Manner, to allure Your Majesty, that it is our fixed Resolution, at the Hazard of our Lives and Properties, to Hand by Your Majesty against all rebellious Attempts, in the Maintenance of the just Rights of Your Majesty, and the Two Houses of Parliament.
