A Petition of Francis Eyre, Esquire, waspresented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, at the last General Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Morpeth, in the County of Northumberland, Peter Dehne, Esquire, the honourable William Byrons Charles Bigge, Esquire, and the petitioner, were Candidates, and Andrew Fenwick and Robert Cooper were Bailiffs and returning Officers; and that the Election came on upon the 13th Day of October last, when a great Majority of Persons, having a legal Right to vote for Members of Parliament for the said Borough, duly gave their Votes in favour of the Petitioner, and the Petitioner and the said Peter Delme were returned duly elected; and re-

citing a Petition of the honourable William Byron, presented to the House upon the 6th Day of December last, and also at Petition of the several Aldermen and Free Burgesses of the Borough of Morpeth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, presented to the House upon the 19th Day of December last: And taking Notice, That the Sclect Committee, appointed to try the Merits of the said Return, have determined, That the Petitioner is not duly returned; and that the said William Byron ought to have been returned: And that the Merits of the Election were not, nor could be, entered into before the said Committee, the Reference being confined to the Return only; whether it was under Fear, or according to the Declaration and Opinion of the Bailiffs, but the Merits ftiil remain to be decided; and that the said Andrew Fenwick solicited Votes for the said Peter Delme and William Byron-, and the said Andrew Fenwick and Robert Cooper did, by their Conduct, manifested by frequent Declarations and otherwise, shew great Partiality to, and a determined Resolution to return, the said Peter Delme and William Byron as duly elected in all Events; and that the said Andrew Fenwick and Robert Cooper refused to allow several Votes which were offered and given in favour of the Petitioner, which were good and legal Votes, and ought to have been admitted; and they admitted several Votes in favour of the said William Byron, which were not good Votes, and ought to have been rejected; and that the said Andrew Femvick acted as Agent for the said Peter Delme and William Byron, and did actunlly bribe and corrupt several Persons to vote for the said Peter Delme and William Byron, and endeavoured to prevail upon several others, by Bribery and Corruption, to give their Votes in favour of the said Peter Delme and William Byrort, and allured several others, that in case they voted for the said Peter Delme and William Byron, their Votes should be good and allowed, but if they voted for the Petitioner, they should be bad and not allowed; and that the said William Byron, and also Germain Lavie, who acted at and previous to the Election as Agent for the said Peter Delme and William Byron, and other their Agents, did bribe, and did endeavour to bribe, others to vote for the said Peter Delme and William , and were guilty of divers other indirect and corrupt Practices relating to the said Election; and that, by such and other partial, illegal, and unwarrantable Practices, a Majority of Votes was pretended, and declared by the said Bailiffs, in favour of the said William , contrary to Truth and Justice, and to the manifest Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had a clear Majority of legal Votes: And therefore praying (as the Merits of the said Election have not been heard by any Committee) the House to take the same into Consideration; and that the Petitioner may be declared duly elected, and have such Relief as to the House shall seem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Wedsufday the 12th Day of July next, at the same Time that the Petitions of Thomas Charles Bigge, Esquire, and of the several Aldermen and Free Burgesses of the Borough of Morpeth, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; are ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ditto> A Petition of the manufacturing Hollers of the Town and County of the Town of , was

presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners with great Humility approach the natural Guardians of all that is valuable to them, and beg leave to represent the impending Ruin of the Trade and Commerce of the said flourishing Town and Neighbourhood; that the Produce of the Manufactories under their Direction has hitherto, in a very great Proportion, been exported to the American Colonies; and on the Demand from thence depends the Employment of many Thousands of their ingenious and industrious Artificers; the entire CelTation of this important Trade has not only (hut up in their Ware-houses a great Part of their Property in different Sorts of Goods provided for the American Market alone, but obliges them daily to dismiss from Employment their dependent Workmen, who have no Resource but in the Exercise of that Trade; every Day will add to the Number, from the utter Inability of the Petitioners to proceed in the Accumulation of an useless Stock; and a short Time mull consign great Part of the moll useful but moll heceflitous Members of their Community to absolute Idieness, and all its dreadful Train of Evils; dillreffed in themselves, they have no Hopes of administering that Relief to their Wants, which, in every ordinary Exigence, Humanity has prompted them to; and, if not prevented by the timely Interposition of Parliament, they fee no Possibility of repelling that Poverty, Distress, and Ruin, in which the said Town and Neighbourhood must be soon involved, whatever be the Fate of the Kingdom at large; abhorring the Thought of {Emulating the Dissentions of this Nation, and urged only by sober important Truth, interesting in its extensive Operation to every Individual, they humbly recur to the Wisdom of Parliament, in this their alarming Situation; trailing that the faithful Depositaries of the People’s Welfare will find fotne temperate and honourable Means of conciliating the Differences of the British Empire, which will revive the Hopes of the Manufacturer, and enable him to call back into the Arms of Industry the poor dillrefled Artificer.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the ^Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

The Orders of the Day being read;

Ditto. Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day

Sevennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, and of the several other Petitions referred to the Consideration of the said Committee.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the several Papers which were presented to the House, by the Lord North, upon the 19th and 3 tft Days of January last, and the ill Day 2

of this Inllant February, by His Majesty’s Command.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Ongley reported from the Committee, to whom Lidlingto the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open and locionve Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, and other Commonable Lands and Grounds, in the Manor and Parish of Lidlington, in the County of Bedford, was committed; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Bills of Inclosure, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same tobe true; and that the Parties concerned had given their Consent to the Bill, to the Satisfaction of the Committee (except the Proprietors of Lands within the said Parish, of the annual Value of £.26; and that the whole of the Lands within the said Parish are of the annual Value of £. 1,694, or thereabouts; and that no Person appeared before the Committee to oppose the Bill) and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were Once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be ingrossed.

Bristol rpHE Hour, appointed for taking into Consideratiort Election. the Petition of Matthew Brickdale, Rfquire, and

also the Petition of divers Persons whose Names arc thereunto subscribed, being Freeholders and Free Burgestes of the City and County of the City of Bristol, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Henry Cruger and Edmund Burke, Esquires, for the City and County of the said City, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said ElecUonand Return, according to the Directions of Twofeveral Acts of Parliament, passed in the 10th and nth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to lerve in Parliament: 1

Vol. 35.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 118 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioner, Matthew Brickdale, Esquire, his Counsel and Agents, who also appeared as Counsel and Agents on Behalf of the said other Petitioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Henry Cruger, Esquire, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Edmund Burke9 Esquire, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee attending also at the Bar; and the said Counsel for the said Sitting Members having severally informed the House, that the said Sitting Members were complained of by the said Petitions now taken into Consideration, upon the Ground of Bribery, at the said Election, which Charge in its Nature would affect them separately, that the Matter fluted in the said Petitions, respecting the Admissibility of a Candidate after the Poll was begun, was applicable only to One of the said Sitting Members; and that, upon the Whole* the Interests of the said Sitting Members being distinct and separate from each other, they therefore desired to separate in their Defence; and no Objection being made thereto by the Counsel foT the Petitioners, and the said Petition having been read, the same was agreed to by the House. '

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Orders of the Day, for taking the said Petitions into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

American Mr. Speaker reported, That both Houses did Yes-Colonies, terday attend His Majesty with their Address; to which His Majesty was jjleased to give this most gracious Anl'wer:

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I thank you for this very dutiful and loyal Address, and for the affectionate and solemn Assurances you give Me of your Support, in maintaining the just Rights of My Crown, and of the Two Houses of Parliament; and you may depend on My taking the most speedy and effectual Measures for enforcing due Obedience to the Laws, and the Authority of the Supreme Legislature.

Whenever any of My Colonies shall make a proper and dutiful Application, J shall be ready to concur with you in affording them every just and reasonable Indulgence; and it is My ardent Wilh, that this Disposition on our Part may have a happy Effect on the Temper and Conduct of My Subjects in America.

A.

That Richard Clarke, Esquire, deceased, by his Will, dated the Third Day of November 1773 (after devising certain Lands and Hereditaments therein mentioned, to the Uses therein expressed) devised all other his Messuages, Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, subject to a Term of One thousand Years therein mentioned, to the Petitioner, for Life, Remainder to his first and other Sons successively in Tail Male; and by his said Will did direct, that the Petitioner and his Heirs Male should (when they respectively, by virtue of the Limitations aforesaid, became entitled to the Rents and Profits of the said Premises) ule and take the Surname of , and bear the

Arms of Clarke; and that the Petitioner hath taken the Surname and Arms of , and is desirous the same may be confirmed to him, and his Heirs Male, by Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Knightley and Mr. Powys do.prepare, and bring in the fame.

A Bill for. naturalizing Charles , was read a Second Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to Mr. Strahan, Mr. Whitworth, &c.: And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve it felt into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into the said Committee.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty;

Ordered, That the Lift of the Reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines entitled to receive Half Pay in Great Britain; with an Etlimate of the Charge thereof, for the Year 1775, be referred to the said Committee.

Mr. Dundas also acquainted the House, that, in the Course of the Examination into the Merits of the Petition of James Calthorpe, Esquire, and Richard Beckford,

Esquire, it having appeared to the Committee, that the most flagrant and notorious Acts of Bribery and Corruption had been practised; and that a very considerable Majority of the Electors of the Borough ol had been bribed and corrupted in a very gross and extraordinary Manner; and that several others of the said Electors had been concerned as Agents for that Purpose; the Committee, desirous that the House may adopt such Measures as may discourage, and, if possible, put an End to a Practice lo subversive of the Freedom of Elections, had directed him to lay before the House the whole of the Evidence given before the said Committee, with their Opinions thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read } and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth:

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Richard Smith, Esquire, by his Agents, has been guilty of notorious Bribery, in procuring himself to be elected and returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That iThomas Brand Hollis, Esquire, by his Agents, has been guilty of notorious Bribery, in procuring himself to be elected and returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Hindon.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That James Calthorpe, Esquire, by his Agents, has been guilty of notorious Bribery, in endeavouring to procure himself to be elected and returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Hindon.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Richard Beckford, Esquire, has, by his Agent, endeavoured, by Promise of Money, to procure himself to be elected and returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Hindon.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Reverend John Nairn, of Hindon, Fasham Nairn, Esquire, late of Bury Street, Saint James's, Francis Ward, of Sherborne Lane, London, Stevens, a

Butcher, at Salisbury, commonly called Jobber Stevens, Francis Mead, John Hart, William Lucas, Thomas Howell, John Becket, Baker, William Penny, William Bye, Senior, William Becket, and William Burnett, of Hindon, have acted as Agents, and been accessary to, and concerned in, the notorious Acts of Bribery and Corruption that have been practised at the last Election for the said Borough of Hindon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill to disfranchise the said Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts.

Mr. Garth reported from the Committee, to whom Devize* the Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, and other the Election. Inhabitants, of the Borough of Devizes, in the County of Wilts, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth i viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

William Salmon, Junior, being examined, said, That the said Borough, being a very great Thoroughfare, and having a considerable Market, the principal Streets there, by means of the many heavy Carriages constantly passing through them, cannot be kept in good Repair by the ordinary Course of Law$ that it would be a great Convenience and Advantage to the Inhabitants of the said Town, and to all Persons having Occasion to relbrt to, or pass through, the fame, if Power was given to amend, regulate, ^nd keep in Repair, the several Streets,

Lanes, and Passages, there, to light and watch the fame, to remove Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions, therefrom, and to prevent the like for the future.

Mr. Samuel Taylor, being examined, confirmed the whole of the foregoing Evidence.

And both the Witnesses being further examined, said. They apprehended the Inhabitants would be able to defray the Expence of executing the several Purposes abovementioned, by a Rate on themselves, assisted by a small Toll to be collected on Sundays on the Turnpike Roads within or near, the said Town.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for amending, cleansing, lighting, watching, and regulating, the several Streets, Lanes, Passages, and Places, within the Town and Borough of Devizes, in the County of Wilts; for removing Annoyances and Obstructions therefrom, and for preventing the like for the future; and that Mr. Garth, Mr. James Sutton, Mr. docke, and Mr. Goddard, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Lord of the Manor of Mevagissey

in the County of Cornwall, of the Owners of Lands Pier, within and near the said Manor, and of several Persons residing in and near the Town of Mcva»i£ey, who are concerned in, and carry on, the Pilchard Fishery, and who trade to and from the said Town, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the said Town has for a long Scries of Years (from the Situation thereof) been found very convenient for carrying on the Pilchard Fishery; and the same has been so done, to the great

Emolument

i 20 140 Februarii. A. 1775.

Emolument and Advantage, not only of the Public in general, but of many Persons concerned or employed therein j and that, for the Safety and Protection of Vessels employed in the said Fishery, and others who might at any Time have Occasion to navigate to and from the said Town, a small Pier was formerly erected and kept in Repair, by the private Owner of the Ground and Soil near to the fame, in respect of which certain small Dues were taken from the Owners of all Vessels as partook of the Protection of the said Pier; and that the said Pier, being found very incommodious, difficult of Access, and inadequate to the Encrease of the said Fishery, and the Resort of Vessels to the said Town, hath been suffered to fall into Ruin and Decay; and that some of the Petitioners and others, seeing the Ne-ceflity of erecting a new Pier upon a morev extended and enlarged Plan, have subscribed and paid the Sum of £. 1,300, or thereabouts, which hath been expended in executing Part of the Work intended to be carried into Execution; and that, in order to make and erect the proper Embankments, Quays, Wharfs, Ways, Passages, and Approaches, to the (kid Pier, and for the Protection thereof, it is necessary to veil in Commissioners the Soil of a sufficient Quantity of Ground; and the Petitioners find, that, for that End, and for completing the several Works aforesaid, and in making Satisfaction to the Owners of the Ground and Soil which will be used in effecting the lame, the further Sum of ,£.3,000, or thereabouts, will be necessary; and that the Petitioners conceive, that, by laying a reasonable Tonnage, or Duty, on all Ships and other Vessels which shall partake of the Benefits refuhing from the said Improvements, and by laying certain other reasonable Tolls, Taxes, or Duties, not only the said further Sum necessary to be raised, but the Interest thereof, and of the Sums already advanced, may be kept down, and the said Pier and Works at all Times kept and maintained in good and sufficient Repair: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations and Restrictions as to the House shall seem proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

ville, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

Supply. Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee: had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the ( Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an additional Number of Two thousand Men be allowed, for Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, including Four hundred and Ninety Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Two thou-/ sand Men, for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Five thousand Three hundred and Twenty-six Pounds Sixteen Shillings and Eight Pence, be granted to His Majesty, upon Account of the Reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eight hundred and Seventy Pounds Three Shillings and Nine Pence, be granted to Voi. 35.

His Majesty, for defraying the Charge for Allowances to the several Officers and Private Gentlemen of the Two Troops of Horse Guards reduced, and to the Superannuated Gentlemen of the Four Troops of Horie Guards, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred and Twenty-eight Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for the paying of Pensions to the Widows of such Reduced Officers of His Majesty’s Land Forces and Marines, as died upon the Establishment of Half Pay in Great Britain, and were married to them before the Twenty-fifth Day of December One thousand Seven hundred and Sixteen, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision be made for the Pay and Cloathing of the Militia, and for their Subsistence during the Time they shall be absent from Home on Account of the Annual Exercise, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, :d to by the House.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Oxford -A Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Ox-Canal. ford Canal Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for , making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, from the

Coventry Canal Navigation, to the City of Oxford, Power and Authority were given, by the Ways and Means therein mentioned, to make, complete, and maintain, such Navigable Cut, or Canal, pafiable for Boats, Barges, and other Vessels; and that the said Company of Proprietors have, by virtue of the said Act, nearly completed the said Cut, or Canal, from the Coventry Canal Navigation, to Naplon, in the County of Warwick, being about 42 Miles, and have made great Progress therein at several other Places, and are now proceeding with great Expedition in the Execution of the remaining Parts thereof; and that the said Company were, for the Purpose of making the said Canal, enabled to raise amongst themselves the Sum of £. 150,000, with Power, if that Sum was not sufficient, by the same Means, or by the Admission of new Subscribers, to raise a further Sum of £.50,000-; and that the said Company have already raised and contributed, amongst themselves, the Sum of £.122,300, which hath been expended in carrying on the Works, and for other Purposes authorized by the said Act; and that the said Proprietors did, at their General Assembly, or Meeting, held by Adjournment at Oxford the 4th Day of July last, set on Foot a Subscription, for raising the Sum of £.30,000 in order to complete the said Cut, or Canal, to the Town of Banbury, which they are at present unable to do; and that some Amendments are necessary to be made to the said Act, and some further and other Pow'ers and Provisions wanting, for carrying on, completing, securing, and preserving, the said Navigation: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the said Company of Proprietors, under their Common Seal, to borrow any Sum or Sums of Money, which they shall think proper, upon the Credit of the Rates, Tolls, and Duties, of the said Navigation, in order to cariy on and complete the 1 1

fame, and that such Amendments may be made to the said Act as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

&c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to lend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

A Petition of the principal Manufacturers of the Borough of Bridpott, in the County of Dorset, on Behalf of themselves and Thousands of others, Inhabitants of the said Borough and Places adjacent, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, being Mailer Manufact urers of Nets, Lines, and Twine, for the Use of the Fisheries carried on, on the respective Shores and Banks of New England, Newfoundland, and other Parts of North America, as also of Canvass for Sails for the Vessels and Boats employed in the said Fisheries, have usually employed, in the said Borough and the neighbouring Villages, several Thousand Labourers in the Manufacture of the said Articles, who solely depend thereon for Subfi Hence, no other Manufactory of any Sort being carried on there; and that, in conference of the Non-importation Agreements lately entered into in America, the Petitioners have not received, and find they are not this Season to cxpect, a Demand for a Shilling’s Worth of Goods for those Parts; and that the Loss of that valuable Branch of their Trade distresses them the more, as, from a Consideration of the Importance of the Fisheries, and the Impossibility of carrying them on without Nets, Lines, &c. they had flattered themselves the Americans, in their Non-importation llesolutions, would have made some Exception in favour of these Articles; and from thence, as well as in Companion to the poor Labourers, were induced to continue their Manufactories, so that they have now large Stocks of Goods on Hand, of a Con-Itruction peculiar to those Parts, which will therefore be of little Value to them without a Return of this Trade; and that, from the Necessity th must be under

of an immediate Supply of these Articles for carrying on the Fisheries, the Petitioners apprehend Manufactories of them already are, or inllantly will be, set up there, or such other Sources of Supply discovered, and Connections formed, as will for ever deprive them of a Return of this Trade; and that, should this be the Cafe, the Petitioners, already much distressed, shall become great and lalling Sufferers, and their Labourers, many of whom are already without Employment, and the rest employed only in Part, mull inevitably be reduced 4o a Condition deplorably miserable, being neither capable, nor having an Opportunity, of turning their Hands to any other Business: And therefore praying the House to take their and their poor Labourers present Distresses and impending Ruin into Consideration, and to grant

such speedy and effectual Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

A Petition of the Merchants* and Mader Manufacturers of Woollen Goods, of the Towns of Wakefield, Halifax, Bradford, Huddersfield, and Country adjacent, intereded in the Trade to America, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, by Means of the North American Commerce carried on directly from the said Towns and Country adjacent, or through the Hands of the Merchants of London, Bristol,

Glasgow, Hull, and other Places, the Petitioners have been enabled greatly to extend their Manufactures, and give thereby a large Employ to many Thousand in-dudrious poor Labourers; and that the North American Commerce, taken collectively and in its full Extent, is an Object of great Concern to the Wed Riding of York-fhtrein general, to the Petitioners in particular, and worthy the Attention of Parliament; and that, by the unhappy Differences subsisting between Great Britain and her American Colonies, the Petitioners labour under the present Stagnation of that Branch of Trade, the Loss of which is feniibly felt, and in Time will be much more so, by the Petitioners and the aforesaid indudrious poor Labourers; and that the Petitioners, thus circum-itanced, are judly alarmed for themselves and Families, at the same Time feeling for the Didreffes of those to whom in Times pad they have been enabled to give Support, humbly represent to the House their present unhappy Situation, confiding in the Wisdom, the Justice, and Moderation, of Parliament, to remove the Causes thereof, in such Manner as to the House may teem meet.

Derby A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are Blc&ion. thereto subscribed. Electors of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of , in the County of Derby, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That at the last Eleilion of a Member to serve in Parliament for tire said Borough, Daniel Parker Esquire, and John Gijbortie, Esquire, were Candidates; and that the Petitioners, and divers others, having a lawful and undoubted Right, by Birth or Servitude, to the Freedom of the said Borough, and to be sworn Burgesses thereof, previous to the said f lection, claimed to be admirted Burgesses of the said Borough; but Christopher Heath the Mayor, and divers Aldermen of the said Borough, with a view to deprive the Petitioners and others of voting at the then next ensuing Election, and in order to procure a Return in Favour of the said John Gisborne, refused to admit them to their Free-

dom, although the said Mayor and Aldermen, at the same Time, admitted several Persons under the like Circumstances with the Petitioners; and that the said Daniel Parker Coke was duly eletted, by a great Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned, but the said Christopher Heath, the Mayor, who presided as the Returning Officer, hath made a Return of the said John Gisborne, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said Christopher Heath, during the whole Course of the Poll, acted with the greatest partiality in favour of the said John Gisborne, by rejecting the Votes of the Petitioners and others who had a Right to Poll, and who tendered their Votes for the said Daniel Parker Coke, and by admitting on the Poll for the said John Gisborne, divers Persons who had no Right to vote, and ought to have been rejected; whereby, and by many undue, illegal, and unwarrantable Practices and Proceedings of the said Christopher Heath, and divers Members of the Corporation of the said Town, as well previous to, as during the Poll, the Petitioners conceive themselves greatly prejudiced, and their Rights and Privileges as Burgesses of the said Borough attacked and violated: And therefore praying the House, on Behalf of themselves and others the Burgesses of the said Borough of Derby, to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall i'eem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Friday the 14th Day of July next, at the same Time that the Petition of Daniel Parker Coke, Esquire, is ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Mr. Gajcoyne reported from the Committee, to whom Clerkenwell the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the *>00ri 4c* Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of Saint James Clerkenwell, in the county of ,

on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared t<j them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Babingtoh, Master of the Workhouse, being

examined, said. That there are now 320 Persons in the House, which was built to receive only 150; by which Means it is crowded to such a Degree as to render it not only extremely inconvenient, but also highly prejudicial to the Health of the poor Persons residing in it: And,

Mr. John Severn being examined, said. The said Parish consists of Two Districts; that the Number of poor Persons has greatly increased of late Years, and is now so large, that the Workhouse being too small to receive them, many are obliged to be maintained as Out Pensioners, which is attended with much Inconvenience and additional Expence; that the Poor’s Rata is now Three Shillings in the Pound at the Rack Rent, and the Parish is in Debt on account of the Poor £.980, and upwards; that if Power was given to raise Money to build a new Workhouse, or enlarge the old bne, for the Purposes of receiving and relieving the Poor, with proper Regulations for their good Government and Employment, it would be productive of many great Advantages to the Parish, and tend to lessen the present heavy Expences.

Mr. John Sawell being examined, confirmed the Evidence of both the said Witnesses.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for building a Workhouse, and for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor, within the Parish of Saint James Clerkenwell, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Gajcoyne and Mr. Macktuorth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Page reported from the Committee, to whom Oxford the Petition of the Company of Proprietors of the Ox~ v-anai.

ford Canal Navigation, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and find that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House of the

25th

13* l\° Februarii. . 1775*

45th Day of April 1774* relating to Navigation Bills; it not being proposed to extend the Navigation beyond the Limits already authorized by an Act of the Ninth Year of His present Majesty, nor to raile any further Sum of Money for that Purpose; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Thomas Walker, Esquire, being examined, informed your Committee, That the said Company of Proprietors have completed great Part of the said Canal, and are now proceeding in the Execution of the said Act; but that the Act is found in many Respects defective, and requires several Amendments and Alterations.

And being asked, What Alterations are necessary to be made in the said Act ? the Witness said, That by the said Act the Proprietors are restrained from raising Money to carry the same into Execution, except by Subscription, which Method hath been found imprafti cable; that they have already raised the Sum of £.123,300 by Subscription; and that a further Sum is wanted to complete the said Navigation, which he apprehends might be raised, if the Company were impowered to mortgage the Rates or Duties granted by the said Act.

And the Witness further laid. That it is necessary that the said Company of Proprietors should have Power to restrain the Owners of Collieries, from working the same within a certain Distance of the said Canal: And he added. That the said Company of Proprietors would be enabled to purchase Lands for making the said Canal, at a less Expence than they can do at present, if Power was given to the Owners of the Lands to be purchased, to sell or exchange the remaining Parts of all such Lands as are separated and divided by the said Canal.

That it would be for the mutual Benefit of the said Company of Proprietors, and of all Persons navigating upon the said Canal, and would prevent many Disputes between them and the Owners of Vessels, if, in all Cases where Vessels do not pass above the Distance of a Mile upon the Canal, the Owners of Vessels were only to pay an equal Proportion of the Rates, according to the Distance they navigate upon the Canal.

And Mr. Walker further said. That some other Alterations and Amendments are necessary to be made in the said Act, in order to enable the said Company of Proprietors effectually to carry the same into Execution.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to amend an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for making and maintaining a Navigable Canal, from the Coventry Canal Navigation to the City of Oxford: And that Mr. Page, the Lord Wenman, and Lord Charles Spencer, do prepare, and bring in, the lame. American A Petition of the Aldermen, Sheriff, principal Ma-Coloniei. nufacturers, and Inhabitants, of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners very sincerely lament the unhappy Differences which have already arisen between Great Britain and her Colonies, and cannot, without great Concern and Abhorrence, reflect upon that seditious Spirit, which hath broken out with such Violence in the Province of Massachuset's Bay, particularly in the Town of Boston, whose Inhabitants, by their t Disobedience, have set at Defiance the Laws and Government of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners having seen the very ungrateful Return made by the Bojionians, for the uncommonly mild and indulgent Kindness testified to them by the British Senate, in the Repeal of the American Stamp Act, are much surprised to find that Petitions have been repeatedly urged in their Favour to the House, and in particular by some of the maftufacturing Hosiers of the Town of Nottingham; and that the Petitioners, from their intimate Knowledge of the Manufactory of this Town, well know that the Allegations of such Petitions are highly exaggerated; and that the Zeal of the Petitioners hath led them beyond the Bounds of sober and important Truth, representing Calamities which have never yet, nor in the remotest Probability ever will be, felt and experienced by the Inhabitants of the said Town in the Degree stated; and that the Petitioners, from the ^relent Disposition of the Americans, apprehend that the Trade and Commerce of Great Britain with her Colonies cannot be effectually restored, and permanently secured, without a due and proper Submission and Obedience to the Laws and Government of this Kingdom: And therefore beseech the House to take such Measures as may seem most likely to secure and maintain the supreme Authority, Honour, and Dignity, of Great Britain, enforce a due Obedience to her l^aws, and restore Subordination, Order, and good Government, in America.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro-poled, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred;

A Petition of James Watt, of the City of Engineer, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner hath employed many Years, and a considerable Part of his Fortune, in making Experiments upon Steam and Steam Engines, commonly called Fire Engines, with a View to improve those very useful Machines; and that, in the Year 1769, the Petitioner obtained His Majesty’s Royal Letters Patent, for the Sale of certain new Steam Engines invented by him, by which very considerable Advantages over the common Steam Engines were proposed to be derived; but, upon Account of the many Difficulties which always arise in the Execution of such large and complex Machines, and of the long Time requisite to make the necessary Trials, he could not complete his Intention before the End of the Year 1774, when he finished some large Engines as Specimens of his Construction, which have fully succeeded, and confirmed the Petitioner in his Opinion of the Expediency and Utility of his Invention; and that, in order to manufacture these Engines with the necessary Accuracy, and so that they may be sold at moderate Prices, a considerable Sum of Money must be previously expended in erecting Mills and other Apparatus; and as several Years, and repeated Proofs will be required before any considerable Part of the Public can be fully convinced of the Expediency of the Invention, and of their Interest to adopt the lame, the whole Term granted by the said Letters Patent may probably elapse before the Petitioner can receive an Advantage adequate to his Labour and Invention; and that the Petitioner apprehends, that, by furnishing mechanical Powers at much less Expence, and in more convenient Forms, than has hitherto been done, his Engines may be of great Utility, in facilitating the Operations in many great Works and Manufactures of this Kingdom; but it will not be in the Power of the Petitioner to carry his Invention into that complete Execution which he wishes, and so as to render the same of the highest Utility to the Public of which it is capable, unless the Term granted by the said letters Patent be. prolonged, and his Property in the said Invention secured for such Time as may enable him to obtain an adequate llecompence for his Labour, Time, and Expence: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such liellriftions and Limitations, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Lord Guernsey Sir Adam Fer-gufon. Sic.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to lend for Persons, Papers, and Records; and all who come to the Committee are to have Voices.

A Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and Over- Barking seers of the Poor, and other principal Inhabitants, of Poor* the Parish of Barking, in the County of Essex, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read;

Setting forth. That the Poor of the said Parish are Very numerous, and are supported and maintained at a great Expence, and that the present Workhouse is too small for their Reception; and that the Method of collecting the Rates for the Relief of the Poor is attended with great Delay, by which Means Losses frequently happen in the Collection; and that the Power of distributing the Money when collected is so general, that the Rates are of late much increased, and become very burthensome to the Petitioners; and that, if the Petitioners were empowered to hire or purchase a convenient Piece of Ground within the said Parish, with Messuages or Tenements^thereon, proper for a Workhouse, or House of Industry, or to build a more convenient Workhouse, or House of Industry, for the Reception, Maintenance, and Employment, of the Poor of the said Parish, under proper Regulations, the Poor would be much better managed, supported, and maintained, and at a less Sixpence than they are at present; and that, if some Method was provided, for the more speedy Collection and better Distribution of the Money to be raised and collected for the Relief of the said Poor, it would be of great Benefit to the Inhabitants of the said Parish; and that there are several Charity Estates belonging to the said Parish, confiding of Lands, Hereditaments, and Money in the public Funds, the Trusts of which are expired; and in order to support the said Charity, it is absolutely necessary, that the vacant Trusts should be filled up, and some further Provisions made for regulating and managing the said Charity Estates: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, interested in the American Commerce, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are deeply concerned, to observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is brought in, to restrain the Trade and Commerce of the Provinces of Massachuset's Bay and New , and Colonies of

Conneliicut and Rhode Island, and Providence,

in North America, to Great Britain, Ireland, and the British Blands in the West Indies, and to prohibit such Provinces and Colonies from carrying on any Fishery on the Banks of Newfoundland, or other Places therein to be mentioned, under certain Restrictions, and for a Time to be limited; and representing to the House, that the said Bill, should it pass into a Law, will, in its Operation, deprive Thousands of His Majesty’s loyal Subjects of their actual Subsistence, and reduce them to extreme Distress, even that of Famine, the said Provinces not generally raising Corn sufficient for their own Support; and by the said Bill they will be prevented from receiving any Supplies from their Sifter Colonies, and precluded from their natural Resource, the Sea; and that the Petitioners have Reason to believe, that very

freat Numbers of Men are bred and employed in the 'ilheries, who, in IJardiness and Intrepidity, are not exceeded by any in this extensive Empire, and may be impelled, by the pressing Calls of Hunger and Want, to such a Conduct as may be productive of Devastation and Blood (bed, which may endanger the Peace and Welfare of that Part of His Majesty’s American Dominions, or be induced to emigrate to the Blands of Miquelon and St. Pierre, there to fish for the French, and give our Rivals the Means of supplying the Markets in Europe, and thereby render it difficult for us to regain thac valuable Branch of Commerce; and that there is now due, from the said Provinces and Colonies,

to the City of London, a very large Sum of Money, and that their Remittances are principally made by Means of the Fisheries,'and consequently the Ruin brought on those Colonies will ultimately fall on Great Britain; nd that amongst the other Grievances of which our Fellow Subjects in Americafo generally complain, is, their being

deprived of Trial by Jury in particular Cafes, and the Extension of the Jurisdiction of the Admiralty Courts; which Grievances, the Petitioners with much Concern find, are not only continued, but extended, by the present Bill; and they think it their Duty to represent to the House, that it is their firm Opinion, that the Disquietude, which universally prevails in the Minds of their Fellow Subjects in America, will not be removed, unless lenient Measures are pursued, and their Grievances redrafted: And therefore praying. That the said Bill may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time.

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Directions of Two several Acts of Parliament, passed in the loth and nth Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament:

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 116 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioner, Alexander Popham, Esquire, his Coun-fel and Agents, who also appeared as Counsel and Agents on Behalf of the said John Holliday, Esquire, and of the said other Petitioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Members, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Sclect Committee attending also at the Bar:

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Orders of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration. And the feme being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and sealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table; and the Seals being inspected by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Outside of the said Box, signed by Mr. Speaker, purporting, " That the said Box was, on the 23d Day of February " 1775, made up in his Presence, in the Manner directed " by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of " His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to regulate " the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns cf " Members to serve in Parliament," was read.

And the Seals being broken, and the Box opened, the Attestation inclosed therein, and signed by the Clerk, purporting, " That the Names of all the Members were " by him, in the Presence of the Speaker, put into " the said Box on the 23d Day of February 1775," was read.

And the said Names, written on distinct Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be of an equal Size, and rolled up in the same Manner, were, by the Clerk, taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers into Six Glasses, placed on the Table for that Purpose, and were there shaken together; and then the Clerk publicly drew’ out of the said Six dalles, alternately, the said Pieces of Paper, and delivered them to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House.

And the Names of Five Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of the honourable Thomas Howard being drawn, the Counsel for the Petitioners declared, that the said Member was intended to be nominated by the said Petitioners; and the said Member having, in his Place, consented to such Nomination, and no Objection being made to his serving on the said Select Committee, as such Nominee, his Name was let aside.

And the Names of other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Seven other. Members, then present, were drawn and let aside, with th Names of those who were absent from the 1 Ioufe, on Account of their being Members against whole; Returns Petitions were depending.

and that the Causes indu&ive of the Acts for suppressing the Name of Gregour, or Mac Gregour are now little known, and have long ago cealed; and the Acts being incapable of Execution ever since the Powers of the Privy Council of Scotland were abolished, many Persons, considering the Acts to be in effect and for the most Part obsolete, do now use the Name of Mac Gregour; and that the Petitioner and his Family, and many others for whom he acts in this Matter, have found disagreeable Inconveniencies arising to them from the said proferibing Acts of the Parliament of Scotland, particularly by being disabled, and apprehending themselves disabled, thereby from suing and defending in their own true Names in Courts of Law and Justice in North Britain; and arq desirous to be relieved from those Proscriptions, to be put on the same Footing with His Majesty’s other Subjects, and to re-assume the Real Name of their Ancestors and Families; but, being unwilling so to do while there is the Appearance of a legal Prohibition against them, and for as much as they cannot be fully relieved but by the Authority of Parliament: Therefore praying, That Leave may be giyen to bring in a Bill to repeal the said Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made Anno 1633, and the said other Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made Anno 1693, f° for as those Acts do affect the People called Mac Gregours, and to revive the said other Act of the Parliament of Scotland, made Anno 1661.

Old A Petition of several Gentlemen, Tradesmen', and Stratford, others, residing near, or frequently travelling, the Road Road from Old Stratford, in the County of , to

Dunchurch, in the County of Warwick, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That several Acts have been passed, in the Sixth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, the 1 xth Year of King George the First, and in the xoth, 13th, and 31st Years of the Reign of his late Majesty, for repairing the said Road; and that Four full Tolls are paid by Travellers passing along the Whole of the said Road, which is in Length about 29 Miles, which Tolls, the Petitioners are informed, amount annually to £. 2,600, or thereabouts; and that the said Road having been made Turnpike a great many Years, they presume that, if the Money collected at the Toll Gates had been properly applied, it ought before this Time to have been completely formed and repaired, and to have been brought into such a State as to require but little Labour or Expence to maintain and keep it in perfect Repair; and that, on the contrary, the said Road is now in a very ruinous Condition, and in many Parts not safe for Passengers and Carriages; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if the said Road was pro*-perly formed and repaired, under the Direction of a skilful and trusty Surveyor, an Income much less than the present would, under proper Management, be sufficient to keep it in very complete Repair, which would be of great public Utility, the said Road being a Part of the great Poll Road between London and Chester, and also opening a Communication from London to Birmingham, and many other great trading Towns in the Midland Part of the Kingdom: And therefore praying the House, That an Enquiry may be made into the Management of the said Trust, and the Application of the Money arising by the Tolls, and proper Provisions made for the effectual Repair and Support of the said Road, and the future good Management thereof.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Cori-sideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

To prpve the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. 'Thomas Clowes, being examined, said, That the Popr are considerably encreased within the Parishe?of the said Hundreds; that Seven Years ago he took an Account of the Average Expence of maintaining the Poor within the said Hundreds for Seven Years preceding that Time, which amounted to about £.,700 a Year; that about Two Months ago he took the like Account for tlje last Seven Years, and finds that the Sixpence is about £. 1,150.-7-And beipg^asked^ To^h^t that Increase was owing ? he said, To various, Causes; — that or late it has become a Practice for poor Persons to keep their Children at home in fdleness. — And being asked. If :the Encrease of the Rates did not arise from the.Dearness of Provisions ? he laid. That, certainly, was one Reason. — "And being farther examined, he laid, That many industrious Poor, and the Old and Infirm, suffer great Hardtbips from the present Mode bf taking Care of them} and that, if the Poor were put under proper Government, and a Place provided for their Reception, the Infirm would ,be more effectually relieved, and the able and industrious better employed, and contribute to the Support of each:other; that the Children of the poor People are not taught to refid; that there is a Foundation at where even

the parents will not fend their Children; that the Number of Children on the Foundation (which he believes is. Twenty) is seldom full; that some few are employed in.Spinning; but that there arc more who pais their Time in Play and Idleness.

Being asked, Whether the Children were kept more in Idleness than they used to be ? he said, he believed so, because poor Persons, with Four or Five Children, more frequently apply for Relief than formerly; that the Price of Labour is in some Instances encrealed within the last Four or Five Years, particularly in Day Work, from is. to 14 d.in' general, and in some Cales to 18 d. — And being asked, In what Cafes it is raised to 18 d.? he said. In Harvest Work, mowing Clover, Marsh Work, Coldeed Work, and various other Works; that the Price of Wheat about Seven Years ago was ao s.a Coomb, and for some Time past has been at an Average of 25*. a Coomb; that if the Old and Infirm are put into the Poor House, they are placed without proper Assistance, and have very poor Support from their Parishes; that the Officers do not allow more than 3 s. a Week for a Man and his Wife who are incapable of Work, but that the Parishes pay for House Rent and Fuel; that the Size and State of the Rooms where they are placed is very bad; that some times more than one Man and his Wife are lodged in one Room; that he has known a Man and his Wife put into a Room with another Family with Children, ' some of whom were 16 Years old, laying in the same Bed with their Father and Mother; that the Floor of titc Rooms arc Brick, and sometimes only Clay; that there are Twenty Parishes within the Two Hundreds,

and in most of them there are Houses for the Reception of the Poor; that the Houses are all in a miserable Condition, but that some of them are better than others; that he does not know what the Rack Rents of the Parishes are; that he lives at , and

occupies a Farm at Caister, of £.210 a Year, which he has held for one Year, and paid one Half Year about £. 7,.and the other Half Year about .9, for the Poors Rate.

The Witness being further asked, If the poor People are able to work, why they are sent to the Houses ? he said. If they apply for Relief, they are sent; that they relieve them, in case of Sickness, out of the House occasionally; that he knew they did at Owlton Poor House; that hp had l'pen several Orders in their Books, of temporary Relief out of the House; that he never saw their Bye Laws, nor did he ever hear they had any Bye Law to restrain giving Relief to Persons out of the House; that he has been at House of

Industry; that he.does not know any thing of relieving poor Persons put of that House; that he was there in January last, when he enquired as to the Health of the Poor, and was told they were remarkably well; that he went into the Mens Infirmary, and found an old Man dying, and Two, Women attending him; that he thinks he was the only lick Perl'on in the Infirmary; that the Room was warm, and was kept very still; that the Apartments were clean and commodious; that their DrelTes were clean and tight; that the poor Persons appeared very happy and eal'y in their Situation; and that there were separate Rooms for the married Persons.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor, within the Hundreds of Raft and West Flegg, in the County of Norfolk: And that Sir Edward AJlley, Mr. Coke, Mr.

Milles, and Mr. Anson, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are subscribed, being divers of the Directors and Members of the laudable Society for the Benefit of Widows, on Behalf of themselves, and the said Society, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Year 1761, a Society was formed, by the Name of " The laudable Society for the Benefit of Widows," with an Intent to secure, to the Widows of such Persons as were and should become Members thereof, certain Annuities, mentioned in the Scheme then adopted, and published by them; and that the Members of the said Society, on their Admission, executed a Deed, containing Articles for the better ordering and regulating tfyeir Affairs; and that the said Society hath increased to a very considerable Number, and now consists of about 624 Members; and that there were at Michaelmas last 74 Widows, Claimants on the Society, to the Amount of about f. 1,760 per and that, the

State of the said Society’s Affairs having been examined, it appears, that several Alterations in their Plan are necessary, in order to establish the same on a permanent Foundation, and effectually to secure the Payments to the Widows; and that the said Society are desirous to secure, in the First Place, to the Widows who are now Claimants, the Annuities promised by the original Plan, or by any subsequent Alterations therein i and to make such Regulations, for the better Government and Management thereof in future, as may put an Institution, calculated for such useful Purposes, on a firm and solid Basis; hut the Petitioners apprehend the same cannot be done under their present Deed of Settlement, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for securing, out of the present Fund of the Society, a sufficient Sum to make good to the Widows, who are now Claimants, the 8

several Annuities promised to them by the original Scheme, or by any subsequent Alterations therein; and for making such further and other Regulations, for the better Government and Management of the said Society, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

The Lord Stanley reported the Conference; and that it was to acquaint this House, That the Lords, being extremely desirous, upon all Occasions, to preserve a perfect good Correspondence with the House of Commons, have asked this Conference, in order to acquaint them, that the Lords, having taken into Consideration a printed Book, complained of to their Lordships, intituled, " The present Crisis with respect to America, " considered," printed for T. Becket, the Corner of the Adelphi, in the Strand, 1775; had come to the following llesolutions; viz.

Resolved, t By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in Parliament assembled, That the Book, intituled, " The present Crisis with respect to America, considered," is a false, malicious, and traiterous. Libel, inconsistent with the Principles of the Resolution, to which we owe the present happy Establishment, with the Rights of the Subject; and is an audacious Insult on His Majesty, tending to subvert the fundamental Laws and Liberties of these Kingdoms, and to introduce an illegal and arbitrary Power.

Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal in Parliament assembled, That One of the said printed Books be burnt by the Hands of the common Hangman, in New Palate Yard, on Monday the 6th Day of March next, at One of the Clock in the Afternoon; and that another of the said printed Books be burnt by the Hands of the common Hangman, before the Royal Exchange, in London, on Tuesday the 7th Day of March next, at the same Hour; and that the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex do attend at the said Times and Places respectively, and cause the same to be burnt there accordingly.

Which Resolutions, together with the said printed Book, their Lordships had directed to be communicated to this House; and desire die Concurrence of this House to the said Resolutions.

And the said Report, and several Parts of the said printed Book, were read.

And the First of the said Resolutions being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Resolution.

And the Blank was filled up with the Words " and " Commons."

The Second of the said Resolutions being read a Second Time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Resolution,

And the Blank was filled up with the Words " and " Commons."

Resolved, That the Lords be acquainted, at a Conference, that this House hath agreed to the said Resolutions.

and that the present Manner of exposing Butchers Meat for Sale, within the said Town, is by putting it on Stalls or Standings, and by hanging it upon Hooks under Sheds, or Penthouses, over such Stalls or Standings, which are fixed before, and project from, the Houses fronting the public Streets within the said Town, which are very incommodious tc*$he Inhabitants thereof; and that proper and convenient Shambles for Sale of Butchers Meat within the said Town maybe erected and made, in or near the little Corn Market, or upon some Part thereof, and upon the Scite of several Messuages or Dwelling Houses, and other Buildings near thereto, which is the most convenient Situation for that Purpose within the said Town; and that there is a very great Thoroughfare, or Passage, through the said Town; and several of the Streets, Passages, and other public Places, are in many Parts very narrow and incommodious} and that it would be very advantageous to the Inhabitants of the said Town and Parish, and the neighbouring Country, to have a more easy, speedy, and less expensive, Method provided for the Recovery of small Debts, and to have a fixed and regular public Market and Shambles for the Sale of Butchers Meat, within the said Town, in or near the little Corn Market, or upon some Part thereof, and upon the Scite of such Messuages, Dwelling Houses, and other Buildings} and it would also be of great Benefit to the Petitioners, to have the said Streets, Passages, and other public Places, lighted, and all Nuisances, Incroachments, and other Obstructions therein, removed and prevented: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of finall Debts within the said Parish; for the fixing and regulating a public Market and Shambles, for the Sale of Butchers Meat; lighting the Streets, and other Places; and for removing and preventing all Nuisances, Incroachments, and Obstructions, within the said Town, with such Powers and Provisions, and under and subject to such Regulations and Restrictions, as to the House shall feera meet.

Bargemasters and others, employed in navigating Boats,

Barges, and other Vessels, upon the said Rivers, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and find that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th Day of April 1774, relating to Navigation.

Bills, the Petitioners only proposing to regulate the Depth of Water,' which Vessels navigating the said Rivers are allowed to draw; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read; and Mr. Thomas Alexander being examined, said, That the Restrictions in the said Acts respecting the Depth of Water, to be drawn by Barges, Boats, or other Vessels, navigating the said Rivers, have been found to be very prejudicial to the Bargemalters, and other Persons employed in the said Navigation, and that the same tends greatly to enhance the Price of Carriage of the Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, navigated thereon; and that he apprehends, that if the Barges, Boats, and other Vessels, navigating the said Rivers, were allowed to draw Three Feet Water between the ill Day of May and the tft Day of

November, and Three Feet and Eight Inches Water between the 1 ft Day of November and the ill Day of May, the Price of the Carriage of Goods, Wares, and Merchandizes, navigated upon the said Rivers, would be considerably less than if the same continue to be navigated according to the Terms and Conditions preferred by the said Acts, anu that the same will be of no Prejudice to the Navigation of the said Rivers.

Mr. Josiah Barnard confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to alter and amend an Act, made in the r ith Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, for improving and completing the Navigation of the Rivers Thames and from the City of London, to the Town of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts, so far as the same relates to the Depth of Water to be drawn by Boats, Baiges, and other Vessels, navigated upon the said Rivers: And that Mr. Griffith and Mr. Elwes do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported American from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it Colonie$* was referred to consider further of the several Papers which were presented to the House, by the Lord , upon the 19th and 31st Days of January (all, and the ill and 15th Days of this Inllant by His Majesty’s Command, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; ayd afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That when the Governor, Council, and Assembly, or General Court, of any of His Majesty’s Provinces or Colonies in America, shall propose to make Provision, according to the Condition, Circumstances, and Situation, of such Province or Colony, for contributing their Proportion to the Common Defence (such Proportion to be raised under the Authority of the General Court, or General Assembly, of such Province or Colony, and disposable by Parliament) and shall engage to make Provision also for the Support of the Civil Government, and the Administration of Justice, in such Province or Colony, it will be proper, if such Proposal shall be approved by His Majesty and the Two Houses of Parliament, and for so long as such Provision shall be made accordingly, to forbear, in respect of such Province or Colony, to levy any Duty, Tax, or Assessment, or to impose any farther Duty, Tax, or Assessment, except only such Duties as it may be expedient to continue to levy or to impose for the Regulation of Commerce; the Nett Produce of the Duties last mentioned to be carried to the Account of such Province or Colony respectively.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Ditto. Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the several Papers which were presented to the House, by the Lord North, upon the 19th and 31st Days of January last, and the 1 ft, 15th, and 24th Days of this Instant February, by His Majesty’s Command.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the *n whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morn- Supply, ing next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Ditto. A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and County of , was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, that a Petition is presented to the House from the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London., in Common Council aflera-bled, against the Bill mentioned in the preceding Petition; and that the Petitioners beg Leave to observe, that the Restraints intended to be laid upon the Newfoundland Fishery of the Colonies, mentioned in the said Bill, if carried into a Law, will not by any Means be injurious to Commerce, as the Petitioners against the Bill conceive, because the Foreign Markets can be amply supplied by extending the Newfoundland Fishery of Subjects resident in England; and that the Annual Produce of the Newfoundland Fishery carried on by Subjects resident in the Mother Country exceeds£.500,000; and that the Newfoundland Fishery of the Mother Country is a constant Nursery of Seamen for the Navy, that great Bulwark of the Nation, every Fifth Man employed being, by the 10th of the Third, obliged

to be a Landman, a Consideration of infinite Weight, the Petitioners imagine, and this the more especially, as the Profits of the Trade center entirely in this Kingdom; and that the Profits of the Newfoundland Fishery, carried on by the Colonies mentioned in the Bill, do not center here, nor is the Newfoundland Fishery of the Colonies a Nursery of Seamen for the Fleet, because the Americans are not obliged by Law to make use of Landmen, nor are the American Seamen compellable, like the Brit if 1 Seamen, to serve their Country in Times of War; the Petitioners are therefore greatly alarmed, left a Petition from so respectable a Body as the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of , should operate not

only to their Prejudice, but to the general Prejudice of the Kingdom, on a Point of such Importance to the National Prosperity; humbly submit the foregoing Fadts to the Consideration of the House, and foliating, no less for their own immediate Advantage, than for the universal Benefit of their Country, such Encouragement of the British Fishery to N as the Parliament shall think proper.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.
