Patent, whom the Petition of James Watty of the City of Glasgow, Engineer, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Letters Patent, dated the 5th Day of January, in the Ninth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, granting an exclusive Privilege to the Petitioner for the Sale of certain new invented Steam Engines, commonly called Fire Engines, for the Term of 14 Years, were read: And,

John Roebuck, M. D. being examined, said, That to his Knowledge £. 2,000 at the lead has been expended in bringing the said Fire Engines to their present State of Perfection; and that if an Allowance was made for the Time that Mr. Watt has already empoiyed, in bringing the said Engines to their present Srate, at all proportionable to what has been paid to him when engaged in other Business, the Expence would greatly exceed £. 3,000; and that to carry this Invention to the Degree of Perfection, which the Witness thinks it capable of, it will be necessary to expend some Thou-iand Pounds more.

That the Petitioner has been employed in this Work 17 Years, and for 10 or 12 Years last pad it has taken up the greated Part of his Time.

That this Engine will not consume Half the Steam that a common Fire Engine does, probably not the Third Part, and produce an equal Effect; that it will at lead do double the Work of a common Fire Engine at the same Expence, and be of general Utility in Collieries and Mines of all Kinds that in the Witnesss Opinion, it may be applied to many mechanical Purposes with greater Advantage than the present Fire Engine, as it works by a circulating, indead of a reciprocating, Motion, and that it may be applied with Advantage wherever any Kind of mechanical Power is wanted; that he is of Opinion, the Money already expended, and which he thinks may with Propriety and Prudence be laid out, together with a moderate Stock to carry this Invention into Execution, may amount to £. x 0,000 j but that it will not be prudent in the Petitioner to expend the Sum necessary for that Purpose, unless some greater Security was given for the foie making and vending the said Machines than is granted by the said Letters Patent.

That he has seen One of these Engines which Mr. Watt has already erected, which was not finished till November lad, and t does double the Execution of a common Fire Engine with the same Expence of Steam and Fuel.

That the Petitioner has not yet received any Advantage from the Engines he has made; that an expensive Apparatus is necessary for making these Engines, particularly boring and turning Mills for making of Cylinders; and Founderies for cading them mud also be erected, in order to bore the Cylinders with sufficient Accuracy, which Mills will cod a very considerabte Sum of Money; and as it mud necessarily be some Time before the Public in general become acquainted with the Utility of this Machine, the Term of the Patent will probably expire before the Petitioner can receive any Advantage from his Invention.

That unless the Term of the Patent be continued to the Extent of 28 Years, the Petitioner will not have spent his Time in the Prosecution of this Invention for his own Profit, whatever Advantage may accrue from thence to the Public, which, in the Witness’s Opinion, will be very great, as these Engines, when finished, will cod less than the common Fire Engines, and do equal Execution t Then,

Mr. Alexander Camming being examined. &id. That he has not seen the Engine, but is acquainted with the Principles upon which it is condruded, and believes them to be the bed that can be made use of for the working of Steam Engines, and a great Improvement upon the Engines now in use.

That the Principle of the circulating Wheel is entirely new, and much more applicable to Mills and other mechanical Operations in general, than the common or reciprocating Fire Engine.

Being further examined, he confirmed all the Evidence given by Doctor Roebuck, except what relates to the Expences which have been already incurred by the Petitioner.

Matthew Boulton, Esquire, being examined, said. That Mr. Watt has been pursuing this Invention "to his Knowledge ever since the Year 1763, and even at that Time had made a considerable Prog refs in it; that these Engines are superior to any. before invented in this Country, even three times better than any the Witness had ever examined.

That a very large Sum of Money will be requisite to carry this Invention into Execution, l'o as to make it of the greated Benefit to the Public, which it is capable of.

That if the Invention was his own, he should think it very imprudent to advance the Sum necessary for this Purpose unless the Term of the Patent were considerably extended.

That he is convinced, from actual Experiments, that this is not only the cheaped mechanical Power yet invented, except Wind and Water Mills, but that it may be applied to an infinite Number of Purposes to which the common Fire Engine is not at all applicable.

It appearing upon Perusal of the said Letters Patent, that the tole Benefit of the said Invention was granted to the Petitioner, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns only, within that Part of Great Britain called England, the Dominion of Wales, and Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and His Majesty’s Colonies and Plantations abroad: Your Committee thought proper to examine, whether it was worth Mr. Watt'% while to go on with the Work unless his Property was equally secured in Scotland ? And

Mr. Boulton being again examined, said. That he had great lleafon to believe, that if this Invention was once established into a regular Manufactory, great Numbers of the Engines would be exported to various Parts of the European Continent, and in that same any Persons in Scotland may avail themselves of this Invention at a much less Expence than the Inventor, and he should think it a very dangerous Undertaking to proceed further, unless Parliament would secure the Property of the Invention to the Petitioner as well in Scotland as in the Places already mentioned.

Mr. Alexander Camming being again examined, said, That if he was in Mr. Watt'% Situation, he would not proceed any further in this Undertaking unless his Property was secureckin Scotland as well as in England.

A Petition of the Merchants, Linen Drapers, and principal Inhabitants, of the City of in the

Kingdom of Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, with the deepest Concern for the unhappy Differences which at present subsist between Great Britain and her American Colonies, and from an Apprehension of the fatal Consequences which may arise from, thence, beg Leave to set forth, that, as their Export Trade with the American Colonies consist chiefly in the Exportation of the Linen Manufacture, and that of White and Brown Linens only, by the Non-importation Agreement they are deprived of this, the only valuable Branch of Export they* are permitted to carry on with the Colonies, and of which they already begin to feel the unhappy Effects; and that, if the Linen Manufacture decays, this Kingdom must be reduced to l'uch a State, as, from want of Employment at Home, to incrcale Emigrations, reduce the Value of Lands, and diminish every Branch of the poor Remains of the Trade they enjoy; and that the chief Commodities which they have Liberty to import from America into this Kingdom, being Flax Seed, . Vol. 35.

t7f

Lumber, Wheat, and Flour, should the Non-injporta-tion take place, they mull necessarily be deprived of Flax Seed, to raise Flax to carry on their Linen Manufacture, of Staves for Calks to contain their Beef,

Pork, and Butter, for the Supply of Great Britain,

His Majesty’s Navy, and the IVef India Islands; and this Train of Consequences, so destructive to the Landed Property, Manufactures, and Commerce, of this Kingdom, and which of course must occasion a very sensible Diminution of His Majesty’s Revenues, from the then absolute Inability of the Inhabitants, forces them to pray the House would take the Premises into their Consideration; hoping that some Expedient may be found out, whereby thei’e Consequences may be prevented, and Harmony restored> and established upon a solid and permanent Foundation.

Ordered, That the said. Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

To prove the Allegations of the Laid Petition, an Act# made in the 29th Year of King he Second, for discharging the Corporation of the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly called Bedford Level, from a Debt due to the Duke of Bedford and Earl of Lincoln, and for enabling the Proprietors of Lands in the North Level, Part of the said Great Level, to raise Money to discharge the Proportion of the said North Level from the Debts of the said Corporation, and for ascertaining and appropriating the Taxes to be hid on the said North Level; and for the more efti’ftual draining and preferring the said North Level, and divers Lands adjoining thereto, in the Manor of Crowland, was read; whereby it appeared, that the Commissioners appointed by the said Act wjerc impowered to assess, rate, tax, and charge, the Owners or Occupiers of all the Lands intended to be drained, except certain Lands in the said Act excepted, by equal and proportionable yearly Rates or Taxes, at the Discretion of such Commissioners, not exceeding, for the first Four Years, to be computed from Midsummer 1754, the yearly Rate of One Shilling for every Acre; and after th^ Expiration of the said Four Years, not exceeding, in any one Year, Sixpence an Acre; and that the Taxes so to be raised, and all Money to be borrowed on the Credit of the said Act, should be applied and disposed of for and towards the General Works of draining and preferring all the Districts in the Act particularly mentioned. Then,

Mr. Emerson Harrison, Surveyor of Part of the Works, being examined, said, That the Taxes of One Shilling for every Acre, charged upon the Lands by the said Act, for the said Four Years, and of Sixpence per Acre, wherewith the same have been yearly assessed by the said Commissioners ever finee the Expiration of the said Four Years, have proved inefficient to support the general Works of Drainage, and a considerable Debt hath been incurred on Account of such Works, which ’ . The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 117 Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee attending also at the Bar:

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and lealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table; and the Seals being inspected by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Out-side of the said Box, signed by Mr. Speaker, purporting, " That the said Box was, on the 6th Day of March 1775, made up in his Presence, in the Manner ,c directed by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the " Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act " to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or " Returns of Members to serve in Parliament," was read.

put into the said Box on the 6th Day of March 1775," was read.

And the said Nanies, written on distinct Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be of an equai Size, and rolled up in the same Manner, were, by the Clerk, taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers into Six GJafles, placed on the Table for that Purpose, fend were there shaken together; and then the Clerk publicly drew out of the said Six GlafiTes, alternately, the said Pieces'of Paper, and delivered them to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House.

To prove the Allegations of the First-mentioned Petition, the said Act was read: And,

Thomas Williams, Esquire, being, examined, . said. That the Trustees have made great Progress' in the

Repairs of the said Road, and have borrowed the Sum of £. 2,600, or thereabouts, which still remains due.

That several Amendments are necessary to be made to the said Act; and that the Road cannot be Completely repaired, noi* any further Sum of Money borrowed, unless the Terrm and Powers of the Ad are further continued and enlarged; and for that Purpose it will be necessary to encrease the Tolls.

That the said Road is the great Communication between England and Ireland, and several Parts thereof are overflowed by the Sea, every Spring Tide, so as to render it impassable for several Hours; that it is sometimes overflowed to the Depth of Seven or Eight Feet, and is therefore very dangerous, and many Risks are run by Travellers j that last Spring a Carriage was overturned by the Tide, and several others have been frequently in Danger; and that the said Road cannot be rendered safe, nor the Sea prevented from overflowing the fame, under the Powers of the present Act.

In Support of the Allegations of the Second* mentioned Petition,

Mr. IVWiams being further examined, said. That the Amendment of the said Road has proved of considerable Utility; and that the Petition is signed by 19 in 20, or thereabouts, of the Owners of Estates, and Inhabitants of Houses lying near the Road.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Henry WhiteJide, being examined, said, That in Consequence of the said Letters Patent, the Petitioner had contrived a Lighthouse of such singular Construction, that the same may at all Times be distinguished from every other Lighthouse in the World; and that the lame, when erected, will be of the utmost Importance to the Royal Navy, and to the Trade of this Kingdom; the Model of which was produced to your Committee.

And being further examined, he said, That the Petitioner had already expended the Sum of£.1,867, and upwards, in taking Surveys, making Models, purchasing Materials, and in the several necessary Works already performed, in order to carry the Purposes of ^the said Letters Patent into Execution; and that it will require the further Sum off. 1,464, and upwards, to complete the building of the said Lighthouse; and that, when completed, it will require the yearly Expence of £. 724, and upwards, to support and maintain the fame.

Mr. William Ferguson, Owner and Mailer of a Vessel called the Neptune, in the Dublin Trade; and,

Mr. William Huntingdon, Matter of a Vessel trading from Liverpool to London, being severally examined, laid. That the said Lighthouse will be of the utmost Importance to the Royal Navy, and to the Trade of this Kingdom.

Mr. William Ferguson, being further examined, said, That when the Petitioner first declared his Intention to apply to this House for the Purpose prayed for by his Petition, he fully intended to have opposed the fame, by reason that the Witness then thought, that the Term granted by the said Patent was fully sufficient for the Petitioner to raise Money for, the Purpose of carrying on the said Work; and upon the Witness applying to the Petitioner, to acquaint him with his Intentions, the Petitioner gave the Witness the Letters Patent, with Authority for him to raise Money upon it; and that the Petitioner applied to many Merchants and others to advance Money upon the fame, and even proposed to advance Part himself, but could not prevail with any Person to lend any Money thereon, by reason of the Sbortness of the Time granted by the said Patent; and that the Witness thinks that the Petitioner will not be able to procure any Money to be lent him upon the said Undertaking, unless a Perpetuity is granted to him, as prayed for by the said Petition.

the West Hiding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read ;Setting forth, That the Petitioners are very elsenfially interested in the Woollen Trade of the Northern Parts of this Kingdom, and particularly in the Narrow Cloths; and that the Trade there has been good the last Year, and is lo at the present, notwithstanding the Difficulties that it necessarily meets with from the Conduct of the , in pre-

fuming to obstruct the Trade from thence to many of the Colonies in America; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that any Submission to their unjust and unlawful Demands would be most prejudicial to the Petitioners, as well as to the Kingdom in general, as it would tend to make them more insolent, and totally to overthrow the lawful Authority which the King and Parliament mull have over all its Dominions; but, should the Petitioners suffer a present Loss, they are willing to do so, rather than a certain future one, which mull involve themselves and their Posterity, and consequently the whole Kingdom, in perpetual Distress: And therefore praying the House will take all such Measures as shall be thought adviseable, to support the lawful Authority of this Kingdom, and maintain the just Rights and Privileges thereof, in Opposition to all its Enemies whatsoever.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Word " whom" to the End of the Question, and inserting the Words " it is " referred tocontlder further of the several Papers which " were presented to the House, by the Lord North, upon " the 19th and 31st Days of January last, the ift, 15th, " and 24th Days of February last, and the 3d and 8th

Days of this Instant March, by His Majesty’s Command," instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words proposed to be left out Hand Part of the Question;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question being put j

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred.

A Petition of the manufacturing Hosiers of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, was presented to the House, and read; renewing their Application to the House, from a deep Sense of the Importance of the Facts contained in their former Petition, from a perfect Knowledge of their Truth, and apprehensive of

the unhappy Influence which art intervening Petition from the other Inhabitants of the said Town, intituled,

A Petition of the Aldermen, Sheriffs, principal Manufacturers, and Inhabitants thereof,’ ’ may have upon the Deliberations of Parliament at this important Juncture; and, knowing no greater Crime to their Country, than to approach their Representatives with Falsehood, and thereby mislead the great Council of the Nation, the Petitioners beg Leave to express their Abhorrence of the unjust Representation of the Manufacturers of this Town and Neighbourhood, which Men, styling themselves its Aldermen, principal Manufacturers, &e. have not been afraid to present to the House; and that the former Petitioners do constitute a very great Majority of the real Manufacturers of this Town, and the present Petitioners are the Committee appointed by them to transact this Business; the Distress they represented in their former Petition is real, has already in some Measure taken place, and they are persuaded mull encrease upon them every Day, beyond their Abilities to support, should the present Cessation of the North American Trade continue; and the contrary Representation of Men, ill capable of judging of their Trade or its Dependencies, has no Foundation in Truth, not One-fifth of the Signers of that Petition being Manufacturers, or any way concerned in the North American Trade; and it is to obviate the Impression which such Misrepresentation may have, to second that Relief which the House may be now meditating for their Distress, and to contribute by their particular Experience to that perfect Knowledge of the real State of the Manufactory of this Town and Neighbourhood, that the Petitioners earnestly entreat that they may be heard, in Proof of the several Allegations in this their present and former Petitions.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House* to whom the Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and others, of the City of London, concerned in the Commerce of North America, is referred; and that these Petitioners be heard, before the said Committee, upon their said Petitions, if they think fit.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Robert Nezvton being examined, said, That Stockport is a populous Town and a Place of great Trade, and that great Inconveniencies arise for want of its being properly lighted.

That the Streets are narrow and incommodious to the great Hindrance of Trade.

That if the Town was lighted, and Obstructions and Annoyances removed, and Power given to enlarge the Streets and Passages, and to purchase Buildings and Grounds necessary for the Purpose of widening the Streets, and rendering the same commodious, and to make Rates and Assessments for defraying the Expence of l'uch Powers, it would tend to the Advantage of the Inhabitants thereof, and to the Public in general.

Mr. Garden reported from the Committee, to whom Aberdeen the Petition of the Provost, Magistrates, and Town Streeu* Council, of the City of Aberdeen, in North Britain, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Longlands, being examined, said. That the City of Aberdeen has of late Years greatly encrealed in Buildings, and is, as well as the Approaches thereto, very badly paved, lighted, cleansed, and not sufficiently supplied with fresh Water; that it would tend greatly to the Safety and Accommodation of the Inhabitants of the said City, and of all Persons resorting thereto, if Power was given (o remedy the above-mentioned Inconveniencies; to remove and prevent Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions; to establilli a regular Nightly Watch; and to regulate the keeping of Gunpowder in Houses and Warehouses.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Rickard Leath being examined, said. That he

A. 1775.

was born within the Hundred of JSIitford, in the County of Norfolk, and had lived there 50 Years, and that he had acted as Clerk to Three Justices for levcra! Years.

And being asked, If he was acquainted with the State of the Poor in the Hundreds of Mitford and Laun-ditch ?he laid, he w'as; and that the Poor within those

Hundreds have greatly encrealed for several Years past; that they are now very numerous, and maintained and supporfed at much greater Charge than formerly, and that the Expences of maintaining them are yearly encreasing.

And the Witness laid. That from the Situation he was in, as Clerk to the Justices, he had had an Opportunity of inspecting the Overseers Accounts; and from that Inspection in particular he grounded his Information of the Encreale of the Expences of maintaining the Poor.

And being asked, Whether he meant to say, that the Poor had encrealed in all the Parishes within those Hundreds? he laid, he meant in the Parishes in general.

And being asked. If the Parish Accounts don’t include other Expences besides the Money disbursed for the Relief of the Poor? he said, they include the Constables Account and the County Rate.

And being asked, If the Expences of the Work-house at Deerhamwere not encrealed ? he said, they

were; and he attributed the Encreale of those Expences to the Encreale of the Poor; and that the Poor within the Workhouse have been farmed to a Governor for .£.305 a Year, who provided them with every Thing, and had the Advantage of their Labour, over and besides his Allowance; but that the Governor’s Allowance has been advanced within these few Months 45 a Year.

And being asked. What Ground he had for saying that the Expence of maintaining the Poor was encreased in the Parishes in general ? he said, from his general Observation of the Amount of the Expences at Rafter, and from the Report of the Parish Officers; and also from the more frequent Complaints of late to the Magistrates for Relief.

And being asked, Whether he usually saw at the Amount of the Poor Accounts of the several Parishes within these Hundreds ? he laid, he did; and that they contain the Amount of the annual Expence of maintaining the Poor in each respective Parish; and that the Expence is in general encreased. Then,

Mr. Robert Suckling, who had occupied Two Farms in the Parish of Soulhburgh, in the Hundred of ford, within a few Years past, being examined, laid.

That he knows the Hundreds of Mitford and Lam-ditch-, that he has known them above Seven Years: and "v that the Poor within the said Hundreds are very numerous, and the Charges of maintaining them greater than formerly, which are still encreasing.

And being asked, If he knew any Thing of the Poor’s Rates in any other Parish than Southburgh I he laid, he knew a great many; that lie had examined the Books of the Overseers of many Parishes, %y which it appeared, that the Poor’s Rates of such Parishes had greatly encrealed. '

The.House proceeded to the Appointment of aSeleft Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Directions of Two several Acts of Parliament, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to lerve in Parliament.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 105 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioners, Samuel Whitbread, and John Howard, Esquires, their Counsel and Agents, who also appeared as Gounfel and Agents on Behalf of the said other Petitioners, and the Counsel and Agents for the Sitting Members, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Car: The Clerk appointed to Attend the said Select Committee attending also at the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day for taking the said Petitions into Consideration, 4

And the same being read accordingly;

The Box, containing the Names of all the Members of the House, and sealed with Mr. Speaker’s Seal, was placed upon the Table; and the Seals being inspefeed by Mr. Speaker, the Attestation annexed to the Out-side of the said Box, ligned by Mr. Speaker, purporting, " That the said Box was, on the 13th Day of " March 1775, made up in his Presence, in the Manner directed by an Act, made in the Tenth Year of " the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to " regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Re+ " turns of Members to serve in Parliament," was read;

And the Seals being broken, and the Box opened, the Attestation inclosed therein, and ligned by the Clerk, purporting, " That the Names of all the Members were by him, in the Pretence of the Speaker, put " into the said Box on the 13th Day of March 1775," was read.

And the said Names, written on distinct Pieces of Paper, being all as near as might be of an equal Size, and rolled up in the same Manner, were, by the Clerk, taken out of the said Box, and put in equal Numbers into Six Glades, placed on the Table for that Purpose, and were there shaken together; £nd then the Clerk publicly drew out of the said Six Glaflbs, alternately, the said Pieces of Paper, and delivered them to Mr. Speaker, who read the same to the House.

And the Names of Thirty-eight Members, then present, were drawn, who were riot objected-to.

And the Name of Lord George Germain being drawn, the Counsel for the Petitioners declared, that the said Member was intended to be nominated by the said Petitioners; and the said Member having, in his Place, consented to such Nomination, and no Objection being made to his serving' on the said Select Committee, as such Nominee, his Name was set alide.

And the Name of One other Member, then present, was drawn, who was not objected to.

And the Name of Richard Jackson, Esquire, being drawn, the Counsel for the Sitting Members declared, that the said Member was intended to be nominated by the said Sitting Members; and the said Member having in his Place, contented to i’uch Nomination, and no objection being made to his serving on the said Select Committee as such Nominee, his Name was let aside.

And the Names of Ten other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

Note, That, in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Fourteen other Members, then present, were drawn and let aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; Eight, on Account of their being Members against whole Returns Petitions were depending; and Six, on Account of their then serving on Select Committees appointed for trying the Merits of controverted Elections.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members so drawn, and not excused, or set aside, being complete, and Two Lists of the said Names having been prepared by the Clerk;

The Door of the House was opened:

A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Merchants, trading to Africa, being offered to be presented to the House;

; The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the House, an Account of the Money granted for the Year 1773, examined and passed by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the 23d of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending " and improving the Trade to Africa-ft and that they have inverted the Money, granted in 1774, for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and Settlements having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State, by the Royal African Company, and the Sums annually granted by Parliament, being nearly expended in the civil and military Establishments, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, several of them still remain in a very ruinous Condition; and that the Petitioners being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa: Therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, and likewise for the Repairs still wanted, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the Clothiers and other principal Inhabitants of Trowbridge, in the County of Wilts, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, certain Persons, styling themselves Reprefeatatives of the People of sundry Provinces in America, assembled in General Congrels, have presented a Petition to His Majesty, in which they question the Authority of the Supreme British Legislature, to enact Laws for raising a Revenue in those Parts of His Majesty’s Dominions; and that the Petitioners conceive, the openly or tacitly giving up, in this Instance, the Authority of the Legislature of Great Britain, over the American Colonies, would be not only highly derogatory to the Honour and Dignity of the Crown and Parliament, but greatly injurious to the Welfare and Trade of Great Britain; and that the Petitioners cannot be insensible that, if their Fellow Subjects in America are exempted from contributing, in such way as the British Legislature shall judge best, and in some equitable Proportion, with the Inhabitants of Great Britain, to the Revenues necessaryTor supporting the Dignity of the Crown, the Administration of Government and Justice in, and the Protection of, the whole Empire, such Exemption to them must occasion the People here being unequitably and too heavily burdened; and, as the Petitioners apprehend, the disproportioned and heavy Share of the public Burdens, which the Inhabitants of this Kingdom have been hitherto called to bear, has been one Occasion of Numbers from different Branches of the Woollen Manufacture already emigrating to America, so they are persuaded the Continuance of such Disproportion would be a Means of drawing from hence to America yet more and more our most useful and industrious Manufacturers and Mechanics, to a Degree, which, in the End, must be pernicious both to the Landed and Commercial Interest of Great Britain: And therefore praying, That the House will ever aftert, and maintain entire, the Supremacy of the British Legislature over His Majesty’s Dominions in America, and provide, by such Laws and Measures as to the House shall appear best, that, whilst the Inhabitants of those Dominions claim and expect Countenance and

under the Management of the Commissioners for paving Westminster, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have advanced considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the said Acts, or one of them, trusting on the Faith of Parliament for their Security; and taking Notice of the Bill to enable the Inhabitants of such Part of Piccadilly as lies between Berkeley Street and Hyde Park , and of such Von. 35.

Part of Park Lane as lies between Piccadilly and the North Side of Hertford Street, to pave, cleanse, and light the fame, and also to water such Part of Piccadilly as aforesaid, and for repealing the several Laws now in being for those Purposes; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the taking the said Parts of Piccadilly and Park Lane out of the said Acts, and from the Jurisdiction of the said Commissioners, will be a manifest Injury to all- Persons possessed of, or interested in Securities made on the said Acts, for Money advanced thereon: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pals into a Law.

A Petition of the Committee appointed for the Parish Ditto, of Saint fames, within the Liberty of Westminster, to put in Execution the several Acts of Parliament for paving,' deanfing, lighting, and regulating, the Squares, Streets, and other Places, in Westminster, and Parts adjacent, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Bill; and Setting forth; That the Petitioners observe a Clause in the said Bill, directing the Surplus of the annual Sum of £. 1000. granted by Parliament in the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, from the Kensington Trull, to the Commissioners 1 for paving Westminster, and Parts adjacent, and also the Surplus which shall from Time to Time remain of the said annual Sum, after satisfying the Interest chargeable thereon, to be applied for the Benefit of the Inhabitants in the before-mentioned Part of Piccadilly and Park Lane; which annual Sum is, by the said Act, directed to be applied for paving, lighting, repairing, and regulating, Part of Piccadilly and Park Lane, and the several other Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Places, under the Care and Management of the said Commissioners; and that, should such Bill pass into a Law, the Petitioners apprehend, they shall thereby be deprived of that Part of the said Surplus which at present is legally vested in them for the Benefit of the Parishioners; and that the Property of the Pavements, Lamps, and other Materials and Things, being within the Limits of the said Bill, and which are now vested in the said Commissioners for the Benefit of the Public, are to bevelled in the said Trullees, who may sell or dispose thereof, if they think proper; and that the said Trullees'are not compellable to new pave the said Places, nor to purchase new Lamp Irons, or other Materials, or to cause the present Number of Lamps to be lighted, or to preserve the Levels in case of new paving, whereby great Inconveniencies, Mischiefs, and Dangers, may arise to the Public; and that the exempting any of the Streets and Places from the general Care and Management of the Commissioners, and allotting or assigning to the Trullees of such Streets and Places the Money granted by Parliament for the Benefit of the whole, mull totally defeat the general Plan, calculated for the Benefit both of the Public and the Inhabitants of Westminster and Parts adjacent; and that the Places comprised in the said Bill are now well paved, repaired, cleansed, and lighted, under subsisting Contracts with the Commissioners; and therefore the Petitioners conceive the said Bill to be unnecessary: And therefore praying. That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the same may not pass into a Law.

and that the said William Blakey did, in pursuance of the said Proviso, cause a Particular to be inrolled in the said Court of Chancery, on the Ninth Day of October 1766, which Description is therein particularly expressed and contained, according to the Drafts or Plans thereunder drawn; and that His said Majesty, by Let* ters Patent, bearing Date the 5th Day of January, in the Ninth Year of His Reign, did' grant unto James Watt, of the City of Glasgow, Merchant, the foie Benefit and Advantage of making and vending certain Engines, therein mentioned to be by him invented, for leftening the Consumption of Steam and Fuel in Fire Engines, for the Term of Fourteen Years, with the like Proviso, to cause a particular Description of the Nature of the said Invention to be inrolled in His Majesty’s High Court of Chancery, within Four Months after the Date of the said last mentioned Letters Patent; and that the said James Watt did, in pursuance of the said Proviso, cause a particular Description-of the said Engine to be inrolled in the said Court of Chancery, on the 29th Day of April 1769; but the said James Watt did not cause any Draft, or Plan, to the said De,-feription, to be drawn and delineated; and that the said William Blakey had no previous Notice of the said James Watt having obtained his laid Let ters.Patent, otherwise he would have opposed the granting thereof; and that, although the said James Watt lo obtained his said letters Patent in the Beginning, of the Year 1769, yet he did not complete any such Machine before the End of the Year 1774, when he alledges to have fur-hished feme large.Engines as Specimens of his Construction; and that the said Machine, so alleged to be invented by the said James W is only an Imitation of the Construction of the said Machine invented by the.laid William Blakey, and contains.no utile Principles whatsoever, further or other than is contained in that of the said William Blakey and although there are fotne Ingredients. and'Things all edged by the said James Watt to be used in the Exercise of the said Machines, never* thelbfs that is Matter of Discretion mthe Persons using the fame, the Experience of which, front the said James Watt's own shewing, has had but a very short Space of Two or Three Months, in which:short Timeik is unlikely such short Experience should be satisfactory; A Petition of several of the Merchants, Tradesmen, Manufacturers, and other Principal Inhabitants of the Town of Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, was prefeiftetL to the House* and read; taking No-

tice of an Application for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Cut, or Canal, from or near the Town of Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, to communicate with the Sta and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, at or near Stourton, in the County of Stafford, and also for making Two collateral Cuts, out of the said intended Canal, to certain Places, called The Fens and The Level, Parcel of Penfnett Chafe, in the Parish of Kingswinford, and County of;

and that the said collateral Cuts will open into very extensive Coal Mines lying between Stourbridge and Dudley, within Four or Five Miles of the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, which are now in a greajt Measure excluded from being brought to Market, for Want of a Water Carriage; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the present great Demand for Coalsdown the Staffordshire Canal to the Severn, supplied from the

Collieries lying upon the Banks of the Birmingham Canal, will tend to distress the Trade and Manufactures of the said Town of Birmingham and Neighbourhood, by advancing the Price of Coals; and that the same will be greatly prevented, by means of the said intended Canal and collateral Cuts, opening a Communication from such Collieries between Stourbridge and Dudley to the Severn, and which will thereby supply Part of the Demand upon the River Severn, and by Means thereof the Trade and Manufactories of the said Town and Neighbourhood will, as the Petitioners apprehend, have a more lasting and plentiful Supply of Coals, and at a more reasonable Rate than at present, and be (ft" great public Utility: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in such Bill for making the said Canal and collateral Cuts, and that the same may pass into a Law, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Sheriffs, and Common Council of the City of Gloucester, in Council assembled, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise taking Notice of the said Application; and setting forth, That the Petitioners apprehend, by Means of such intended Canal and collateral Cuts, a more commodious and cheaper Communication will be opened between the said City and the said Town of Stourbridge, and Parts adjacent; and that Coals may thereby be supplied cheaper than at present, and great Advantage will ante to the Trade of the said City, and to the Inhabitants, and more especially the Poor, who will be considerably benefited; and that other public Advantages will be derived therefrom: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to &ring in such Bill for making the said Canal and collar tcral Cuts; and that the same may pass into a Law, with such Powers, and under such Terms and Conditions, as to the House shall seem meet.

Widows A Petition of several Members of the Laudable Society. Society for the Benefit of Widows, whose Names are theieunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That a Petition has been presented from several Directors and Members of the said Society, for Leave to bring in a Bill for securing to Widows, who are now Claimants upon the said Society, the several Annuities promised to them by the original Scheme, or any subsequent Alterations therein, and for making further and other Regulations for the better Government and Management of the said Society; and that it appears to the Petitioners, that the Principles upon which the said Society was formed are erroneous, and that the Annuities engaged to be paid will be much greater than the annual Payment from the Subscribers can answer, which Engagement must end in the Ruin of the Society, and in the very great Distress of many of the Parties interested, without the Interposition of Parliament; and that the Petitioners are desirous to secure to the Widows who are now Claimants their several Annuities, as promised, and that all future Annuities may be secured, either by encreasing the Annual Subscription so far as to answer the Payment thereof, or by reducing such future Annuities, and that such of the Subscribers as shall be dissatisfied with the Terms proposed may be at Liberty to withdraw, receiving an equal Proportion of the Money already subscribed by them, after securing the Payment of the Annuities to the present Claimants; and that the immediate Interposition of the Legislature appears to the Petitioners to be absolutely necessary, as the Fund provided for the Payment of the said Annuities becomes every Day more inadequate to that Purpose t And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall appear reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom (he Petition of the several Persons whose Names are subscribed, being divers of the Directors and Members of the Laudable Society for the Benefit of Widows, on Behalf of themselves and the said Society, is referred.

Ditto. A Petition of the several Persons whole Names are thereunto subscribed, being divers of the Directors, Trullocs, and Members, of the Laudable Society for the Benefit of Widows, on Behalf of themselves and the said Society, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that divers of the said Society have presented a Petition, for Leave to bring in a Bill for these Purposes in the Prayer of the said Petition; and that these Petitioners apprehend there is no good Reason for such Application;

and that the Members who have subscribed to the same are only Three Directors and Eight other Members out of above Six Hundred of the whole Body; and that, by an Article in the Deed of Settlement of the 18th Day of March 1761, a General Meeting of the Members thereof (haying Twenty at leail present) have Power to determine all Matters relating to the Society, and to alter and amend the Deed, and make any additional Rules or Articles, jo as they be confirmed by a Second General Meeting; and that, in the Beginning of the Year 1774, a Petition was presented to the House, by divers of the said Society, for dissolving the said Society, and other Purposes therein mentioned, and a Counter Petition w^s» presented, by others of the said Society, against the fame; when it was recommended to the Parties differing, to endeavour to accommodate Matters; and accordingly divers Meetings were had, and Proposals made, for that Purpose; and that, at a Special General Meeting of the said Society, upon the Second Day of June 1774, a Plan for the Reformation of the said Society was proposed, and agreed to by a Majority, and confirmed at another Special General Meeting, upon the 23d Day of the said Month: And therefore praying, That a Bill be not permitted to pass, to make any Alteration in the reformed Plan of the said Society; and that the Petitioners may be heard by Counsel.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names are subscribed, being divers of the Directors and Members of the Laudable Society for the Benefit of Widows, on Behalf of themselves and the said Society, is referred.

Ordered, That all have Voices, who come to the Committee, to whom the said Petition is referred.

American A Motion was made, and the Question being pro-Colonies. posed, That the Colonies and Plantations of Great Britain, in North America, confiding of Fourteen separate Governments, and containing Two Millions and upwards of free Inhabitants, have not had the Liberty and Privilege of electing and fending any Knights and Burgesses, or others, to represent them in the High Court of Parliament.

And the previous Question being put. That that Question be now put j

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

Tellers for the Yeas, j } ?8-

Tellers for the Noes, ^^C^opey0^9 \ 270.

So it passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed. That the said Colonies and Plantations have been made liable to, and bounden by, several Subsidies, Payments, Rates, and Taxes, given and granted by Parliament, though the said Colonies and Plantations have not their Knights and Burgesses in the said High Court of Parliament, of their own Election, to represent the Condition of their Country; by Lack whereof they have been oftentimes touched and grieved by Subsidies, given, granted, and afiented to, in the said Court, in a Manner prejudicial to the Commonwealth, Quietness, Rest, and Peace, of the Subjects inhabiting within the lame.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out from the Word " Country" to the End of the Question.

And the Question being put. That the Words proposed to be left out stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Then the main Question, so amended, being proposed, That the said Colonies and Plantations have been made liable to, and bounden by, several Subsidies, Payments, Rates, and Taxes, given and granted by Parliament, though the said Colonies and Plantations have not their Knights and Burgesses in the said High Court of Parliament, of their own Election, to represent the Condition of their Country;

And the previous Question being put. That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, That, from the Distance of the said Colonies, and from other Circumstances, no Method hath hitherto been devised, for procuring a Representation in Parliament for the said Colonies.

And the previous Question being put, That that Question be now put;

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being pro-poled, That each of the said Colonies hath, within itself, a Body chosen in Part, or in the Whole, by the Vox.. 35.

Freemen, Freeholders, or other free Inhabitants thereof, commonly called the General Assembly, or General Court, with Powers legally to raise* levy, and assess, according to the several Usages of such Colonies, Duties, and Taxes, towards defraying all Sorts of public Services;

And the previous Question being put. That that Question be now put

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That the said General Assemblies, General Courts, or other Bodies legally qualified as aforesaid, have, at sundry Times, freely granted several large Subsidies and public Aids, for His Majesty’s Service, according to their Abilities, when required thereto by Letter from One of His Majesty’s principal Secretaries of State; and that their Right to grant the fame, and their Chear-fulness and Sufficiency in the said Grants, have been, at sundry Times, acknowledged by Parliament,

It passed in the Negative.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That it hath been found by Experience, that the Manner of granting the said Supplies and Aids, by the said General Assemblies, hath been more agreeable to the Inhabitants of the said Colonies, and more beneficial and conducive to the public Service, than the Mode of giving and granting Aids and Subsidies in Parliament, to be raised and paid in the said Colonies;

It passed in the Negative.

The Lord Hinckingbrook reported from the Committee, Huntingdon to whom the Petition of several Noblemen, and also Clergymen the humble Petition of several Gentlemen, Clergy, and fcc

others, of the County of Huntingdon, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, John Clementfort, Esquire, informed Your Committee, That there a,re, within the said County, several small Benefices, and great Numbers of Widows and Orphans of Clergymen left in distressed Circumstances; that many Donations have been set on foot in the County for their Relief; and that he thinks they might be better relieved, if a Corporation was established under proper Regulations.

A Member present confirmed the above Evidence; and Mr. Clementfon added. That there are many Persons desirous of contributing to the Charity; and that there are some Charity Trusts that cannot be applied without the Aid of Parliament; and that the Trustee of a Charity for the Relief of poor Widows and Children of Clergymen within the said County, is desirous <?f resigning the Trust to this Charity, if enabled fb to do by Authority of Parliament.

Upon the whole Matter, Your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the poor Widows and Children of Clergymen within the said County of Huntingdon, would be better provided for if certain Persons were incorporated for receiving and managing such charitable Donations as have been, or shall be, given or bequeathed for the Relief of such poor Widows and Orphans.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Chairman be directed to move the House for

Cricklade A Petition of the Subscribets, Electors of the Bo-Election. rough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilis, in Behalf of themselves, and others, Electors of the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting* forth. That, at the last Election of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the room of William Earle, Esquire, deceased, Samuel Peach, John Dewar, and Samuel Petrie, Esquires, were Candidates; and that Thomas Carter, Bailiff of the said Borough, who presided as Returning Officer at the said Election, during the Poll, acted with the greatest Partiality, in Favour of the said Samuel Peach, ejefting the Votes of many who had an undoubted Right to poll, and who tendered their Votes for the said John Dewar, or the said Samuel Petrie, and admitting many to poll for the said Samuel Peach, who were in the same Situation with those who were refused to be admitted'for the Other Candidate^, as well as many others who had no Right to vote at all; and thereby the said Thomas Carter, in a most arbitrary, illegal, and unwarrantable Manner, deprived great Numbers of the Electors of the said Borough of that Right and Franchise, which they had heretofore exercisedfor Time immemorial and that, by those and other undue Tracr tices, the said Samuel Peach has* been unduly returned to serve for the said Borough, in Defiance of the Law, and gross Violation of the Freedom of Election: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation, and to grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem just. ... '

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Cohfi-deration upon Monday the 17th Day of July next, at the same Time that the Petition of John Dewar, Esquire, is ordered to be taken into Consideration. Memorandum:

A Petition of the Manufacturers, Traders, and prin- Stourbridge cipal Inhabitants, of the Town of lVolverhamptony in Canal, the County of Stafford, was presented to the House, and read 3 Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented,. for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a navigable Cut or Canal, from or near the Town of St our bridge, in the County of Worcester, to or near a Place called Stourton, in the County of Stafford, there to communicate with the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal 3 and also for making Two collateral Cuts, out of the said intended Canal, to certain Places called The Fens, Parcel of Penfnet Chafe, and The Level, other Parcel of Penfnet Chafe, in the Parish of Kingswinford, in the County of Stafford3 and that a very extensive Manufactory of Iron Goods and other Branches of Trade are carried . on in and about the said Town of Wolverhampton, wherein many Thousands of Mechanics and Labourers are employed, the Success and Extension of which Trade depends in a great Measure upon a cheap and plentiful Supply of Coals; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the making and maintaining such navigable Canal and collateral Cuts will cause many Mines of Coal, lying between the Towns of Dudley and Stourbridge, near the intended Course thereof, to be opened and ( worked, and great Quantities of Coal brought to.

Market, which at present are excluded for want of a Water Carriage, by which Means the said Town of Wolverhampton and the Neighbourhood thereof, as well as many other Parts of the said County, may be supplied with Coal in a more plentiful Manner, and at a much cheaper Rate, than at present, which will be of great Public Utility, and essentially serviceable to the Manufacturers, Trade, and Poor, of the said Town of Wolverhampton and Neighbourhood; And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in such Bill for making the said Canal and collateral Cuts, and that the same may pass into a Law, with such Powers, and under such Terms and Conditions, as to the House shall seem meet.

To the First Amendment made by your Lordships, Press 18, Line 12, the Commons do agree.

The Commons disagree to the Second Amendment made by your Lordships, Press 8, Line 39 and 40; and to the Third Amendment made by your Lordships, Press 9, Line 1:

Because, by the said Amendments, the Commanders of His Majesty’s Ships of War, Rationed for the Regulation and Pro ted ion of the British Fisheries, on the Coasts of North America, and the Commanders of any other of His Majesty’s Ships or Vessels, employed on the said Coasts, maybe involved in great Difficulty and Perplexity, in carrying the Ad into Execution, with respect to the Colonies of New Jersey, Pensylvania, Maryland, Virginia, and South Carolina, and in the Performance of the Duty required of them by a Law, which in the Title and Preamble of it purports only to restrain the Fisheries of the Provinces of Maftachu-set's Bay and New Hampshire, and Colonies of Connecticut and Rhode Island.

Sir Thomas Clavering reported from the Committee, Tweed to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Bur- Fitherie*. geffes, of the Town of Berwick upon Tweed, and of the several other Persons whose Hands are thereunto subscribed. Owners, Proprietors, and Tenants of Fisheries in the River Tweed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, made in the nth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for regulating and improving the Fisheries in the River Tweed, and the " Rivers and Streams running into the fame, and also within the Mouth or Entrance of the said River;’* was read. And,

Mr. Anthony Lambert being examined, said. That the Regulations and Provisions established by the said Act have been found of great Utility to the Owners and Proprietors of Fisheries in the said River, but that many Complaints have lately been made by several of the Proprietors, that feme of the Provisions in the said Act have been found ineffectual; that he was present at a Public Meeting at Berwick, held pursuant fb Advertisement, when the Necessity of an Application to Parliament for making the said Act effectual was universally acknowledged; and that the Petitioners, who had signed the Petition, were considerable Proprietors in the Fisheries on the River Tweed. Then,

A Member present informed your Committee, That upon the passing of the said Act, several Fisheries on the River Tweed were let soon after, upon the Idea that

the

15 Geo. III. 270 Martii.

the Act would have proved effectual for the Purpose of ' preserving the Fish, and detesting Persons that should be found fishing in the prohibited Months; that the Fisheries on the said River role thereupon very considerably; that the same Fisheries have since very much fallen, but not quite so low as they were before the passing of the said Act, which the Member said he had reason to believe is to be imputed in a great Degree to the Act not having proved so effectual for preserving the Fish as was at first imagined; and he added, that he understood, from the bell Intelligence he had been able to procure, that it is the general Wilh of far the moll considerable Proprietors, that a new Act should be obtained for making such Alterations as may be found necessary, and rendering the Provisions in the last Act more effectual.

Then another Member present informed your Committee, That he was present with a Justice of the Peace when several Persons were brought before him, in consequence of his Warrants, for taking and killing Fish in the River Tweed at the Time prohibited by the Act; and that the Justice found the greatest Difficulty in convicting the Persons lo informed against, though the Fish were found upon them, owing to the Darknels of the Night, so that the Informers could not fee them take and kill the Fish.

to the Benefit of the Towns of Port Glasgow and Newark to have a regular Police; that the Streets of the said Towns are ill paved, cleansed, lighted, and watched; that there are no public Markets; that the Breast and East and West Quays of the Harbour of Port Glasgow are out of Repair, nor are the Inhabitants supplied with fresh Water; and that it Provision was made for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, for erecting public Markets, and repairing the Breast and East and West Quays of the Harbour, and for supplying the Inhabitants with fresh Water, it would be of great Benefit to the said Two Towns, and to the Public.

And the Witness added, That if the Duty of Two Pennies Scots in the Pint, now payable on Ale and Beer brewed or fold within the said Town of Port Glasgow, was extended over the said Town of Newark, and a Tax was laid on the Rents of the Houses of the Inhabitants of the Towns of Newark and Port Glasgow, the above Regulations might be carried into Execution.

Mr. James Watt confirmed the above Evidence.

A Member present informed the Committee, That he very frequently travels the Cud Turnpike Road, and has done so for many Years past; that during his Knowledge of the Road it has been in very bad Condition, very inconvenient, and at many Times dangerous to Travellers; that he has taken more particular Notice of it for Three or Four Years last past, and has observed from Time to Time, that it has been very ill managed by the Surveyor; that it has never been properly formed; and that the Materials which have been put upon it have endured but a short Time, as they have for the most Part lain wet, and the Wheels of the Carriages having formed a Sluice on each Side that has retained the Water, have soon ground the Materials into a Pbddle.

That when he last came along the Road, he found it in very bad Condition, and believes many Travellers and Carriages quit the Road at Stony Stratford on one Side, and at Dunthutch on the other, and go through Northampton, which is several Miles farther, in order to avoid this bad Road.

That he apprehends, that if proper Powers were given to get Materials of a better and more durable Nature than those heretofore used, and a skilful Surveyor was; to be employed, there would be a very considerable Saving in the Expence, and the Road might be effectually repaired.

Another Member present also informed the Committee, That he apprehended, unless necessary Powers. are granted for the getting proper Materials for the Repair of the said Road, and some Method taken to reduco the Weights on Broad Wheeled Waggons, the same cannot be effectually repaired.

for the better maintaining, relieving, and governing, the Poor, within the said Hundreds; and representing to the House, that several Meetings, for considering the Plan of an Application to Parliament, for incorporating the several Parishes within , the said Hundreds, with regard to their Poor, have been held; at the last of which Meetings, it was determined, that no Bill for the Purpose of incorporating the Poor within the said Hundreds should be applied for; and that, if such a Bill pafles into a Law, it must very considerably affect the Property of all Penons who are afiefled, and contribute to the Maintenance of the Poor, and will, from the Extent and Size of the said Hundreds, put the Poor under peculiar Circumstances of Hardship in applying for Relief: And therefore praying. That a Bill, so introduced contrary to the Sense of the Owners and Occupiers present at the said last Meeting, and which will, as they apprehend, so very materially affect all Persons contributing to the Rates for the Relief of the Poor within the said Hundreds, may not pass into a Law; and that they may be heard, by themselves or Counsel, against the said Bill.

levant A Petition of the Governor and Company of Mer-

Ctmpany. cjiants of England trading into the Levant Seas, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord Norths by His Majesty’s Command, acu quainted the House, That His Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Trade between this Kingdom and Turkey has for a long Series of Years been carried on by a Society of Merchants, incorporated by Charters, and regulated by Acts of Parliament; and that, in order to carry on the said Trade with Safety, and to protest His Majesty’s Subjects in the Turkish Dominions, it has been found necessary that there should be an Ambassador sent from England, to reside at Constantinople, and that there should be Consuls and Vice Consuls, and other Officers and Servants, in the other Parts of Turkey, where any British Subjects reside, and where the Ertglish Carry on Trade, the whole Expence whereof has been borne by the Turkey Company; which, together with other necessary Expences incident to the carrying on the said Trade, has of late Years amounted to about 10,000 per Annum; and that the said Trade, once so flourishing, is now, from many unavoidable Events and concurring Circumstances, much reduced; and that the Assistance which has been granted to the Petitioners by Parliament has enabled them to pay off the Debt which they had incurred, and to lower their Duties, which were so high as to be a Burthen that the Trade was not able to support; and that the Trade has for some Time past been encreasing, which has been beneficial to His Majesty’s Revenue, and likewise of Advantage to the Manufacturers of this Kingdom; and that the Petitioners have Reason to apprehend, that, if they should raise their Duties again, such ah Alteration would tend to diminish the Trade, and consequently that they should be less able to support the Expences of it; and that the Petitioners, having found themselves, by the former Bounty of Parliament, in a Situation to support their Expences, during the last Year, without immediate Assistance, did not then make any Application; but they are sensible that they should not discharge the Duty incumbent upon them by their Charter, nor the Justice they owe to the Public, for whom they consider themselves as Trustees, if they did not declare their present Inability to support their necessary Expences, unless relieved by Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Assistance as may be~ thoughtmeceflary and proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

THE Hour, appointed for taking into Cohsideration SVafteftwry the Petition of Hans Witttrop Mortimer, Esquire, fekBlon. complaining of the undue Election and Return of ! Thomas Rumbold and Francis Sykes, Esquires, for the Borough ot Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset, being come j

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a §e-left Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Election and Return, according to the Dii eft ions of Two lever.il Acts of Parliament, passed in the Tenth and Eleventh Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for the regulating the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament:

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Business of the House:

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 107 Members being found to be present;

The Petitioner, Hans Wintrop Mortimer, Esquire, and his Counsel and Agents, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Mr. Rumbcld, and the Counsel and Agents for the said Mr. Sykes, who attended at the Door, were called in to the Bar: The Clerk appointed to attend the said Select Committee attending also at the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked;

The laid Counsel for the Sitting Members severally informed the House, That the said Sitting Members were delirous of appearing by different Counsel, in respect that the Charge stated against them, in the said Petition, was that of Bribery, which, in its Nature, mull affect them separately; that the Numbers on the Poll for the Sitting Members were different; and that in the Course of hearing the Matter of the said Petition, their Interests might prove opposite to each other; and they proposed, that if the Counsel for the Petitioner should not agree to this Request, he ought to consent not to give any Evidence before the Committee, which did not equally afi'eft both the Sitting Members.

And the said Counsel having been heard thereto;

The Counsel for the Petitioner was heard; and having dated to the House, that the Sitting Members were Joint Candidates at the Election, and having opposed their separating in their Defence; -

The laid Petitioner, and the Counsel and Agents on both Sides, were directed to retire some Way from the Bar.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Thomas Rumbold and Francis Esquires, be at Liberty to appear as separate Parties on distinct Interests.

It passed in the Negative.

And the Petitioner, with the Counsel and Agents, being again called to the Bar, Mr. Speaker acquainted them with the said Resolution.

And then the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to

Mevagissey Mr. Grenville reported from the Committee, to whom Pier. 1 the Petition of the Lord of the Manor of Mevagissey, in the County of Cornwall, of the Owners of Lands within and near the said Manor, and of several Persons residing in and near the Town of who are

concerned in and carry on the Pilchard Fishery, and who trade to and from the said Town, whose Names are thereunto lubscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Stephen Rice informed your Committee, That the Town of Mevagissey is situated on the South Side of the County of Cornwall, contiguous to the British Channel, that it is a very convenient Situation for carrying on the Pilchard Fishery, and the same has been carried on there for a long Series of Years; that a small Pier was formerly erected and kept in Repair by the private Owner of the Ground and Soil near the said Town, in respect of which certain small Dues were taken from the Owners of such Vessels as partook of the Protection of the said Pier.

That the said Pier being found very incommodious, difficult of Access, and inadequate to the Increase of the Fishery, and the Resort of Vessels to the said Town, the same has been fullered to fall into Ruin and Decay; and that it hath been judged necessary to erect a new Pier upon a more enlarged Plan, for which Purpose the Sum of £. 1,300, or thereabouts, has been subscribed and expended in executing Part of the Work intended to oe carried into Execution.

Vol. 35.

That, in order to make the proper Embankments,

Quays, Wharfs; Ways, Passages, and Approaches to the said Pier, and for the Protection thereof, the Wit-nels apprehends it will be necessary to vest in Commissioners the Soil of a sufficient Quantity of Ground; for which Purpose, and for completing the several Works before-mentioned, and for making Satisfaction to the Owners of the Ground and Soil which will be necessary for effecting the fame, the further Sum of £.3,000, or thereabouts, will be wanted: And,

Mr. Thomas Richardson, being exahiined, said, That by laying a reasonable Tonnage Duty on all Ships and Vessels which shall partake of the Benefit resulting from the Improvements before-mentioned, and by laying other reasonable Tolls or Duties, not- only the said Sum of £. 3,000, but the Interest thereof, and of the Sums already advanced, may be kept down, and the \ said Pier and Works at all Times kept and maintained in good and sufficient Repair.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for completing and maintaining the Pier at the Town of Mevagissey, in the County of Cornw And that Mr. Grenville and the Lord Bulkeleydo prepare, arid bring in, the lame.

A Petition of the Merchants, Mariners, and Trades- Ditto; men, of the Port of Liverpool, whose Names are subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed a Bill is expending, to impower John Phillips, Proprietor for a determinate Number of Years of certain Rocks called The Smalls, in Saint George's Channel, to levy a perpetual Tax upon all Ships or Vessels that shall pass a Lighthouse, proposed to be by him erected upon one ot those Rocks; and that the Petitioners have great Cause to doubt, whether the eretting and maintaining a sufficient Lighthouse upon any of the said Rocks be at all practicable; but, if the Futility of those Doubts should from Experience appear, they apprehend that a Lighthouse so situated will not be of such general Use as to authorize a general Taxation, nor can the Petitioners conceive that the alledged peculiar Conllruttion of the intended Building will be attended with any peculiar Advantage to Shipping, or that the Means proposed will render it distinguishable at Sea from other Lights; and that the Petitioners hope it will not appear reasonable to impose upon Shipping a certain perpetual and almoll general Tax, for an uncertain and limited Advantage ' And therefore praying, That they may be permitted by the House to be heard, by themselves and Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Petition of the Merchants of Glasgow, was also Dittos presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, from the Votes, that a Petition has been presented, in the Name of John Phillips, of Liverpool, to grant to him a Perpetuity, or in such Manner as the House shall think proper, of a Lease of the Rock or Rocks called The Smalls, in Saint George's Channel, for eretting a Lighthouse or Lighthouses thereon; and that the Petitioners are of Opinion, that a Lighthouse, erected on the said Rock or Rocks, and of such Conllruttion as at all Times to be distinguished from any other Lighthouse, upon a moderate and 3 S reasonable

150 5* Apr ills, A. .1775.

reasonable Toll, maybe of great Advantage >'but the Petitioners apprehend it would be improper and dangerous, to veil Mr. John or any private Person whatever, with Power to levy a perpetual Tonnage; for the Lighthouse may never be erected, or, after it is erected, it may prove insignificant and ineffectual, or may be suffered to go into Decay, while the Tax on Trade remains certain, heavy, and perpetual; and no Remedy for Redref3 is left to the Petitioners, or others interested, but by tedious and expensive Law-suits against Mr. Phillips or his Heirs; and when every trading Town in the Kingdom is interested in applying for Redrel’s against any Abase that may be committed, it will probably be neglected b'y all: And therefore praying the Bill may not pals into a Law.

A Petition of the Merchants of London, and of Dublin and Liverpool now ii\ London, and others immediately interested in the Trade carried on in Saint George’s Channel, from the Port of London, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe a Petition from John Phillips before the House, praying to be enabled to erect a Lighthouse or Lighthouses on The Smalls; and that the Petitioners are well informed by the Masters of Vessels in their Employ, and others, that his Design, when executed, will be of the greatest Comfort and Safety to Trade: And therefore praying he may be enabled to carry the same into Execution.

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Council, of the Corporation of Liverpool, assembled in Council, was also presented to the House, and read; likewise Taking Notice of the Petition of the said John Phillips; and Setting forth, That, if such a Lighthouse was erected upon the said Rocks, the Petitioners are of Opinion the feme would be of great Benefit to all Ships of War, and Merchant Ships, passing by, or in Sight of,‘the said Lighthouse, and would be the Means of preserving the

i Lives of many useful Seamen: And therefore praying the House, That they will give such Encouragement to the said John Phillips, as may enable him to carry his Invention into Execution, as the House shall think proper.

jrjitto A Petition of the Masters of Vessels now in London in actual Employ, and trading in Saint George’s Channel, or well acquainted therewith, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have observed, that His Majesty has given his Consent, for perpetuating the Grant of The Smalls, to John Phillips, in order to enable him to carry his Design on that dangerous Rock or Rocks into Execution; and that the Petitioners are at a Loss to account for the Principle, which militates against that Design, as expressed in Petitions from Lancaster and Liverpool, as they never knew of any Seamen conversant in Saint George’s Channel, but wished that a Lighthouse, or Lights, may be erected on one of the said Rocks, agreeable to the Design of the said John Phillips: And therefore praying, That the said John Phillips may be enabled to carry his Design into Execution, in such Wife as shall appear meet to Parliament.
