Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: W here the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as followeth; viz.

Mr. John Hornbuckle, who has been an Alderman of

Bedford Thirty Years, being examined, your Committee found from his Evidence, that he always understood Bedford to be a Borough by Prescription; that he was present at a Common Council in September 1769, when the Corporation made 513 Freemen in One Day, none of whom were Householders of Bedford, or ever exer-tiled any Trade, or served any Office, there; that they were admitted just before the Choice of a Mayor, and acted in that Matter immediately after; that they had continued to make such Freemen every Year since, and he was certain they would go on doing so, unless some Stop is put to it, by which the Inhabitants of Bedford will entirely lose their Right of electing Members to serve in Parliament; that at the Time of making the said 513 Votes several desired to be admitted to their Freedom, thinking themselves legally entitled to it by Birth or Servitude, although they had not been reported lb entitled from the Court Leet, and were refuted; that, at the Time of making the said Votes, Fourteen of the Common Council were for it, and Ten against it; that the Members of the Common Council must be Inhabitants; that at the above Council it was objected by the Lord Recorder, ‘ that the making the said £13 ‘ Freemen was depriving every One who had a Right ‘ to his Freedom by Birth or Servitude of that Right, Children born and unborn;’ that some honorary Freemen were made in 1749; that when he came into the Corporation, they never made any body free for leis than Five Guineas and their Fees; that he often objected to the making of honorary Freemen; that the taking of Five Guineas of honorary Freemen was left off about the Year 1750, because the Corporation wanted Freemen for certain Purposes, and could not find enough to pay that Sum; that the said 513 paid One Guinea for Fees, and nothing to the Chamber; that those who are made free by Right are entitled to 'it only for their Fees; that the Guinea paid by the said 513 was divided amongst the Officers of the Corporation; that of the Freemen who claimed their Freedom and were rejected, some applied to the Jury, were reported, and afterwards admitted; that he never remembered any honorary freemen admitted without a Fine, till 1769, when the 513 were made; that he did not oppose the making of honorary Freemen, as understanding the Corporation had no Right so to do, he always deeming them possessed of frich Power.

It further appeared to your Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. John fVkitworth, Mr. Edward Wells, and Mr. Benjamin King, that they had paid Fines, besides their Fees, when they Were admitted to their Freedom; the First £. 17. 5 s. the Second £. 10. and the Last £.12.

It also appeared to your Committee, from the Evidence of Mr. Theed, who has lived in Bedford ever since the Year 1740, was Clerk to the Town Clerk there Six Years, of the Common Council in 1769, and present at the making of the said great Number of Freemen in that Year; that at the Common Hall, when they were made, the Town Clerk produced a Paper with' a Number of Names very" much confused; that he was ordered to read them over, which he did, and was challenged by the Witness with reading them wrong, which was the Fa<ft; and that he was of Opinion that they were not read right at last; that the Council Chamber is so small, that not a Quarter of those whose

Names were on that Paper could possibly be in it at that Time; that it had always been usual for Freemen to come in by Petition, and that he never ‘knew any other Way till that Lift came; that he used to write the Petitions; that they always described the Profession of the Persons, and named his Place of Abode, and were addressed to the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council; that in the Lift above mentioned, the Place of Abode was mentioned; that those who were on that Lift, and made free at that Time, were to pay 19 6

but gave £. 1. is.; that Mr. John Heaven was Mayor at that Time, and the Money was paid to him as they were lworn in; that he never saw the original Lift since, but liipposed they were entered fair in the Council Books afterwards; that in his Remembrance all honorary Freemen paid something to the Chamber Stock on their Admission, besides their Fees; that it was got as low as Three Guineas, but several paid a great deal more; that at the Council in 1769 a Question was put, whether the honorary Freemen should be made ? and carried Fourteen to Ten; that all who voted at that Time were Inhabitants of Bedford, except the Duke of Bedford, who told them they were doing wrong, for that the Intention was not to, introduce Foreigners; that he did not recollect whether the Bye-Law of the Year 1693 was mentioned then or not; that he voted against admitting the honorary Freemen, not as objecting to the Corporation’s Right to admit them, but only to the Manner of doing it j that he never knew the Number of honorary Freemen was limited, but always understood it to be at the Pleafore of the Corporation to make what Number they thought proper; that he had seen the Bye-Law of 1693, and believed it never was repealed; that before the making of the great Number of honorary Freemen in 1769, he believed such had been admitted for left than Five Guineas Fine, but never without paying something; that he did not recoiled! that any who were proposed in 1769 were rejected; that the Common Council consists of the whole Corporation, that is, the Mayor, Aldermen, Two Bailiffs, Recorder, and Common Council; that about Thirty had a Right to attend in 1769, and Twenty four or Twenty-five did; that he never knew any Man to be of the Council who was not an Inhabitant of Bedford; that in 1769, when the great Number were made free, the Names were not put singly, but all in a Lump; that he apprehended they could not be entered in a Book till some Days afterwards; that it was the Business of Mr. Hill, the Town Clerk, to enter them; that Freemen admitted by the Corporation are good Voters if they have paid to the Corporation Stock; that the Admission of the Freemen in 1769 was very different from the Admission of any other; that it was without Form; that on other Occasions they were proposed separately, and all who had not a Right used to have it by Petition; that he was not against admitting those who claimed their Freedom in 1769, but were not reported from the Court Leet; that the whole Council was fom-moned in 1769, and he never knew it otherwise; that the Notice on all Occasions is only, ‘ That there will ‘ be a Common Council,’ without Specifying the Bufi-nefe; that he is not of the Corporation now, having resigned; that the Transactions of the Corporation were always entered in a Book when he was there; that at the Time of making the honorary Freemen in 1769, the Lord Recorder laid, in his Speech, ‘ He wished the ‘ Corporation would take Care what they were about; ‘ that they had no Right to admit so extraordinary a

Number; that the Intention of making honorary Free-

men was to compliment neighbouring Gentlemen, and

if they would proceed he must take Notice of it in

another Place,’ or to that Effect; meaning, when the Town itself would not supply a sufficient Number to keep up the Credit of the Corporation, they then might

make

i5 Geo. III.

5’ — 8* Mail

make honorary Freemen: That before 1769 he believed most of the honorary Freemen were neighbouring Gentlemen; that he could not recolieft whether the Minority of the Corporation ever talked of taking Counsel’s Opinion on the Legality of that great Number of Freemen, though they wished it; nor was any Prosecution commenced against the Majority for that Act, to his Knowledge.

And your Committee further found, by the Evidence of Mr. Leech, That he had lived in Bedford since the Year 1750, and served his Apprenticeship there^ that he is not in the Corporation, but was made free on paying Five Guineas, besides his Fees, and f. 1. ioj. for a Treat; that no Common Council Man, or other Officer (except the Recorder) of the Corporation, can be elected, unless they are resident in the Borough; that'in 1769 the Corporation consisted of the following Persons; viz. a Mayor, Recorder, Thirteen Aldermen, Two Bailiffs, and Thirteen Common Council-Men; of which Number John Heaven (the Mayor), Gedny Phillips, William Parker, Senior, fViUiam Parker, Junior,

Thomas Cave, John Cave, Richard Cave, John Howard, Thomas Knight, William Palmer, William Webb, John Hill (Town Clerk) all Aldermen; William and Robert Clements (the Two Bailiffs) and Thomas Salmons, John Rcfe, William Parker, Thomas

Eagle, William Harris, and John Palmer, (Common Council Men.) voted for making the said great Number of honorary Freemen; that he was pretty certain they were present on the Monday, but not quite -sure with respect to the First Day; that at -that Time there was no Want of Freemen at -there-being then about

400, of which about 150 were resident in the Towns that he did not hear any of the Corporation declare for what Purpose the.(kid Number of honorary Freemen were made; that Freemen are appointed by the Common Hall; and that it is usual for honorary 'Freemen 4o attend the Election of Mayors,

A Petition of Thomas Howell, now a Prisoner in the Gatehouse, Westminster, by Order of the House,

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioner being examined, before a Committee of the whole House, relative to a Bill depending to incapacitate certain Persons, therein mentioned, from voting at Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, and for preventing Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, touching the Absence of Thomas Spencer and , John Beckett, Two Persons who were ordered to attend the House, did on such Examination (partly through Ignorance, and partly through Fear, the Petitioner not having been used to give Evidence before so great an Assembly) prevaricate in giving his Evidence; for which Offence he was committed to Prison; and that the Petitioner is very poor, and, if not released from his Confinement, himselfand a large Family mull soon be in a deplorable Situation, they having but the Petitioner’s daily labour to depend on; and alledging, that the Petitioner was not any Way privy to the absconding of the said Spencer and Beckett, or either of them; And therefore praying the House to take his unhappy same into Confederation, and to discharge him from his Confinement, being willing and desirous to alk Pardon at the Bar of the House for such his Offence, and sincerely promises never to offend in the like or any. other same for the future; and that the House will take his great Poverty into Consideration, and order his Discharge from the said Prison, without paying the usual Fees attending the Commitment of a Prisoner by the House, which said Fees the Petitioner is wholly unable to pay.

A Petition of William Lucas, now a Prisoner in the Prison of the Gatehouse, by Order of the House, Was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner being in London, on his own private Business, and accidentally attending at the Lobby

Vol. 35.

of the House (to hear, what wa? done with respect to the Bill now depending for the Extension of the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, and for other Purposes therein mentioned) was examined touching the Absence of Thomas Spencer and John Beckett, Two Voters of the said Borough, who were ordered to attend the House, to give Evidence relative to the said Bill; and that, on such Examination, the Petitioner did, though unintentionally, prevaricate in giving his Evidence, but informed the House all he knew concerning the said Spencer and s

Absence; and that he was not privy to, or advised them, or either of them, to abscond, nor does not now know what is become of them; and that the Petitioner, by having drawn down the Resentment of the House for such his Prevarication, hath already suffered much in his private Business and Affairs in the Country, in so much that it must be a Work of much Time and Labour to reinstate and put them again in Order; and, if his Imprisonment is further prolonged, he mtift be ruined: And therefore praying the House to grant his Enlargement from his present Confinement; and in respedh the Petitioner hath been (by his imprudent, though not wilful, Behaviour) already so great a Sufferer in his private Affairs, that the House will take the same into their serious and humane Consideration, and order his Difchirge, without Payment of Fees, he being willing and desirous to ask Pardon for such his Offenrt, at the Bar of the House, and sincerely promises never to offend in the like or any other same for the future.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

The Serjeant at Arms being called upon to give Ditto* an Account of what he had further done, in relation to the taking Thomas Spencer and John Beckett;

The Messenger, who was sent in search of thetn, informed the House that he had made a further very strict Inquiry, in order to apprehend the said Thomas Spencer and John Beckett; but that they could not yet be found.

And Richard Smith, Esquire, and Captain Fafham Nairn, attending, according to Order, were severally called in, and, at t e Bar, examined in relation to the Non-Atfendance of the said Thomas Spencer and John Beckett.

And then they were severally directed to withdraw.

The other Order of the Day being read, for the j^tto. House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Bill to incapacitate certain Persons, therein mentioned, from voting at Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, and for preventing Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Hindon in the County of Wilts;

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that, from the Absence of the said Thomas Spencer and John Beckett, Two material Witnesses in Support of the said Bill, it will not be expedient to proceed further in the said Bill in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, Nenrine contradicente. That this House will take the Report, which was made from the Select Committee who were appointed'; to try and determine the Merits of the Petition of James Callhorpe, Esquire, and Richard Beckford, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the Borough of Hindon, in the County of Wilts, into further Consideration as early as possible in the next Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That this House will not order any Warrant to be issued for a new Writ for electing Members for the said Borough of Hindon, until the House shall have proceeded to take the said Report into further Consideration.

A Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that no Trustee shall be concerned in a Contrail.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks; which being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that no Meeting shall be held unless Notice is sent to the Trustees.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to' be added to the Bill, that if a Trustee shall become a Bankrupt, or remove out of the Parish, he shall be no longer a Trustee.

And the said Clause was Twice read, with Blanks; which being filled up, the said Clause was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that One Half of the Trustees shall be elected by the Parishioners.

And the said Clause was Twice read’; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that no Victualler shall be appointed an Overseer.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

Another Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, that nothing in this, or the former Act, shall extend to a Beadle, or other Officer, appointed by the Minister or Parishioners.

And the said Clause was Twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made Part of the Bill.

A Petition of the several Potters and Dealers in Earthen Ware and Porcelain, whole Names are subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill is depending for enlarging the Term of Letters Patent, granted to William Cookworthy, of Plymouth, Chymist, for the sole Use and Exercise of a Discovery of certain Materials for making Porcelain; and that the Petitioners arc informed, that the said Letters Patent were unduly obtained by the said William Cookworthy, and were, at the Time of granting thereof, contrary to Law; and that the Petitioners are also informed, that the said William Cookworthy hath not, by an Instrument in Writing under his Hand and Seal, described and ascertained the Nature of his said Invention, and the Manner in which the same is to be performed, nor caused the same to be enrolled, within the Time, and in the Manner, directed by the said Letters Patent; and that the Petitioners apprehend that the extending the Term of the said Monopoly will be injurious to the Petitioners, and the several other Potters and Dealers in Earthen and Porcelain Wares in this Kingdom, will tend to discourage future Improvements in those Manufactures, and’ be disadvan-tagcous to the Public in general: And therefore praying, they may be heard, by themselves or their Counsel, against the said Bill.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term of Letters Patent, granted by His present Majesty, to William Cookworthy, of Plymouth, Chymist, for the lole Use and Exercise of a Discovery of certain Materials for making Porcelain, in order to enable Richard Champion, of Bristol, Merchant (to whom the said Letters Patent have been a Aligned) to carry the said Discovery into effectual Execution, for the Benefit of the Public, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Eden, according to Order, reported from the

Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be applied the Sum of Ten thousand Nine hundred and Seventy-six Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Two Pence, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, of the Monies arilen by the Duties on Rice exported, the Duties on Apples imported, and on Cambricks and Sugars, granted by an Act of the Sixth Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, the Monies paid by the Receivers General of the several Counties which have not raised the Militia, and also of such Imprest Monies as remain there for the Disposition of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Duty of Two Shillings Sterling Money be laid upon every Gallon of Rum, or Spirits, imported into the Island of Newfoundland, from any of His Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations on the Continent of America.

Vol. 35.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words " Two Shillings" and in-lerting the Words " One Shilling" instead thereof.

And the Question being put, That the Words " Two Shillings" stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " One " Shilling" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That the House do agree with the Committee in the said Resolution lb amended, That a Duty of One Shilling Sterling Money be laid upon every Gallon of Rum, or Spirits, imported into the Island of Newfoundland, from any of His Majesty’s Colonies of Plantations on the Continent of America.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the Encouragement of the Fisheries carried on from Great Britain, Ireland, and the British Dominions in Europe, and for securing the Return of the Fishermen, Sailors, and others, employed in the said Fisheries to the Ports, thereof, at the End of the Filliing Section, is committed, that they have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, pursuant to the last of the said Resolutions, as agreed to by the House.

Resolved, That this, House will, at the Riling of the Adjournment. House this Day, adjourn till Monday Morning next.

Ordered, That all Committees have Leave to fit, not- Committees* withstanding any Adjournment of the House.

A Petition and Memorial of His Majesty’s ancient Subjects, the Seigneurs, Freeholders, Merchants, Traders, and others, settled in H is Majesty’s Province of Quebec, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, under the Sanction of His Majesty’s Royal Proclamation of the 7th Day of 1 763, which

promises to all Persons inhabiting in, or rclorting to, the said Province, the Enjoyment of the Benefit of the Laws of the Realm of England, until Assemblies should be called therein, the Petitioners settled themselves in the said Province, having intruded their own Properties, as well as very considerable Sums of their Friends, in Goods and Merchandize from Great Britain, and intruded the same into the Hands of the Canadians, as well for the Purpose of internal Trade in the Province, as for Out-

17

lets in carrying on the Traffic of Furs and Peltries in the Indian Countries and Fisheries below Quebec, many of them having purchased Lands and Houses, and been employed in Agriculture, and the Exportation of Grain and other Produce to Foreign Markets, to the great Benefit and Emolument of the said Province, which has ftourished chiefly by the Industry and enterprizing Spirit of the said Subjects, who, under the Protection of British Laws, and by the Assistance of Annual Supplies of British Manufactures, and other Goods and Merchandize, obtained upon Credit from the Merchants of Great Britain, have been enabled to carry oh at Icaft Four Parts in Five of, all the Imports and Exports, which are principally made in British Bottom^ the latter consisting of Furs, Peltries, Wheat, Fish, Oil, Pot-afh, Lumber, and other Country Produce > and for the more convenient carrying on the said Trade and Commerce, they have built Wharfs Store-Houses, at a very great Expence, in lb mqplpi [that the Property, Real and Personal, now in British Hands, or by them intrusted to Canadians at a long Credit, is One Llalf of the whole Value of the Province, exclu-five of the Wealth of the different Communities, which the Petitioners have in Part set forth in their Petition to His Majesty, dated at Quebec, the 31 ft Day of December 1773, praying, that He would be graciously pleased to require His Governor or Commander in Chief to call a General Assembly, in such Manner, and of such Constitution and Form, as to His Majesty should seem best adapted to secure the Peace, Welfare, and good Government, of their Province; wherefore, with Concern, the Petitioners observe, that, in certain Examinations taken before the House, the British Subjects at Quebec have been grossly abused and misrepre-fented, as well as to their Numbers as in their Importance in the said Province, for the Numbers of the new Subjects have, the Petitioners conceive, been greatly exaggerated; it being by the last Computation about 75,000; and that, by an Enumeration of the British Subjects, they amount at this Time to upwards of 3,000 Souls, besides many, that the Petitioners cannot immediately ascertain, that are dispersed in the Indian Countries, carrying on Traffic with the Savages, besides the Merchants and Traders, with their Families, settled at Detroit and its Dependencies, and at the Fisheries below Quebec-, and that an Act has lately passed, for the making more effectual Provision for the Government of the Province of Quebec, in North America, which is laid to have been passed upon the Principles of Humanity and Justice, and at the pressing Instance and Request of the new Subjects, signified to His Majesty, by a Petition, setting forth their Dislike to the British Laws and Form of Government, and praying, in the Name of all the Inhabitants and Citizens of the Province, to have the Institutes in

their Stead, and a total Abolition of Trials by Jury, together with a Capacity of holding Places of Honour and Trust, in common with His Majesty’s ancient Subjects; and the Petitioners beg Leave to inform the House, that the said Petition was never imparted to the Inhabitants in general, that is, the Freeholders, Merchants, and Traders, who are equally alarmed with the Petitioners, at the Canadian Laws being to take Place, but was in a secret Pdanner carried about, and signed by a few of the Seigneurs, Chevaliers, Advocates, and others in their Confidence, at the Suggestions, and under the Influence, of their Priests, who, under Colour of French Laws, have obtained an Act, which deprives His Majesty’s ancient Subjects of all their Rights and Franchises, destroys the Habeas Corpus Act, and the inestimable Privilege of Trial by Juries, the only Security against the Venality of a corrupt Judge, and gives unlimited Power to the Governor and Council to alter the Criminal laws; which Act has already struck a Damp upon the Credit of the Country, and alarmed the Petitioners with the just Apprehensions of

arbitrary

"V »

i5 Geo. III.

arbitrary Fines and Imprisonment, and which, if it takes place, will oblige them to quit the Province, or in the End it rauft accompli fh their Ruin, and ithpoverish or hurt their generous Creditors, the Merchants in Great Britain, &c.; to prevent which, the Petitioned pray. That the said Act may be repealed or amended; that they may have the Benefit and Protection of the Laws, in so far as relate to Personal Property; and that their liberty may be ascertained, according to their ancient Constitutional Rights and Privileges heretofore granted to all His Majesty’s dutiful Subjects through-out the Britt fh Empire.

The House was moved, that an Act, made in the Fourteenth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for making more effectual Provision " for the Government of the Province of Quebec, in " North America," might be read.

And the same was read accordingly.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to repeal the said Act;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Mr. Speaker,

" turns of Members to serve in Parliament," that there was the moll notorious Bribery anti Corruption at the last Election of Members to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough: This, the House of Commons were of Opinion, required the moll ferrous Consideration of Parliament; but, as it appeared to them too late to proceed in this Consideration in the present Session, and highly expedient to proceed as early as possible in the next, the House of Commons thought it essentially necessary, that, until they Ihoukl have an Opportunity of making a further Enquiry into that Matter, no Election for that Borough should , eventually take place, which might in any Manner afied that Enquiry, or prevent the Parliament from taking such effectual Measures for discouraging Bribery and Corruption in the Election of Members of the House of Commons, as upon mature Deliberation should seem moll proper.

After which* His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth, biz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot, in Justice to you, forbear to express My Hi> Majkiy* entire Satisfaction in your Condu.dl, during the Course Speeth* of this important Session.

You have maintained, with a firm and steady Refb-lution, the Rights of My Crown, and the Authority of Parliament, which I shall ever consider as inseparable t You have protedled and promoted the Commercial Interests of My Kingdoms; and you have* at the same Time, given convincing Proofs of your Readiness (as far as the Constitution will allow you) to gratify the Wishes, and remove the Apprehensions, of My Subjedb in America; and I am persuaded, that the most salutary Effects must, in the End, result from Measures formed dnd conduced on such Principles*

The late Mark of your affectionate Attachment to Me, and to the Queen, and the Zeal and Unanimity which accompanied it, demand My particular Thanks.

I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that, as well from the general Dispositions of other Powers, as from the solemn Assurances which I have received, I have great Reason to expect the Continuance of Peace 2 Nothing on My Part, consistent with the Maintenance of the Honour and Interest of My Kingdoms, shall be wanting to secure the Public Tranquillity.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

It gives Me much Concern, that the unhappy Dif-turbanoes in some of My Colonies have obliged Me to propose to you an Augmentation of My Army, and have prevented Me from completing the intended Reduction of the Establishment of My Naval Forces. I cannot sufficiently thank you for the Cheerfolness and public 'Spirit with which you have granted the Supplies for the several Services of the current Year.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have nothing to desire of you, but to use your best Endeavours to preserve and to cultivate, in your several Counties, the same Regard for public Order, and the same Discernment of their true Interests, which have in these Times distinguished the Character of My faithful and beloved People; and the Continuance of which cannot fail to render them happy at Home, and respected Abroad.

After which, the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said j

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this £arI,amu^ Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the 27th Day of roro*uc July next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 27 th Day of -July next.

They have raised Troops, and are collecting a Naval Force, they have seized the Public Revenue, and affomed to themfehres Legislative, Executive, and J udicial Powers, which they already exercise in the most arbitrary Manner, over the Persons and Properties of their Fellow Subjects; and although many of these unhappy Peopfe may still retain their Loyalty, and may be too wile not td fee the fatal Consequence of this UluTpation, and wish to resist it, yet the Torrent of Violence has been strong enough to compel their Acquiescence, till a sufficient Force shall appear to support them.

The Authors and Promoters of this delj>erate Conspiracy have, in the Conduct of it, derived great Advantage from the Difference of our Intentions and theirs; they meant only to amuse by vague Expressions of Attachment to the Parent State, and the strongest Protestations of Loyalty to Me, whilil they were preparing for a General Revolt: On Our Part, though it was declared in your last Session that a Rebellion existed within the Province of the Majjathufet's Bay, yet even that Province We vfifired rather to reclaim than toiubdue; the RefoUtions of Parliament breathed a Spirit of Mod era-51 tion

The rebellious War now levied, is become more general, and is manifedly carried on for the Purpose of edab-lishing an independent Empire: I need not dwell upon the fatal Effects or the Success of such a Plan; the Object is too important, the Spirit of the British Nation too high, the Retources, with which God hath blessed her, too numerous, to give up so many Colonies, which die has planted with great Industry, nursed with- great Tendernefe, encouraged with, many commercial Advantages, and protested and defended at much Expence of Blood and Treasure.

It is now become the Part of Wifoom, and (in its Effects) of Clemency, to put a speedy End to these Dif-orders by the most decisive Exertions: For this Purpose I have increased My Naval Establishment, and greatly augmented My Land Forces, but in such a Manner as may be the lead burthensome to My Kingdoms.

I have also the Satisfaction to inform you, that I have received the most friendly Offers of Foreign Affidance; and if I shall make any Treaties in consequencp thereof, they shall be laid before you: And I have, in Tedimony of My Affection for My People, who can have no Cause in which I am not equally intereded, sent to the Garrisons of Gibraltar and Port Mahon a Part of My Electoral TrOops, in order that a larger Number of the Edablished Forces of this Kingdom may be applied to the Maintenance of its Authority; and the National Militia, planned and regulated with equal Regard to the Rights, Safety, and Protection, of My Crown and People,' may give a farther Extent and Activity to Our Military Operations.

When the unhappy and deluded ^Multitude, against whom this Force will be directed, shall become sensible of their Error, I shall be ready to receive the Milled with Tendernels and Mercy: And in order to prevent the Inconveniences which may arise from the great Didance of their Situation, and to remove as soon as possible the Calamities which they differ, I shall give Authority to certain Persons upon the Spot to grant general or particular Pardons and Indemnities, in such Manner, and to such Persons, as they shall tjirnk fit, and to receive the Submission of any Province or Colony which shall be disposed to return to its Allegiance: It may be also proper to authorize the Persons so. commissioned to redore such Province or Colony, so returning to its Allegiance, to the free Exercise of its Trade and Commerce, and to the same Protection and Security as ifr such Province or Colony had never revolted.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Edimates for the ensuing Year to be laid before you; and I rely on your Affection to Me, and your Resolution to maintain the jud Rights of this Country, for such Supplies as the present Circumdances of Our Affairs require: Among the many unavoidable ill Gonsequences of this Rebellion, none affects Me more sensibly than the extraordinary Burthen which it mud create to My faithful Subjects.

A Motion was made, and the: Question being pr<3-» posed, That an humble Address be presented to His Ma- ... -r jedy, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne:

To assure His Majesty, that we have long lamented the Condition of our unhappy Fellow Subjects in America; seduced from their Allegiance by the grossed Mif-representations, and the most wicked and insidious Pretences, they have been made the Indruments of the Ambition and traiterous Deligns of those dangerous Men, who have led them Step by Step to the Standard of Rebellion, and who have now assumed the Powers of Sovereign Authority, which they exercise in the most despotic and arbitrary Manner, over the Persons and Properties of this deluded People:

To declare, that His Majesty’s faithful Commons took a sincere Part in His Majesty’s benevolent and paternal Desire, rather to reclaim, than to (ubdue, the most refractory of His Colonies; and that, excited by His Majesty’s great Example, we were anxious to prevent, if it had been possible, the Effusion of the Blood of our Fellow Subjects, and the Calamities which are inseparable from a State of War; we dill hoped that his Majesty’s People in America would have discerned the traiterous Views of their Leaders, would have considered how ruinous even their Success mud be to themselves, and been convinced that Conditional Subjection to Great Britain is the freed and happied Condition of any Civil Society in the known World: But we now fee with Indignation, that no other Use has been made of the Moderation and Forbearance of His Majesty, and His Parliament, but to drengthen the Preparations of this desperate ConspiraGy; and that the rebellious War now levied is become mora general, and manifedly carried on for the Purpose of establishing an independent Empire:

To assure His Majesty, that we entirely concur with His Majesty, in thinking it is now become the Part of Wisdom, and (in its Effects) of Clemency, to put a speedy End to these Disorders, by the most decisive Exertions; and that we learn with the greated Satisfaction, that for this Purpose, His Majesty has increased His Naval Eda-blidiment, and greatly augmented His Land Forces, in such a Manner as may be the lead burthensome to His Kingdoms: And that we will'chearfully and effectually support His Majesty in such necessary Measures; and enable His Majesty, when the Occasion shall require it; to avail Himself of the friendly Offers, which His Majesty has received, of Foreign Affidance: That we thankfully acknowledge the gracious Gonsiderations, which induced ’His Majesty to fend a Part of His Elect-toral Troops to the Garrisons of Gibraltar and Port Mahony in order that a larger Number of the Edablished Forces of this Kingdom might be applied to the Maintenance of its Authority; and that we arc bound in Duty to return His Majesty our particular Thanks, for pointing out to us, from the Throne, the Condi tutional Resource of our well-modeled and well-regulated National Militia; which upon every great Emergency, cannot fail of affording Security to His Majesty’s Realm, and-of giving, at the same Time, Extent and Activity to His Military Operations: '

" We are satisfied by Experience, that this Misfortune has in a great Measure arisen from the want of " full and proper Information being laid before Parliament, of the true State and Condition of the Colonies, by Reason of which, Measures have been carried into Execution injudicious and inefficacious, from " which no salutary End was reasonably to be expected, and which necessarily tended to tamish the Ludre of " the British Arms, to bring Discredit on the Wisdom

of His Majesty’s Councils, and to nourish without " Hope of End, a most dangerous Civil War.

Halifax, Nova Scotia, July 4th, 1775.

Sir,

I am directed by the House of Assembly of this Province, to inclose you this Address, Petition, and, Memorial, today before the House of Commons.

I have the Honour to be. Sir,

Your most obedient, and Most devoted

Humble Servant,

IVn Nesbitt, Speaker*

The Right HonMe Sir Fletcher Norton, Knight, Speaker of the House of Commons of Great Britain.

To the King’s most Excellent Majesty, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled.

The Address, Petition, and Memorial, of the Representatives of the Freeholders of the Province of Nova Scotia, in General Assembly.

Your loyal and ever dutiful1' House of Assembly of the Province of Nova Scotia, most humbly beg Leave to address our Gracious Sovereign, and both Houses of Parliament, at this dreadful ana alarming Crisis, when Civil Discord, and its melancholy Consequences, are impending over all British America:

Actuated by the warmest Ties of Duty and Affection to the Person and Family of our most Gracious Sovereign; animated with the firmest Attachment to the Mother Country; zealous to support her Power and Consequence over all the Britif Dominions, and dreading a Separation from her Government and Protection as the greatest Political Evil which can befal us or our Posterity. -:

Influenced by the Principles of Humanity, and the just Rights of Mankind in Civil Society, we tremble at the gloomy Prospect before us; we feel for our Gracious King; we feel for our Mother Country, of which many of us are Natives; we feel for the British American Race, once the most loyal, virtuous, and happy, of M.affkind: Animated with such Principles, may. we not approach the -Supreme Legislature of the Empire ?- And,

as dutiful Children of just and indulgent Parents,* may we not most humbly solicit for such Regulations, as we conceive most likely to preserve the Inhabitants of this Province in Duty and Allegiance to our King, in rendering permanent their Connexion with, and Dependance on, the Supreme Legislature of Great Britain, and preferring inviolably to us and our Posterity, the just Rights of Men in Civil Society ?

We are fully sensible, that we have no Right to pray for Redress of Grievances, to request Privileges or Regulations, unless we acknowledge Y’our Right over us: Therefore, we the Representatives of the Freeholders of the Province of Nova Scotia, do Unanimously most humbly acknowledge our Gracious Sovereign, George the Third, King of Great Britain, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Commons of Britain, in Parliament assessibled, to be the Supreme Legislature of this Province, and of all the British Dominions; and that it is our indispensable Duty to pay a due Proportion of the Expence of this Great Empire.

Having thus, as obedient Subjects, acknowledged our Duty to our King, and our willing Submission to the Supreme Legislature of the British Empire, we humbly request the Right of being heard, in respect to our Grievances or Withes; and as our Proceedings in this Assembly may possibly have tome Influence with other Assemblies in America, we humbly hope if will not seem presuming if we enter on the Subject.

We humbly conceive it will be necessary to the Peace and Happiness of the British Empire, That the Tax to be raised in the Colonies, and which shall: be at the Dilpolal of the British Parliament, and the Proportion

N«ra Scotia. Office, and the Number of His Deputies must be excessive; and whose Power in Ek&ions is absolute. If we are not relieved in this Particular, we can have no Pretensions even to the Name of Freemen.

We humbly pray, That Your Majesty will graciously permit, and order, that a Recorder of Deeds and Conveyances be appointed in each and every County, and not a Deputy to a Principal residing elsewhere.

Our Gracious King cannot be insensible of the great Necessity there is, that the 'most respectable Persons in the Community be appointed to the Commissions of the Peace; Legal Authority, unless aided by the good Opinion of the People, can have but little: Probably the Reason why the most relpe&able Persons

decline the Office, is, because they are liable to be dismissed unheard. The Want of Power in the Magistrates to execute, or enforce the Laws, has been a general Complaint in America.

We humbly pray, That the Governor, Council, and Judges, of the Supreme Court, may constitute a Court of Vice Admiralty throughout the Province, to determine all Causes cognizable in such Courts, agreeable to Law and Equity, and to receive no Fees therefor.

We humbly pray, That any Two or more of the Judges of the Supreme Court, and a Jury ballotted for and struck by the Parties, shall constitute a Court of Equity, in all Civil Cafes throughout this Province, subject only to Appeals to His Majesty in Council, where the Property contested may amount to Five hundred Pounds Sterling, or upwards.

We humbly pray to be delivered from the Oppression of Practitioners in the Law, and pray, That in all Civil Actions, their Fees, Charges, and Perquisites may be limited to Five per Cent, on all Sums declared for, or defended. It is not the Desire of our Good King to have His quiet and inoffensive Subjects in this Quarter of the Globe, given up to be persecuted by a few rapacious Men.

Most Benign King, Your Majesty was graciously pleased to grant Tracts of Land in this Province upon various Conditions of Settlement, and Payment of Quit Rents; many of the Conditions of Settlement were impracticable, and others so expensive, that the Grantees were not able folly to effect: them: We humbly pray to be exonerated from those feve.re Conditions, and that You will graciously limit the Power of the Court of Escheats to Defaults in the Payment of the Quit Rent only.

This House is forty to observe. That most cruel Use has- been made or this Power of efeheating Land, even to the depriving of Two Old Officers of the Gratuity given them by Your Majesty, for near Forty Years of Military Service, and that to gratify Two Domestics of that Governor who ordered the Escheat-ment; and at this Time a Tract of Land is advertised to be escheated, on which the Proprietors have laid -out near Four thousand Pounds.

Finally, we most humbly request, That the Aflem-bfy of this Province may be called together annually, and that no Governor may be allowed to diflfolve or prorogue them when he shall be informed that they are preparing a Petition to our Gracious King, and Parliament, of Great Britain.

Most Gracious Sovereign, We have unhappily experienced, that the Redress of our Grievances, and those requested Regulations, could not come from us in the Constitutional Mode of Laws, which must have passed a Council, fbme of them without Property in the 'Province, or Interest in our Welfare.

May the God of all Goodnefc ftiower down on our Gracious Sovereign, and His beloved Family, every Temporal Blessing!

May the Spirit of Concord, Justice, and Public ' Virtue, direct the Councils of the British Senate; and may the Father of Mercies preserve Constitutional 20

Freedom to the British Race in every Part of the Globe!

Halifax, Wm Speaker.

June 24th, 1775.

Usual Orders. Ordered, That all Persons who will question any Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, do question the same within Fourteen Days next, and so within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in; and that all Members who are returned for Two or more Places, do make their Election by this Day Three Weeks for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be no Question upon the Return for that Place 5 and if any Thing shall come in Question touching the Return or Election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate; and that all Members returned upon Double Returns do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where this House flpall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the \itmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving 1 Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great tain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time to be appointed by the House, deliver to the 'Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the feme against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the feme Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Behalf of themselves and others, the Electors of the Borough of Cricklade, in the County of Wilts ,was also read; Setting forth. That, at the late Election of a Representative to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the Doom of Samuel Peach and John Dewar, Esquires, John Dewar, Samuel Peach, and Samuel Petrie, Esquires, were Candidates; and that Thomas Carter, a known Friend of the said Mr. Peach, and under the Direction of his Agents, prelided as Bailiff and Returning Officer of the said Borough, to which Office the said Carter was appointed by Arnold Nesbitt, Esquire, the Lord of the Hundred or Manor of Cricklade, and Friend to the said Mr. Peach, and the Person who introduced the said Mr. Peach as a Candidate for the said Borough; and that the Petitioners, and many others duly qualified, as well by the general Laws and Customs of the Land, as by the particular Usage and Constitution of the said Borough, offered to give their Voices for the said John Dewar, Esquire, but were rejected by the said Returning Officer, who, under the Directions of the Agents of the said Mr. Peach, took upon himself arbitrarily and illegally to return the said Samuel Peach, although the said John Dewar, Esquire, had a large Majority of unquestionable legal Votes for the said Borough; and that the said Returning Officer did likewise partially admit many Votes for the said Mr. Peach, which stood precisely in the same Predicament with many which he rejected when offered for Mr. Dewar: and did1 likewise admit many Persons to vote for Mr. Peach, whom he ought not to have admitted, several of whom were the immediate and avowed Agents of Mr. Peach, having no Connexion whatever with the said Borough, but who, under fraudulent and colourable Conveyances, were admitted to vote, to the great Injury of the Rights and Franchises of the Petitioners and others the Electors of the said Borough; and that, by these and other undue, corrupt, and illegal Practices, the said Samuel Peach, Esquire, did procure himself to be returned a Representative to Parliament, in manifest Injury to the Rights of the Electors, and in open Violation of the Law and Constitution of Parliament: And therefore praying, that the Freedom of Election may be restored, and that the said Mr. Dewar may be received as duly elected; and that the House will grant them such other Relief and Redress as they shall thmk meet.

Malden A Petition of the Right honourable Drigue Lord Ejection.- IValt ham of the Kingdom of Ireland, was read; Setting forth, That, at the late Election for the Borough of Malden, iti the County of Essex, the Honourable Richard Savage Nassau, John Strutt, Esquire, and the Petitioner, were Candidates; and upon the Poll the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned to serve the said Borough in Parliament; and that the said Mr. Nassau, Mr. Strutt, and their Agents, or some of them, by and with their or One of their Di-redtions and Privity, previous to the said Election, and during the Poll, were guilty of Bribery and Corruption, and attempting to bribe and corrupt those who had a Right to vote in the said Election, and made use of Threats and Intimidations, in order to procure the said Mr. Nassau and Mr. Strutt to be elected to serve the said Borough in Parliament; and that, by Means of the great Mobs, Riots, and Disturbances, at the said Election, many Persons who had a Right to vote, were deterred and prevented from polling for the Petitioner; and that the Person who acted as Deputy to the Returning Officer of the said Borough, to take the Poll, before and during the said Poll, was guilty of great Partiality and Unfairness, in rejecting good Votes for the Petitioner, and admitting Persons not qualified to vote for the said Mr. Nassau and Mr. Strutt, and by entering many Votes for the said Mr. Nassau and Mr. Strutt who voted for the Petitioner; and that, by these and other corrupt, undue, illegal, and unwarrantable, Practices, many Persons voted for the said Mr. Nassau and Mr. Strutt, who would otherwise have voted for the Petitioner; and the said, Mr. Najj'au and Mr. Strutt were unduly returned as Burgefle$ for the said Borough, in Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in open Violation of the Rights of the said Borough, and the Freedom of Election; And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioner such Relief as to the House shall seem just.!

Southampton A Petition of many of the Inhabitants of the Town EJc&ion. of SoutHampton, having a Right to vote at the Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Town, on Behalf of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, though the Regulation and Government of the said Town is in the Mayor and Corporation, yet the Right of Election, or choosing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Town, is vested in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot; and that the Honourable Charles , commonly called Lord Charles , the Right honourable Hans Stanley, and John , Esquire, offered

themselves Candidates, at the lad Election of Burgesses, to represent the said Town in Parliament, and Mr. Stanley znA Mr. Fleming were returned as duly elected; and that, though the Town of Southampton is governed by a Mayor, Bailiffs, and Burgesses, and has a Sheriff* 01 its own, and the Sheriff of or County of

Southampton, has no Office to execute within the said Town, yet it has been usual, Time immemorial, for Persons having Freeholds there, to vote, in Right of such Freeholds, for Knights of the Shire, or County at large; and one Battalion of the Militia of or County at large, is annually trained and exercised within the Town of So which seem to imply that the said Town is (till a Part of the County at large, and not totally distinct or independent of the lame; and that the said Mi. Flemings when he offered himself a Candidate, and at the Time he was returned as a Burgess to represent the said Town in Parliament, was Sheriff of Hampshire, or the County of Southampton; and the Petitioners are informed, that all Sheriffs are difebled from being elected, not only by an ancient Resolution of the House, but by the express Letter of His Majesty’s Writ or Summons, directed to the Sheriffs, in which, the Petitioners observe, are the following remarkable Words, " Willing neverthelefe, that " neither you, nor any other Sheriff of this our said " Kingdom, be in any wise electedThe Petitioners H

therefore think themselves much aggrieved, and apprehend that the said Election and Return, so far as respects the said Mr. Fleming, is an undue Election and Return, and (latter themselves that the same will be deemed by the -House null and void; and hope that the Honourable Charles Montagu, commonly called Lord Charles Montagu, will be permitted to fit in the House,

as one of the Burgesses for the said Town of Southampton, in the room of the (kid Mr. FlemingAnd therefore praying, That they may be heard by their Counsel, and have such other Relief in the Premises as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Cois-sideration upon Friday the 9th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and 11th Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cates, were lent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their.

Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or -Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

Sir Charles Whitworth, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it Was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty j the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Tabic: Where the same were read, and are as followed!; viz*

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Number of Land Forces, including Three thousand Two hundred and Thirteen Invalids, amounting to Twenty thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-two effective Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included, be employed for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred Fifty-nine thousand Two hundred Pounds Two Shillings and Ten Pence and Seven-eighth Parts of a Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Twenty thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-two effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other His Majesty’s Land Forces, in Great Britain, Jersey, and Guernsey, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred Twenty-three thousand Four hundred and Thirty-two Pounds Eleven Shillings and Seven Pence Three Farthings, be granted to His Majesty, for maintaining His Majesty's Forces and Garrisons, in the Plantations and Africa, including those in Garrison at Minorca and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Forces in North America, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, Gibraltar, the Ceded Islands, and Africa, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-two thousand Five hundred and Thirty Pounds Nineteen Shillings and Four Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the Difference of Pay between the Brt~ tish and Irish Establishment of One Regiment of Light Dragoons and Six Regiments of Foot, serving in North America, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Eleven thousand Five hundred and Five Pounds Seven Shillings and Three Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for the Pay of the General and General Staff Officers in Great Britain, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One hundred and Four thousand One hundred and Thirty-six Pounds and Six Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Levy Money, for the Augmentation to His Majesty’s British and Irish Forces, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six*

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Fifteen thousand and Seventy-two Pounds and Twelve Shillings, be granted to His Majesty (out of the Monies, or Savings, remaining of the Grants in the last Session of Parliament, for j8

the Charge of art Augmentation to His Majesty’s Forces, and for the Charge of Levy Money for the Augmentation to Major General Preston's Regiment of Light Dragoons) towards defraying the Charge of Levy Money for the Augmentation to His Majesty’s British and Irish Forces, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy fix.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty-six thousand Seven hundred and Eighty-three Pounds Fifteen Shillings and Two Pence Halfpenny, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Five Hanoverian Battalions of Foot, at Gibraltar and Minorca, from the First Day of September One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five, to the Twenty-fourth £)ay of December following, both inclusive, being One hundred and Fifteen Days.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum not exceeding Forty-six thousand Eight hundred and Thirty-eight Pounds One« Shilling and Nine Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Five Hanoverian Battalions of Foot, at Gibraltar and Minorca, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six*

Resolved, That it is the Opirlioh Of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred and Forty nine thousand Six hundred and Fifty*five Pounds Eighteen Shillings and Six Penjcc, be granted to His Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six.

Resolved, That it is' tile Opinion Of this Cortimittee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Twenty-three thousand One hundred Seventy*one ’ Pounds Eleven Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Expence of Services performed by the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, and not provided for by Parliament, in One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-five*

The Five First Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Sixth Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time, an Amendment was proposed to be made thereto by leaving out the Words ^One hundred and Four thousand One hundred and Thirty-six Pounds and Six Shillings," and inferring the Words Eighty-nine thousand and Sixty-three Pounds Fourteen Shillings,0 instead thereof;

And the Question being put. That the= W'ords One hundred and Four thousand One hundred and Thirty-six Pounds and Six Shillings" stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Words Eighty-nine thousand and Sixty-three Pounds Fourteen Shillings" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, That a Sunij not exceeding Eighty-nine thousand and Sixty-three Pounds Fourteen Shillings, be granted to His Majesty, for defraying the Charge of Levy Money, for the Augmentation to His Majesty’s British and Irish Forces, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Seventy-six*

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of Sir Alexander Gilmour, Baronet, was read $ Stirling Setting forth. That, at the last Election of a Member Ele&iqo. to serve in Parliament for the District of Boroughs of Stirling, Inverkeithing, Dumfermline, Culrofs, and ferry, held at Dumfermline, the presiding Borough, ora Monday the 31st Day of October 1774, the Petitioner and Archibald Campbell, Esquire, were Candidates; and that Commissioners attended from all the Boroughs of the District, and produced their Commissions; and that, besides the said Commissioners, John Wilson, Junior, the Commissioner" duly elected for the Borouglx of Dumfermline, Sebastian Swinton, Senior, the Commissioner duly elected for the Borough of 9

and James Bunkell, pretending to be Commissioner for the Borough of Queensferry, attended at the said Election, and claimed to vote for the Member of Parliament; and that the Commissioners for the Boroughs of Stirling and Queensferry, and John fVilfon and SebaJHart Swinton, Senior, the Commissioners duly elected for the Boroughs of Dumfermline and Inverkeithing, voted, for the Petitioner; and the pretended Commissioners for the other Boroughs, together with the said James Bunkell, voted for the said Archibald Campbell, and He is returned by the Sheriff, in wrong to the Petitioner, who had the Majority of legal Votes; and that the Election of the said Archibald Campbell was brought about by Bribery, Corruption, and undue Influence, and is liable to sundry other Objections, whereby He is rendered incapable of fitting in Parliament; And therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant him such Relief as shall appear just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 13 th Day of Febrmry next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts-, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were lent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read. And,

Mr. Thomas Hart., the Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, laid. That there is now due upon the Credit of the said Act, the Sum of 10,75©, together with ah An ear of Interest of Two Years and an Half, at £ 4 PerCent, which Money has been duly applied in the Repair of the Roads.

That the Term of the said Act is near expiring; and that unless it is further continued, and the Tolls increased, and some further Powers and Authorities given to the Trustees, the present Debt cannot be paid off, and the Roads kept in Repair.

And the Witness further aid. That the Payment of the Tolls have been frequently evaded, and that in order to prevent the same for the future, it will be necessary to shut up a Lane called Gravel Lane, in the Parish of Leatherhead, and also occasionally to shut up a Lane called Parsonage , in the said Parish, and that the Shutting up the said Lanes will be no Inconvenience to the Public.

That the Tolls will be better, and more easily collected, if Power was given to remove the present Side Gate in the Parish of in to the End

of a Lane called Friday Street, near the present Turnpike Road.

That the Trustees propose, for the better Accommodation of Travellers, to shorten the Road in the Parish of Warnham, by making the same in a more direct Line

Standing Mr. Frederick Montagu reported from the Committee, Order*. who were appointed to take into Consideration the Standing Orders of this House, relating to Private Bills, which were made in the last Session of the last Parliament, and to re]x>rt the lame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; That the Committee had considered the same accordingly, and had come to federal Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and, he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee find, that the said Orders relate principally to previous Notices to be given in the re-ipeftive Counties, of Applications intended to be made to this House, for Bills for inclosing, draining, or improving Lands or Commons; Bills for making navigable Canals, or for making or improving the Navigation of Rivers; and to Bills for making Turnpike Roads, or for the Renewal or Alteration of any Act of Parliament passed for that Purpose.

Your Committee fee great Utility to arise from previous Notices to be given in the Country, of such in-, tended Applications, in order that Persons interested may have an Opportunity at their Leisure of examining into the Propriety of, and Advantages to be derived from such Bills, and may come prepared to offer their Objections or Amendments.

Many Members of your Committee cannot but remember the great Inconveniencies which were felt, and much complained of, before the making of these Orders; Persons residing at a Distance had their Estates cut thropgh by a Canal, or were put to great Expences lor an Inclosure, almost without any Notice at all, or at least too late to have an Opportunity of considering the Proposition maturely, and of laying their Observations upon such Bills before Parliament with Effect; and for thele Reaions, your Committee have been of Opinion, that the said Orders are highly necessary, and ought to be strictly observed.

Your Committee beg Leave to suggest to the House, that if the Resolutions agreed to by-them should be adopted by the House, it would be expedient that printed Copies of such Orders should be lent to the Sheriffs and Clerks of the Peace of the respective Counties, and to the Mayors and Bailiffs of Cities and Towns, to be published by them for the Information of Persons intending hereafter to make such Applications.

Upon the Whole, your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the 25 th Day of April 1774, "That, after this Session of Parliament, before any Petition is presented to this " House, for inclosing, draining, or improving any " Lands, Fens, or Commons, a printed or written " Notice of such intended Application to Parliament be " affixed on the Church Door of the Parish, or Parishes, " in which such Lands, Fens, and Commons do lie, " for Three Sundays in the Months of and Sep-

" tember, or either of them, immediately preceding the " Session of Parliament in which such Petition is to be " presented," be adhered to.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the said 25th Day of April 1774, " That after this Session of Parliament, in all Bills for inclosing Lands or Commons, " the Names of the Commissioners proposed to be " appointed, and the Compensations intended for the M Lord of the Manor and the Owners of Tythes, in " lieu of their respective Rights, where any Bargains f‘ or Agreements have been made for such Compenla-Vot. 35.

" tions, be inserted in the Copy of the Bill presented to " the House; and that all Copies of such Bills, whether " printed or written, which shall be font to an of the " Persons interested in the said Manor, Tythes, Lands, " or Commons, for their Consent, do contain the Namh " of such proposed Commissioners, and also such. intended Compensations," be adhered to.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the said 2 5 th Day of April 1774, " That, after this Session of Parliament, before any Petition is presented to this House,

" for making a Turnpike Road, or for the Renewal or " Alteration of any Act of Parliament passed for that " Purpose, Notice of such intended Application to " Parliament be given, at the General Quarter Sessions " of the Peace, which shall be held for every arid each " County or District through which such Road palles,

" or is intended to pals, it the Michaelmas immediately " preceding the Session of Parliament in which such.

" Petition is to be presented," be adhered to.

County, Three Times at least, in the " Months of August and September, or either of them,

" immediately preceding the Session of Parliament irx " which such Petition is to be presented," be adhered to.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Standing Order of the House, of the said 2.5 th Day of April 1774, " That after this Session of Parliament, when any Petition is presented to this Hocafe, " for making a Navigable Canal, or for making or irnproving the Navigation of a River, or for altering any Act of Parliament passed for either of those Purposes, " thorebe presented with such Petition a Plan describing the Line of such intended Canal or Navigation, " and the Lands through which the same is to be carried; and that previous Application be made to the " Owners and Occupiers of such Lands, for their ^VlTent " to the proposed Canal or Navigation; and that £eparate Lists of the Names of such Owners and Occu-. A Petition of Sir John Glynne, Baronet, Lord of the Manor of Haivarden, in the County of the Reverend Stephen Glynne, Rector of the Parish and Parish Church of Hawarden, and several others. Freeholders and Proprietors of Lands in the said Lordship and Parish, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, from which they claim a Right of Commoning on a certain Common called Saltney Marsh, within the said Lordship and Pari fh, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the said Common contains about 2,000 Acres of rich Padure Land; and that, by an Act of the Sixth Year of his late Majesty, to recover and preserve the Navigation of the River. Dee, in the County Palatine of Chester, the Undertakers therein named did, by vir-20

tue of the Powers thereby granted, cause the said Channel to be turned through the Middle of the said Marsh, and made the said River navigable through the same; in consequence whereof, and for want ot proper Sea Banks and Fences being made, the then Commissioners were apprehendve that the said Common, on the South Side the said River, would in Time be walked away, and therefore came to an Agreement with the said River Dee Company for their supporting the said Banks, which Agreement was confirmed by an Act of the 17th Year of his said late Majesty; and, that other Disputes afterwards arising between the Petitioners and the said Company, they entered into Articles of Agreement, which were confirmed by an Act of the 26th Year of his said late Majesty, that, for and in Consideration of the Sum of £. 600 to be paid them by the Proprietors of the said Navigation, the Petitioners were impowered to make a Sea Bank on the South Side the said River, to preserve the said Common, on the South Side thereof, from being destroyed by the Flux and Reflux of the Tides} and there was also to be paid £. 50 a Year for ever, to support and maintain the said Bank -, all which the said Petitioners, at that Time, thought might be sufficient for those Purpafcs; and that the Petitioners did not only carry on the said Bank, according to the Directions of the said Act, but have at a considerable Expence extended the same further, and have applied the said £. 50 a Year for the Repairs of the fame, as directed by the said Act; all which the Petitioners find is ineffectual for preservirsg the said Mar(h Land; for, so long as the same lies open and uninclosed, it will not be possible so prevent its being entirely wasted and de (troyed, which will be not only a very great Loss to the Petitioners, but to the Public in general: and therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for inclosing the said Common, and dividing the same amongst the several Persons having a Right of Common thereon, agreeable to their respective Intereds therein, and for effectually securing the same irom the Depredations of the said River.

THE Hour appointed for taking into Considera- Peterborough tion the Petition of James Phipps, of the City Eleaioe. of Peterborough, in the County of Northampton, Esquire, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Matthew Wyldbore, Esquire, for the said City, being come;

The House proceeded to the Appointment of a Select Committee, to try and determine the Merits of the said Petition.

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members- on the Business of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 126 Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar,

And the Door of the House being locked, the Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

And the same being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six GlafTes, and were then drawn by the Clerk, in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House

And the Names of Fifteen Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Elwes, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Petitioner, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Thirty-four other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not ohjc&ed to.

Note, That in the Course of drawing the said Names, the Names of Seven other Members, then present, were drawn, and set aside, with the Names of those who were absent from the House; One, on account of his being Sixty Years of Age, or upwards, which he had before verified on Oath; One, on account of his Return to serve in Parliament not having been brought in Fourteen Days; Three, on account of their being Members against whose Returns Petitions were depending; and Two, on account of their then serving on a Select Committee, for trying the Merits of a controverted JEieftion.

And the whole Number of Forty-nine Members, so drawn as aforesaid, and not excused or set aside, being complete; the Counsel for the Sitting Member nominated Lord John Cavendish to serve on the said Select Committee.

And Lists of the said Forty-nine Names were delivered by the Clerk, to the said Counsel.:

And the Door of the House being opened;

The Counsel and Agents ort both Sides withdrew.

Staffordshireand Worcestershire Canal Navigation, already made between the Rivers Severn and Trent, at or near Stourton, in the said County of Stafford) in which, and other considerable Estates adjoining thereto, are contained very valuable Mines of Coal and Iron-Hone, and where Fire Engines and Gins have been erected, Pits lunk, and all necessary Means used, at a very great Expence, in order to get the said Mines for the Accommodation of the Public, as well as with a View to private Profit; and that, if the above-mentioned Branch of the proposed Canal should end at Black Delph, the Petitioners Hand upon very unequal Ground with their Neighbours, through or near to whose Lands the said Branch is meant to pass, and the Public will be debarred the Privilege of a Conveyance by Water from their Mines; and that, in and about the Town of Dudley, large Quantities of heavy Iron Goods are manufactured, and an extensive Trade in Glass and various Kinds of Merchandize carried on; and that, from Levels taken from Black Delph, it appears that the said intended Branch may easily be continued into the Estate of Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire: And therefore praying, That the Branch which is to be made to Black Delph may be extended into the Estate of the said Thomas Talbot Foley, Esquire, at Netherton, near Dudley aforesaid, according to the Plan annexed to the Petition, with such Provisions, and upon such Terms, as to the House shall seem meet.
