And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners, during the present Year, have suffered very great Inconvenience and Loss, in carrying on their Trade and Fisheries at Newfoundland and Places adjacent, by their usual Rclource of Bread, Flour, and other Necessaries, being totaly interrupted, by the unhappy Differences between Great Britain and her American Colonies; and that, although the present Price of Corn leaves the Exportation of Bread and Flour entirely open, and seems to make this Application unnecessary, yet as the Price of both may advance, so that the Prohibition may again take Place, the Petitioners may thereby sustain much Loss and Di(appointment in their Business, unless a timely and proper Relief is provided by the House, in case of such Exigency; and that, as the Quantity of Bread, Flour, Pease, and other Provisions, allowed to be exported from certain Ports in this Kingdom to Newfoundland, under the Act of the.

14th of His present Majesty, will not be a sufficient Supply to carry on the Trade and Fisheries, while an Interruption continues' in their Supply from America, the Petitioners cannot pursue their Business, unless they have Liberty to exjxtrt, under certain Limitations and Restrictions, a sufficient Quantity of Bread, Flour,

Pease, Grout, Oatmeal, and other Necessarics; and as confining the Export to particular Persons and Dill rifts, has been found injurious in a general commercial View, the Petitioners hoj)e that the House will think it expedient to allow the Exportation of the necessary Articles to be extended to any Port or Ports in Great , >

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. John Harrifonbeing examined, said, That he knows the several Vallies between Bridge and Sandwich, commonly called The General Follies; that the Lands therein consist of upwards of Seven thousand Acres; that great Part thereof is frequently under Water, occasioned not only by the overflowing of the River Stour, but by Land Floods; that the Witnds has known Part of the General Follies overflowed for six Months together; and that the same have, been sometimes overflowed in Harvest.

Mr. William Long, Clerk to the Commission of Sewers

for the Eastern Part of the said County, being examined, laid. That Application had lately been made to the Commissioners of Sewers, by the Owners and Occupiers of Lands within the General Follies, requesting them to make proper Works for more effectually draining their Lands; that the Commissioners are very desirous of making such Works as shall be sufficient for draining the said Lands; but, by the Report of their Engineer, it appears, that certain Works are necessary for that Purpose, which the Commissioners apprehend they are not impowered to do by the Laws now in being relating to Sewers.

Then to prove the Allegations of the last mentioned Petition, Mr. Thomas Yeomans, Engineer, being examined, as to the Practicability of draining the Lands within the said General Vallies, laid, That he apprehends, that if a Cut or Drain was made from the River Stour, at or near the Salt Works at Stonar, across a Neck of Land into Sandwich Haven, (which Cut or Drain will not be quite a Furlong and an Half in Length) with Floodgates, and other proper Works, the Lands within the General Follies might be much better drained than they are at present.

Mr. William Long, being further examined, laid. That the Commissioners of Sewers find great Difficulties in collecting the Scotts authorized to be raised by them within the Limits of their Commission, where Owners and Occupiers of Lands change their Places of Reli-dence: And the Witness said, that he apprehends the Commission would be better executed, if some further Provision was made to enable the Commissioners to collect the Scotts from the Owners or Occupiers lo removing.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put, That, although the Terms of the Resolution of this House, of the 27th Day of February 1775, relative to the Colonies in Americado fecm literally to require, that the Offer therein mentioned should be made by the Governor, Council, and Assembly, or General Court of any Province, the true Intent and Meaning of the same does not require any thing more, in order to be accepted by this House, than that it should be made by the House of Representatives of such Province; and also, though the said Resolution fee ms to require that the said Offer should be a Proportion, according to the Condition, Circumstances, and Situation of such Province, yet that the true Meaning of the find Resolution doth purport, that any Duties which this House shall approve, will be accepted as a Compliance with the aid Resolution, although no Grounds for determining the said Proportion be laid before this House; and also, although the said Resolution does seem literally to require that they should engage to make Provision for the Support of the Civil Government and Administration of Justice in such Province, the same doth not require that any other Provision for Civil Government should be made, than what such Province hath been accustomed to make;

It passed in the Negative.

Richard Owen Cambridge, Esquire, being examined, laid. That the making the new Canal Navigation will be of great Benefit to the adjacent Roads; that a River Navigation mud be prejudicial to the Mills, which, he apprehends, the present intended Navigation will not; and that the making the Canal Navigation will be of public Utility.

John CapeI, Esquire, being examined, said, That the making the intended Canal Navigation will be of great public Utility, particularly by the great. Consumption of Coals for the Use of the Manufacturers; and that if this Navigation takes place, it will be of great Use to the Poor, as within his Memory, he believes, Half the Woods in that Neighbourhood have been destroyed, which has rendered Fuel much dearer.

From the House of Commons, the 6th Lecemlrer 77 J

SIR,

1 am commanded by the House of Commons to acquaint you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County and Boroughs within the same, to attend their Service in Parliament on Monday the 29th Day of January next and you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said House.

I am. Sir,

Your humble Servant,

Fir Norton, Speaker*

From the House of Commons, the 6th December 1775.

A Petition of the Planters of His Majesty’s Sugar Colonies residing in Great Bri, and of the Merchants of London trading to the said Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners having, upon a former Occasion, dated and laid before the House, with all the Accuracy and Precision of which they were capable, the Worth and Value of His Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in West , their national Magnitude, and Importance to Great Britain, their Situation as depending upon their Sifter Colonies in North America for the Maintenance of Property and Support of Life, the Petitioners Fears and apprehensions of Dangers and Dill refs arising out of the unhappy Disputes subsisting between Great Britain and America, they firmly tiufted, if Conciliation did not render it unnecefl'ary, that thele substantial Motives would have made them the Objects of the Confederation and Attention of the House; and that, in the Mid ft of the flattering Expectation that Application might meet a forward Disposition in the House to relieve, the Petitipners Hopes are at once blasted and cut off, by the bringing in of a Bill to prohibit all Trade and intercourse with the Colonies of New Mi'jjlichiifel's Bay, Rhode Island,

New jersey, PenJ'ylvania, the Three lower Counties on jDela ware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia; and that, when the American Congress adopted their Non-importation and Non-exportation Resolve, the Fears naturally arising to the Petitioners from thence, were somewhat abated'by a Reliance, on the Petitioners Parts, of a Relaxation on theirs, at lealt with regard to the Petitioners; but left, happily for the Petitioners, this Event might succeed, the present Bill not only deprives the Petitioners of the Probability, but establishes the Impossibility likewise: And therefore praying, That, upon this Ground, the Petitioners may be allowed to be heard at the Bar, by their Agents and Counsel, against the said Bill; relying on the Wisdom, Goodness, Justice, and Mercy of the House, not only for special Relief in this Instance, but for such further Assistance as the House can give.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report be received from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill to prohibit all Trade and Intercourse with the Colonies of New Hampshire, chnfct's Bay, Rhode Island, Connecticut, Nezv York,

Nezv Jersey, Pensylvania, the Three Lower Counties on

A Motion was made, and the Quo ft ion being put.

That an humble Address be- presented to His Majesty, humbly setting forth. That His Majesty’s Subjects in North America, having, in the most dutiful Manner, laid their Grievances before His Majesty, and having humbly belbught the gracious Interpol! tion of His Royal Authority and Influence to procure them Relief from their alflifting Fears and Jealousies, and having in the most earned Terms declared their Attachment to His Person, Family, and Government, with all the Devotion that Principle and Afleftion can inspire; and having solemnly allured His Majesty, that, connected with Great Britain by the strongest rl'ies that can unite Societies, and deploring every Event that tends in any Degree to weaken them, they not only most ardently desire that the former Harmony may be restor6d between them, but that a Concord may be ' established upon so firm a Basis, as to perpetuate its Blessings, uninterrupted by any future Diflensions, to succeeding Generations in both Countries; and having further allured His Majesty, that, notwithstanding their Sufferings during the Course of the present Controversy, their Breads retain too tender a Regard for the Kingdom frdm whence they derive their Origin, to request nich a Reconciliation as might in any Manner be inconsistent with her Dignity or Welfare; and that the- A^pprehen-fions which now opprels their Hearts with, unspeakable Grief being once removed. His Majesty will find His faithful Subjects in America ready and willing, at all Times, as they ever have been, with their Lives and Fortunes, to assert and maintain the Rights and Interests of His Majesty and of their Mother Country; and having, with all Humility, submitted to His Majesty’s wife Consideration, whether it may not be expedient, that His Majesty be pleased to dire<51 some Mode, by which the united Application of His Co-lonifts may be improved into an happy and permanent Reconciliation: His Majesty’s Faithful 1 Commons humbly beg Leave to represent, that, howtrver well-disposed His Majesty’s Subjects in North America may be, according to their most earned Professions, to return to their former Obedience and constitutional Dependance, yet that the Horrors of War and Blood Hied raging in their Country, must drive them to Dif-traction and Dispair: And further. His Faithful Commons beg have to recommend it to His Afa-jesty’s paternal Consideration, that a Return to their Duty of their own free and voluntary Compliance would ensure a more cordial and permanent Reconciliation than any reluctant Submission, which, through much Bloodshed of His Majesty’s Subjects, could be enforced by the Sword: Therefore His Faithful Commons most humbly beseech His Majesty, That He will be graciously pleased to give Orders for putting a Stop to the further Prosecution of Hostilities in America, thereby to prevent the further Destruction of the Lives of His Majesty’s Subjects, and to afford the wished-for Opportunity to His Colonists, of evincing the Sincerity of their Professions, by every Testimony of Devotion, becoming the most dutiful Subjects, and the most affectionate Colonists;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

That the Persons interested in the said Moor are very numerous, residing in many distant Places; ’and that the Number of the Persons-so interested, who have' already subscribed the said Petition against: the said Bill, amounts to 749; and that many others, finding the said Bill materially to differ from what they were ar first given to understand it would impoit, and several who have but very lately had Notice thereof, are now also delkous of petitioning the House against the said Bill: and that the Petitioners have been informed, and believe, that the Number, both of the Manors and of the several Persons interested, and having Right of Common in the said Moor, has been misrepresented to the Committee to whom the said Bill hath been committed, as well as that the Rights of Common of the Persons (in Number only 213) who have figried their Names as consenting to the said Bill, and of such others who are only supposed to have verbally signified their Consents thereto, have in no wife been legally proved, though in the Re-presentation thereof they have been much exaggerated and enhanced in Number; and that the Moor itself is a large and spaeiousTraft of Country, extending not so little as Twelve Miles in Length, on the Produce of which many Hundreds of useful People totally subsist, who mull inevitably feel the most fetal Consequences from a Deprivation of their present Mode of Subsistence, the ill Effects of which would necessariiy extend themselves throughout the Neighbourhood in

general, and would materially affect the Property of all other Persons interested in the said Moor; and that the Magnitude of the present Unde’taking, the Ex-tenfiveness of its Operations, and the Conicqu nces which may and most probably will follow the puffing such a Law, arc more than fufiieient Rcaions against the hurrying on the present Bill, and in Prudence equally evince the Necessityof moll seriously and maturely considering, thoroughly understanding, and impartially and equitably weighing the fame, in the present -State thereof; and that all Parties, whole Rights or Properties are attempted to be altered, changed, or taken away, against their Consents, ought in justice to be solemnly, fully, and fairly heard, before any Law shall be suffered to pass, by which the Country in general, and the many such Parties in particular, will be so very deeply affected; and that it will be impossible for the Petitioners and others, who have already petitioned against the said Bill, to be fully and properly prepared to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, by the Time appointed by the House for taking the Report of the said Committee into Consideration: And therefore praying, on Behalf of themselves and the said other Petitioners against the said Bill, That they may be indulged with a reasonable 'Rime, suitable to the Exigency of the Business, for fully preparing themselves to be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill; and that the said Bill may be printed and circulated in the Neighbourhood of the said Moor, that the Persons interested therein may be apprized thereof; and that the House will grant them such further Relief in the Premises as shall leem meet.

That the Petitioners are employed in some of the moll dam gerous Parts of Building, and that, on account of the Seasons, Masons can only work about nine or ten Months in the Year, and are in a great Measure unemployed the Remainder of it; and that the Petitioners are obliged to serve an Apprenticeship of Seven Years, with a Premium, to their laid Trade, before they can work thereat; and that the Mages of Journeyman Masons are Fifteen Shillings a Week, but that the Kind of W’ork such Journeyman are employed in subjects them to daily Expences in keeping their Tools in Repair, which, on an Average, amounts tct One Shilling per Week, besides being obliged to make good all Accidents in their Work, however unavoidable, or lose their Employ; and that the Danger of the Business is much greater than that of most other Handicraft Trades, and the Labour thereof is so great, that in old Age they cannot work thereat; and that the Petitioners apprehend the present Wages are not adequate to their Labour and Danger, and the increased Price of Provisions and every Convenience of Life makes that Sum not proportioned to the Difference of the Two Periods, it being near 70 Years since their Wages were settled at the F*rices they now are; and the present Wages of the Labourers employed in the Masons Business, who serve no Apprenticeship, nor are liable to any Expence by Tools, are from 12s. to 14J. a Week; and the Petitioners are advised that there is no Law in being, by which the Magi it rates are empowered to settle their Wages, as in many other Trades; they therefore hope for the Interposition of the House in an Augmentation of their Wages to i8r. per Week, or such other Sum as the House shall think proper: And therefore praying.

That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as to the House shall seem just and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition clo lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords by Mr. Leeds and Mr.

Pepys:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prohibit all Trade and Intercourse with the Colonies of New Hampfmre, Massachuset's Bay, Rhode Island Connecticut, Nezv York, New Jersey, Pensylvania, the Three lower Counties on Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, during the Continuance of the present Rebellion within the said Colonies respectively; for repealing an Act, made in the 14th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, to discontinue the landing and discharging, lading or shipping of Goods, Wares and Merchandize, at the Town, and within the Harbour of Boston, in the Province of Massachuset's. Bay, and also Two Acts, made in the last Session of Parliament, for restraining the Trade and Commerce of the Colonies in the said Acts respectively mentioned; and to enable His Majesty, or any Person or Persons appointed and authorized by His Majesty, to grant Pardons, and to issue Proclamations, in the Cafes, and for the Purposes therein mentioned; with some Amendments; to which Amendments the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for giving a public Reward unto such Person or Persons, being His Majesty's Subject or Subjects, as shall discover a Northern Passage for Vessels by Sea, between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, and also unto such as shall first approach by Sea within One Degree of the Northern Pole; without any Amendment: And also. The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, an Act for naturalizing Charles Quifi; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Regulation of His Majesty's Marine Forces while on Shore; without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing certain Commons, or Pieces of Waste Ground, in the Parishes of Bonsall, Wirkf worth, and Matlock, in the County of Derby $ without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of Rickard Brown and Inigo William , on* Esquires, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, 'TTiPt on the 14th Instant the Election of Two Burgesses to ferye in Parliament for the Borough of Ivelchester, in the County of came on; and

that Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury Brereton, EC* quires, and the Petitioners, were Candidates; and that Mr. Thomas Palmer, Bailiff and Returning Officer of the fil'd Borough, a known Friend of the Sitting Members, presided at the said Election, and shewed a great Partiality in Favour of the Sitting Members; and that the said Returning Officer admitted many Persons to poll for the said Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury who had no Right to vote, and rejected several others who had good Right, and who offered to poll for the Petitioners; and that the said Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury Brereton, by themselves, their Friends, and Agents, were guilty of Bribery, Treating, and other undue and illegal Means to' procure their Election; by which Means the said Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury Brereton were returned as having a Majority^ although the Petitioners had a Majority of legal votes, and ought to have been returned; And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give them such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered \That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Friday the 16th Day of February next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections, or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were sent to the Parties; accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant, or Warrants, for such Persons, Papers, and Records, as Shall be thought necessary by the several Parties, on the Hearing of the Matter of the said Petition.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Stourbridge A Petition of the Bailiff, Justice, Aldermen, and <.an»L Burgesses, of the Borough of Kidderminster, in the County of PVorcester, in Common Hall assembled, under their Common Seal, and of the principal Inhabitants residing in the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Leave is given to bring in a Bill, for making a navigable Canal, from or near the Town of Stourbridge, in the County of cester, to join ttie Staffordshire and Canal

Navigation, at or near a Place called Stourton, in the County of Stafford, and also for making Two collateral Cuts, the one from a Place called The Fens, to communicate with the said proposed Canal, and the other from a Place called Black Delph, to communicate with the said first-mentioned collateral Cut; and that the said collateral Cuts will open to very extensive Coal Mines, which, before the making of the Stafford-shire and Worcestershire Canal, supplied the said Town , of Kidderminster with Coal by Land Carriage, and in

Return large Quantities of Grain and other Necessaries, purchased at the Market in the said Town, were forwarded to a very populous Country near to such Mines, but that the Demand for Coals to the said Borough and the Iron Works in the Neighbourhood is now chiefly supplied by Water Carriage from Works at a more remote Distance, on the Banks of the Birmingham Canal, and from whence there has been so great a Demand, that they have not been able to supply that and the neighbouring Markets in a regular Manner; and that the Sale for Coals from the said first-mentioned Coal W orks is in other respects greatly taken otf, for Want of a like Conveyance by Water; and that the Petitioners apprehend, the opening of such Car.al and collateral Cuts will not only afford a more plentiful Supply of Coals to the said Borough, but will be a Means of restoring and establishing a mutual Intercourse between the fame, and the said Town and Neighbourhood of Stourbridge, by Means whereof Coals, as well as Corn and other Necessaries, W. 35.

supplied by the said Market, will be handed tb the Consumers at easier Rates; and the Petitioners apprehend the Staffordshire and Worcesterjhir Canal (for the obtaining of the Act whereof the Corporation and Inhabitants of this Borough were Petitioners to the House) will become of more general Utility by Means of a Junction with the said intended Canal and collateral Cuts; And therefore praying. That the said Bill may pals into a Law, with such Powers, and under such Terms and Conditions, as to the IToufe shall seem meet.

Stroudwater a PETITION of several Persons whose Names avigation, j^ are tkereullt0 subscribed, being Owners and Occupiers of Mills upon the River Stroudwater, between Framiload and Wallbridge, in the County of Gloucester, was prefen ted to the House, and read; Taking Notice of the Bill for amending an Act, passed in the Third Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for making navigable the River Stroudwater, in the County of Gloucester, from the River Severn, at or near Framiload\ to W'allbridge, near the Town of Stroud% in the same County; and also to give other Powers for the Purposes of making a Navigation from Framiload to Wall-bridge aforesaid; and setting forth, that there are, upon the said River, between Wallbridge and Framiload, several Mills wrought by Wheels turned by the Water of the said River, for which Purpose a great Force and Weight of Water is necessary; and that the said Mills, upon a moderate Calculation, afford Employment for Five Thousand, and thereby give Bread to above Nine Thousand Persons, and during the Summer Months in general have not a sufficient Supply of Water to keep them going more than Two-thirds, and sometimes not more than Half, their Time; and should the proposed Navigation take Place, it would deprive the Petitioners of a great Quantity of Water, and render the said Mills of little Use 5 and, that at the Time of passing the said Act of the Third Year of his late Majesty, Provision was made that the intended Navigation should not be worked during Two Months in the Summer; and by an Act, made in the 32d Year of his laid late Majesty, for amending the said Act, the Undertakers thereby appointed are expressly prohibited from making or using any J/x:k* and a Method is therein prescribed-ibr answering the Purpose of Navigation without any Waste of Water whatsoever; and that the Petitioners apprehend that the Advantages to arise from the proposed Navigation will not be adequate to the Injury thereby done to private Property; and that making the same in the Manner proposed by the said Bill will be highly injurious to the Woollen and Iron Manufactures now carried on within the said County to a very considerable Extent: And therefore praying, That the Petitioned may be heard, by their CounfeJ, against the said Bill, and that the same may not pafi into a Law, or that they may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That Counsel be admitted to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition, i?

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read. And,

Mr. Richard Slater, Clerk to the Didrift of Road between Sheffield and Duffield, being examined, said. That the Trustees have made great Progress in repairing the several Districts of Roads in the said Act mentioned; but that several Amendments are necessary, and that many of the Restrictions contained in the said Act have proved of great Detriment to the Road, particularly that of the Gates being fixed at particular Places; and likewise, that many of the Exemptions enable Persons to travel upon the Road Toll-free, who ought to contribute, upon Account of the Didance they go; that there is owing on the Didfift of Road between Sheffield and Duffield £. 8,750, or thereabouts; and on the Didrift of Road between Duffield and Derby 300, or thereabouts; and that the Act is very near expiring, and the Roads cannot be effectually amended, nor the Money owing repaid, unless the Term and Powers thereof are enlarged. Then,

Mr. Thomas Ittce, Clerk of the Didrift of Road between Wirksworth and Duffield, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of the above Witness, except as to the Sums borrowed upon the said Two Didrifts; and he further added. That there is owing on the Didrift of Road between Wirksworth and Duffield, the Sum of £. 1,840, or thereabouts.

A Petition of the Traders and other Inhabitants of Stourbridge the Borough of Bridgnorth, in the County of Salop, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that Leave hath been given to bring in a Bill for making and maintaining a navigable Canal, from or n6af the Town of Stourbridge, in the County of Wore fie", to join the Staffer dshire and Worcestershire Canal, at or near Stoartonf

in the County of Stafford, and allb Two collateral Cuts, one from a Place called The Fens, upon Penfnet Chace, to communicate with the intended Canal neaf the Juntftion of Wordesley Brook with the River St outs and ^he other from a Place called Black Delph upon the said Chace, to join the First mentioned collateral Cut at or near certain Lands called The Lays, in the Parish of Kingswinford, in the said County of Stafford: and that the Trade of the aforesaid Borough (which is situated upon the River Severn) greatly depends upon a numerous Part of the inhabitants thereof, who are Barge Owners and Bargemen employed ,in navigating their Vessels upon the said River, many of which are wholly engaged in the Coal and Iron Trade, by which they are enabled to acquire a competent Subsistehce for themselves and Families, and to contribute towards the Support of their Poor, who are at present very numerous; and that, should such Bill pals into a Law, the Petitioners are apprehensive that a great Number of the said Inhabitants, who are concerned ill the Navigation of the said River, and are able healthy Men, will be reduced to the Necessity of seeking Employment in distant Parts, leaving the Aged and Infirm, as allb many Women and Children, to be supported by the different Parishes, by which Means they will be liable to an exorbitant Poor’s Rate, when many of the inferior Traders, by the Lois of their Trade, will be rendered incapable of paying their Quota of the excessive Demand, and be probably reduced to the Necessity of seeking a Maintenance in other Places, or become an Addition to a numerous and burthensome Poor, in Consequence of which, the Petitioners apprehend, the said Borough will be greatly depopulated, their Trade much prejudiced, and the Householders and House Owners very fnaterially injured: And therefore praying, That the said BUI may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said BUI be read a Second Time.

A Petition of several Persons whole Natnes are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read j Taking Notice of the Bill for amending and keeping in Repair the Road leading from Doncaster to Bawtry, in the Counties of York and Nottingham; and Setting forth. That such Part of the great Northern Road as lies between the Turnpike Road leading from Retford to the South End of Bewdley, and the Road intended to be repaired by the said Bill, is not directed to be repaired by any particular Act of Parliament; and that the repairing and keeping the said Road in Repair would be a great Convenience to Travellers; and that there are Two Roads branching out of the Road intended to be repaired by the said Bill near Roffingtox Bridge, being the Place where a Turnpike is proposed to be erected, One of which Roads leads towards Blyth, and the other towards Thorne; and the Petitioners apprehend, that it will be necessary, in order to prevent evading the Tolls to be collected for repairing the said Road, to erect Side Gates upon the Roads lb branching out as aforesaid; and that it would be a great Saving in the Collection of the said Tolls, if Power was given to change the Course or Path of the said Roads,' near :the Ends thereof, so as to enable One Person to collect the Tolls at the said Turnpike, and also at those Side Gates: And therefore praying* That Provision may be made in the said Bill for the several Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the ‘Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir Cecil Wray, Sir George Savile, &c.: And they are to meet upon Monday Morning next, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speakers Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

That there is great Reason to believe, that the Money to arise from the Carriage of Goods upon the said Navigation will be insufficient to answer the Expence of making and maintaining the some, *and therefore the Petitioners are apprehensive that the Undertaking may probably be abandoned, after great Damage done to the Lands, through which the said Navigation is intended to be carried, and the Proprietors of such Lands left without Remedy for recovering Satis&ftion for such Damage; and, that supposing the said Navigation should ever be completed, the Petitioners apprehend that the Price of Carriage would be very little reduced thereby, and that the Damage done to the Public, and to private Property, by making the lame, wiH be greater than any Advantage that can be reasonably pefted to arise from such Undertaking: And therefore praying the House, that they may be heard, by their Counsel* against the said Bill, and that the some may not pals into a Law*

in the Twenty-third Year of his Reign, incorporate the Freemen of the Society of the Art or Mystery of Butchers within the City of London, and all Persons who then did, or thereafter should, use or exercise the said Art or Mystery within the said City, and within the Space of Two Miles thereof, by the Name of, " The " Matter, Wardens, and Commonalty, of the Art or " Mystery of Butchers of the City of London," with Power for the said Corporation to overlook, inspect, and govern, all Persons exercising or using the said Art or Mystery, and all Flesh exposed for Sale within the Limits aforesaid, and with full Power and Authority to make Bye Laws for the better and more effectual carrying the Intent of the said Letters Patent into Execution; and that, notwithstanding all Endeavours of the Petitioners to the contrary, unwholesome Flesh Meat is frequently exposed for Sale within the Limits aforesaid, which Practice, the Petitioners apprehend, they are not sufficiently empowered by the said Charter to prevent; and that the Petitioners conceive, the exposing to Sale unwholesome Flefti Meat might be prevented, if they were enabled to allow Salaries to the several Persons they employ as Inspectors of the Markets, and other Places within the Limits aforesaid, where Flefti Meat is ulually fold and exposed for Sale; but Doubts have arisen, whether the Petitioners are empowered, by their Charter, to enforce the Payment of the like Sums of Money from such of the Persons incorporated as aforesaid, who are not Freemen of the Company of Butchers within the said City of London, as are paid by the Freemen of the said Company, towards defraying the Expences of carrying the Intentions of the said Letters Patent into Execution: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for obviating all such Doubts for the future, and forgiving the Petitioners such further and other Powers, to enable them to prevent the exposing for Sale all unwholesome Flefti Meat within the Limits of their Charter, as the House shall think just and reasonable.

Stourbridge A Petition of several Proprietors of Salt Works, and Canal. of the Chief Magistrates and principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Droitwich, in the County of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Bill hath been brought into the House, for making a Navigable Canal, from or near the Town of Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, to join the Staff or dshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, at or near Stow ton, in the County of Stafford; and also for making Two collateral Cuts, the one from a Place called The Fens, to communicate with the said proposed Canal, and the other from a Place called Black Delph, to communicate with r the said first-mentioned collateral Cut; and that the Petitioners apprehend, by Means of the said intended Canal and collateral Cuts, large Quantities of Coals will be navigated, from the Coal Mines lying near such Canal and collateral Cuts, down the Staffordshire and Worcesterjhife Caftal, into the River Severn, and up the Droitwich Canal, to the said Borough; and thereby the said Borough, and the Salt Works within the same, as also the adjacent Neighbourhood and certain Lime Works near the said Borough, may be furniQied with Coal at a much cheaper Rate than at present, which may be the Means of extending and promoting the Trade of the said Borough, the Improvement of Land, and a mutual Advantage to the Proprietors of Salt 15 "

Works and of the adjacent Neighbourhood; and the Petitioners also apprehend, the same will *be in other respects of great public Utility: And therefore praying,

That the said Bill may pass into a Law, with such Powers, and under such Terms and Conditions, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Town Stourbridge and'Neighbourhood of Upton upon Severn, in the County Caaal* of Worcester, whose Names- ar^ thereunto subscribed, was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that L^ave is given to bring in a 'Sill, for making a Navigable Canal, from or near the Town of Stourbridge, in the County of Worcester, to join the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal Navigation, at or near a Place called Stourton, in the County of Stafford; and also for making Two collateral Cuts, the one from a Place called The Fens, to communicate with the said proposed Canal, and the other from a Place called Black Delph, to communicate with the said first-mentioned collateral Cut; and that, by Means of such Canal and collateral Cuts, a more ready and cheap Communication will be opened between the said Town of Upton and the said Town and Neighbourhood of Stourbridge, for the Conveyance of Goods and Merchandizes, whereby the said Town and Parts adjacent may be supplied with Coals at a more reasonable Rate than at present; from which great Advantages will be derived to the said Town of Upton and its Inhabitants; and that the said Canal and Cuts will, as the Petitioners conceive, be otherwise of public Utility: And therefore praying. (Cambridge) cution an Act of Parliament, made in the Seventh Year

Drainage. of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, "An Act for draining and preserving " certain Fen Lands ani Low Grounds, lying in the " South Level, Part of the Great Level of the Fens, commonly called The Bedford Level, and in the County " of Cambridge, between the River otherwise

" Grant, West, and the hard Lands of,

" Swaffham Bulbeck, and Swaffham Prior, East, and " for impowering the Governor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the Company of Conservators of the " Great Level of the Fens, commonly called The " ford Level, to fell certain Fen Lands, lying within " the Limits aforesaid, commonly called Invested " Lands " and of fereral other Owners and Occupiers

of Fen Lands and Low Grounds, lying within the Limits aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Commissioners appointed by the said Act have been obliged, from Time to Time, to borrow considerable Sums of Money upon the Credit of the Taxes charged and to be charged by the said Act, great Part of which Money has been laid out in scouring and deepening the Loads, and in making and repairing the Banks by the Sides thereof, and on the East Side of the River Grant; but that the Tolls granted by the said Act for those Purposes are found inadequate to the Expence; and that the Land Owners in the said District are not able to support the said Works, and to pay the interest of the Monies already borrowed and laid out in the Erection, Making, and Maintenance thereof, without a larger Toll; and that, at the Time of passing the said Act,

" many of the said Lands having been dug out into Hods or Turf Pools, it was thought necessary, in order to encourage the Improvement of such Lands, that, the same should be assessed or charged with only one Half of the lax wherewith the other Lands of the . 'fame Sort should-be charged during the first Seven Years after passing the said Act; and that the said Term of Seven Years is now expired, and it appears to the Petitioners, that scarce any of the said dug Lands have been at all improved, or are capable of such Improvement (at least for many Years) as to enable them to bear an equal Tax with the whole Grounds, or that many of them can be sold for the Amount of such Taxes as are already due thereon; and that the turning of Bottisham and Swaffham Loads into Reach Load, as near as conveniently may be by the Skirts of the Uplands, and so make but one Oytfall into the River Cam, would be the most secure. Way of Drainage, and also a Saving to the Undertaking, by sparing some Miles of Embanking; for which Purpose it may be necessary to take into the /Boundary some other Lands, which may be done without any Prejudice to the Proprietors; and others, which have received no Benefit from the Drainage, may be left out; and as it is apprehended that the Taxes now levied on the whole District may be more equally laid out and assessed by a further Assortment of the Lands into more different Sorts or Degrees of Taxation, and that some of the Commonable Parts of the said Fen Lands by becoming mowable, and other Parts thereof that are now mown by being fed by Cattle, may, it is apprehended, be rendered of more general Utility and Service; and that it is found, by Experience, that the Power? and Authorities in the said Act contained are not sufficient for the Purposes for which they were intended; And therefore

praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for granting larger Tolls, and for amending the said Act in such other Respects, as to the House shall fcem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Sir John Hynde Colton, Sir son Gideon, &c.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.

to a Place called Autherly, in the said County of Stafford, where the said Navigable Canal joins and communicates with a certain other Navigable Canal, called the Staffer dshire and Wircejlershire Canal Navigation; such latter Canal communicating also with the Rivers Severn and Trent; and that the great Object, in making the said Birmingham Canal, was, as the Petitioners apprehend, to reduce the Price of Coals at the said Town of Birmingham, and in other Parts of the County of wick, but particularly in the said Town of Birmingham,

the Trade and Manufactures of which Place depend in a great Measure upon the Cheapness of Coals, and that the Proprietors, -in executing the said Canal, have extended it through a large d raft of Country, at or near the above Places, abounding in Coal, great Part of which before the making of the said Canal could not be got and brought to Market, but which in consequence thereof are now raised and vended; and that many Persons (Owners of such Coal Land) and others, who have bought or rented tho lame, have, in consequence of the Conveyance rendered them by the said Canal, expended very large Sums of Money in planting such Coal Works and in erecting Engines, Gins, and other Structures, for the Purpose of railing and vending such Coals lying near to the said Canal; in purl'uance of which mutual Accommodation to the Public, by the making the said Birmingham Canal, and by opening such Mines m consequence thereof, the great Objects of making the said Canal have been answered, and the Petitioners, as well as all other the Inhabitants of the said Town and the neighbouring Parts of , have been enabled

thereby to purchase Coals at about Two Thirds of the Value for which they could buy the same before the making of the said Canal; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the several Coal Works already opened, and which may be opened in the Vicinity or the said Canal, will be sufficient to liipply the Demand for the feme for many Centuries to come; and that the said Owners of such Coal Mines do now render the feme at Market at as cheap a Rate as in the Nature of their Undertakings it is possible for them to do; and that, in consequence, any Scheme which may have a Tendency to compel the present Owners or Workers of Coal Mines, upon the Line of the said Birmingham Canal, to desert and decline the Working of such Mines, will eventually tend to the Prejudice of the Public, but alarmingly lb to the Petitioners and the other Inhabitants of the Town of Birmingham: and that the Petitioners are informed, by the Votes, that a Petition hath been presented for Leave to bring in a Bill for making a Navigable Canal from the Town of Stourbridge, and certain Coal Works in that Neighbourhood, to communicate with the said and

Canal, at a certain Place called Stourton, in the said County of Stafford, at a Distance of about Sixteen Miles (measuring along the respective Birmingham and Staffor dshire and Worcestershire Canals) from greatest Part of the several Coal Mines now at Work, and from which the Markets are now so reasonably supplied; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, a Monopoly will focceed: And therefore praying, That the feme - may not pass into a Law; and that the Petitioners may be heard against the feme, by their Counsel, at the Bar of the House.

thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Streets, Lanes, and other public Psflages, within the said Town, are in general very ill cleansed, lighted, and watched, and the Paths and Passages thereof are greatly obstructed by Nuisances and Annoyances, and the Foot Ways of great Parts thereof, which are Turnpike, are very inconvenient for walking thereon, and cannot be remedied by the said Turnpike; and both the Horse Ways and FootWays, of such Parts thereof as are not Turnpike, are in a very ruinous Condition; and that, on the 11 th Day of July last, there happened in the East Street of the said Town a sudden and terrible Fire, which, by reason of the many thatched Houses in that Part of the Town, in a very ftiort Time burnt down and consumed Twenty-two Dwelling Houses, besides Out Houses and other Buildings, and the whole Town was in imminent Danger of being burnt and destroyed; and that it would tend greatly to the Health, Safety, and Advantage of the Inhabitants of the said Town, and be of great public Utility, if the said Streets, Lanes, A Hep, and other public Passages, were properly cleansed, lighted, and watched, and the Nuisances, Obstructionss; and Annoyances removed, and the Foot Ways of such Parts thereof as are Turnpike were rendered more convenient for Foot Passengers, and the Horse Ways and Foot Ways of such , Parts thereof as are not Turnpike were better repaired;

and k would conduee to the preventing future Dangers by 1 Fire, if thatched Houses and Buildings were prohibited in

the said Town: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets, Lanes, Alleys, and public Passages, of the Town of aforesaid,

and the paving the Foot Wap thereof as are Turnpike; and for the repairing both Lire Horse and Foot Wap of such Parts thereof as are not Turnpike, and for re* moving Nuisances and Annoyances therein, and for preventing ffoufes and Buildings, hereafter to be built, from being, covered with any Thatch or Straw, for the greater Safety of the Inhabitants, and better Security from Danger by Fire.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read; whereby it appeared, that certain Lands, which were, at the Time of passing the lame, dug out into Hods or Turf Pools, were charged with only Half Rates for the Space of Seven Years, which Term is near expiring.

Mr. Camforth Manning, being examined, laid, That the Commissioners appointed for putting the said Act in Execution, have borrowed considerable Sums of Money on the Credit of the Rates thereby laid, all which have been duly expended in the several Works of draining and embanking thereby directed, which has been a great Benefit to the Navigation of the said River Cam; that the Rates and Tolls by the said Act granted have been found very inadequate, and that the several Works thereby directed to be done cannot be completed, unless some additional Tolls are laid; that the Lands dug out into Hods or Turf Pools, are incapable of paying the ' Proportion of Taxes charged thereon, and that, if they were to be sold, the Produce of them would not amount to the Sum due in Arrear; that the turning of Bottifham and Swaffham Loads into the Reach l oad, in order to make but one Outfall into the River Cam, would be the' fefeft Way of Drainage, and a Saving of some Miles of Embanking; that for this Purpose it may be necessary to take into the Boundary some other Lands, which may be done without any Prejudice to the Proprietors; and others, which are at present within the Line, but have not receved any Benefit from the Drainage, may be left out; and he concluded with laying, that the Powers of the said A Cl, in m^ny Particulars, want to be enlarged and amended.

Mr. William Poulter, being examined, confirmed the*

Whole of the foregoing Evidence; and added, that the Sum due on the Credit of the Act, amounts to near Four thousand Pounds, together with a large Arrear of Interest thereon.

Anglesey A Petition of Sir John Stanley, Baronet, was pre-

Roads. (ented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That,

in the last Session of Parliament, an Act was passed for continuing and enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act of the Fifth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, for repairing and widening the Road leading from Porthaethwy Ferry to Holyhead, in the County of Anglesey; and representing to the House, that there are certain Powers contained in the said Act, which, the Petitioner conceives, are not necessary, and, in Consequence of such Powers, the said Trustees have ordered a Wall or Embankment to be made, at a Place called Cricklas, in the Parish of Llanynghenedle, under Pretence that the same is necessary for the Safety and Convenience of Persons and Carriages passing to and from Holyhead, but such Wall or Embankment is not yet made; and that the Petitioner is Owner of certain Lands and Grounds lying near the Place where the said Wall or Embankment is proposed to be made, and should the same be made the Petitioner and his Tenants must be great Sufferers; and that a Road may be made shorter than the present Road, and which would at all Times be convenient and lafe for Travellers and Carriages, without making the pro-poled Wall or Embankment, which will be a leis Expence than the proposed Wall, or Embankment, and Road, proposed to be made by the said Trustees; and that, during the passing of the Bill in the last Session of Parliament, being, from several Circumstances, under Apprehensions that some additional Powers might be given which would affect his Property, he had intended to petition the House against the said Bill; but on receiving Assurances from the Person who was employed as Agent for, and solicited, the said Bill, that nothing was intended that could at all affect the Property of the Petitioner, and the Clauses under which the Trustees think themselves authorized to make the said Wall or Embankment being only in general Words, without specifying the particular Work which is now intended to be made, the Petitioner, relying on those Assurances, did not make any Application to the House, or oppose the Bill, which he would have done if he had understood that, under any general Words, the Trustees could be authorized to make such Wall or Embankment, or do any other Work to the Prejudice of his Estate: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to restrain the said Trustees from making the proposed Wall or Embankment, or any other Work whatsoever, to the Prejudice of the Petitioner, or that the Petitioner may have such other Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of John Hend, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner and James Oswald, Esquire, were Candidates at the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the County of Fife, in Scotland, in place of General Scott, which was held on Wednesday the 24th January 1776; and that, at the said Election, Sir John Anjlruther, Baronet, was chosen Prsefes of the Meeting by the Petitioner’s Friends, who were a clear Majority upon the Poll, as made up at the previous Meeting; and, after the Choice of Praefes and Clerk, the Freeholders present having next proceeded to adjust the Roll, by striking off such as were dead or diverted of their Estates, or such as refused to take the Oath of Trull and Possession, in Terms of the Act in the 7th of the late King, Four of the Petitioner’s Voters, and the same Number on the other Side, were thereby found disqualified, which still left the Majority with the Petitioner; Fifty-nine of the Freeholders present being for him, and only Fifty-five against him; and that an Objectioti having been moved against another of Mr. s

Voters, viz.William Melvil, of Greigston, the same was

unjustly over-ruled by the Meeting, and the said William Melvil was continued on the Roll, although he ought to have been expunged, having been admitted as the Husband of an Heirels, who was now diverted of her Estate, in Favour of her Son, by her former Marriage; and that the next Step was to admit such Claimants for new Inrolment as produced sufficient Titles; Three appeared on the Side of the Petitioner, and Six for Mr. Oswald; Two of the Petitioner’s Claimants were admitted without Objection, the Third was objected to, and, upon examining his Titles, it was thought that they were insufficient, and therefore the Meeting refused to inrol him; of the Six Claimants, on the other Side, Four were admitted without any Objection: the Fifth, James Rutherford, was objected

to,.

duced a legal Title, and it came to a Vote of the Meeting, whether he should be inrolled or not at this Period; including those who had been newly inrolled, the Petitioner had Sixty-one Voters on the Roll, and Mr. Oswald had Sixty; but one of the Petitioner’s

Friends having declined taking the Oath, commonly called the Meeting House Oath, tendered to him by virtue of the Ad 19th Geo. II. Cap. 38, his Vote was difeounted, and other Two of the Petitioner’s Friends, not understanding the Question, threw away their Votes, whereby it carried by a Majority of Two to inroll Captain Dalrymple, though he had been kept off at a former Meeting; and that Mr. Oswald came thereby to have Sixty-one Voters on the Roll, including the said William Melvil, James Rutherford, and Hugh Dal-

rymple; and the Petitioner had Sixty, including the Prefes, and exclusive of the Person who refused taking the Meeting House Oath; and that, the Roll having been then called for the Choice of Member, Mr. Oswald's Sixty-one Friends voted for him, and the other Sixty for the Petitioner, whereby the Election was apparently carried for Mr. Oswald, by One of Majority; but the Petitioner entered a Protest against Mr. Oswald's being returned, and that he himself was duly elected by the legal Majority, in respect of the Ob-jedions that lay to some of Mr. Oswald's Voters; and Sir John Anfruther, the Praefes, did at the same Time declare publicly that he gave his calling Voice in Favour of the Petitioner, in case, upon any After-dif-cuffion of the Votes, it should appear there was an equal Number on each Side; and, in Token thereof, he signed the Protest; notwithstanding which, the said James Oswald has been returned as duly elected to serve in Parliament for the said County of Fife, to the manifest Injury of the Petitioner; who therefore prays the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and grant him such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Consideration upon Tuesday the 19th Day of March next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

Memorandum:

In pursuance of Two Acts, made in the 10th and nth Years of His present Majesty’s Reign, to regulate the Trials of controverted Elections or Returns of Members to serve in Parliament, the like Notices, as in the former Cafes, were lent to the Parties, accompanied with Orders for their Attendance, by themselves, their Counsel, or Agents, at the Time on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Addenbrooke, being examined, laid. That he knows Colebrooke Dale, Madeley Wood, Bent hall, Brofeley, and Places adjacent, in the County of Salop; that there is a considerable Traffic carried on in that Part of the Country in Iron, Lime, Potters Clay, and Coals; and that Persons carrying on the feme are frequently put to great Inconveniences, Delays, and Obstructions, by reason of the Insufficiency of the present Ferry over the River Severn from Bent hall to Madeley Wood, particularly in the Winter Season, when it is frequently dangerous and in very high Floods it is impassable:

That if a Bridge was erected across the said River from Benthall to Madeley Wood, the Witness apprehends the aforesaid Branches of Trade would be much improved, by a quicker Conveyance of Goods, particularly the China Manufacture at Cauthley, near and the Communication between the several Places before mentioned rendered sese and commodious.

And the Witness further feid. That the said Ferry is only passable for Horses and Foot Passengers, by reason of which Carriages are obliged to go Eight Miles about; and that the building of the said Bridge will be of public Utility.

Complaint being made to the House, That the Earl Harcourt. Lord Lieutenant General and General Governor of Ireland, did, on the Twenty-third Day of November last, in Breach of the Privilege, and in Derogation of the Honour and Authority, of this House, fend a written Message to the House of Commons of the Parliament of Ireland, signed with his own Hand, to the following Effect:

" That he had His Majesty’s Command to acquaint " that House, That the Situation of Affairs in Part of " His Majesty’s American Dominions was such, as to " make it necessary, for the Honour and Safety of the British Empire, and for the Support of His Majesty’s " just Rights, to desire the Concurrence of His faithful Parliament of Ireland, in fending out of that " Kingdom a Force not exceeding Four thousand " Men, Part of the Number of Troops upon that Efta- blishment, appointed to remain in that Kingdom for " its Defence; and to declare to them His Majesty’s " Most Gracious Intention, that such Part of His Army " as shall be spartd out of that Kingdom, to answer the " prrient Exigency of Affairs, is not to be continued a " Charge upon that Establishment, fe> long as they " shall remain out of that Kingdom.

" And that he was further commanded to inform " thit House, That, as His Majesty has nothing " more at 1 (cart than the Security and Protection of "'His People of Ireland, it is His Intention, if it shall " be the Deli re of that Parliament, to replace such "Forces as maybe lent out. of that Kingdom, by an " equal Number of Foreign Protestant Troops, as " loon as His Majesty shall be enabled lb to do, the 21

" Chafge of such Troops to be defrayed without any " Expence to that Kingdom."

THE Hour, appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Richard Brown and Inigo William. Jones, Inquires, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury Brereton, Esquires, for’ the Borough of Ivelchester, being come;

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Buli-ness of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 91 Members only being found to be present;

Mr. Speaker directed the Clerk to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration; and immediately adjourned the said Order, without a Question first put, till Tomorrow, Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

And then the House was adjourned by Mr. Speaker, without a Question first put, till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock.

Prayers.

THE Hour, appointed for taking into Consideration the Petition of Richard Brown and Inigo William Jones, Esquires, complaining of the undue Election and Return of Nathaniel Webb and Owen Salusbury Brereton, Esquires, for the Borough of Ivel* chester, being come; .

And Mr. Speaker having taken the Chair;

A Member, in his Place, informed the House, That he had an Authority from the Petitioners, to desire of the House, that they might be at Liberty to withdraw their said Petition.

One of the said Sitting Members, in his. Place, consented thereto.

And another Member, in his Place, informed the House, That he had an Authority from the other of the said Sitting Members, to give his Consent to the withdrawing of the said Petition.

And thereupon Mr. Speaker dated to the House, the Proceedings of the House on the 28th Day of February 1774, with respect to the House having given Leave to withdraw the Petition of John Roberts, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the City of London, on the Day on which the said Petition was ordered to be taken into Consideration.

And the Act, made in the 10th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act to regulate the Trials of controverted Eieftions or Returns " of Members to servein Parliament," was read.

But it appearing to be the Sense of the House, That the Order of the Day ought to be proceeded on, and that the House could not suffer any Question to intervene;

The Serjeant at Arms was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to go with the Mace to the Places adjacent, and require the immediate Attendance of the Members on the Bud-ness of the House.

And he went accordingly.

And being returned;

The House was counted by Mr. Speaker, and 138 Members being found to be present;

The Counsel and Agents on both Sides were called in to the Bar.

And the Door of the House being locked, die Clerk was directed, by Mr. Speaker, to read the Order of the Day, for taking the said Petition into Consideration.

' And the feme being read accordingly;

The Names of all the Members of the House were, by the Clerk, taken out of the Box (which had been before prepared) and put into Six Glades, and were then drawn by the Clerk, in the usual Manner, and read by Mr. Speaker to the House.

And the Names of Four Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to.

And the Name of John Morton, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Select Committee, by the Counsel for the Sitting Members, and his Name was set aside.

And the Names of Forty-five other Members, then present, were drawn, who were not objected to *

Translation of a Treaty between His Majesty and the

Reigning Duke of Brunswick. Signed at,

the 9th of January 1776.

Be it known unto all’whom it does or may concern, That His Majesty the King of Great,

having judged propier to propose to1 His Most Serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick arid Ltthetrburgh, the1 Cession of1 a Body bf his Troops, to be employed in the Service- of Great Britain, and His’ Most vSerene Highness having yielded with Zeal and:Readi- riels to His Majesty’s Views,' the High contracting ' Parties1 have given' Otders -for1 'this! Purpose to"their Tespective- Ministers, that- isto-fay,- His Majesty to Colonel William Captain' of the

Guards, and the Most Serene’ Duke of Brmjhvick "and Lunenburgh to the Privy CouriciBor; Feronce, \\ho, after (he Exchange1 of Yheir: fair Powers havel agreed upon the following Artifcles.

Art: 1.

The Molt Serene Duke of Brunswick yields' to5 His Briiaiiriick Majesty a’--Gorps of--Infantry of his TrOops, of Three thousand'Nirfe hundred Sixty-four Men, Which Corps shall be entirely at the-Dispo'fition of the' King, as well in Europe as in' America.

Art. 2.

His' Most Serene 'Highness allb yields to His Bri-‘ tamiick Majesty a Body of ’ Light Cavalry of Three hundred Thirty-six’ Men; but -as ’His 'Britandick Majesty will not have Occasion for the'Horses of this Corps, ' the said Coirps shall lerve as1 a Corps of Infantry; and if the Service requires them to -be mounted. His Majesty engages to do it at His own Expence.

Arti 3-

The Most Sercnfe Duke engages to equip completely both these Corps, except the Horses for the Light Cavalry; His Moll Serene-Highness will keep iri Readi-nels for marching, towards-the Fifteenth of next at fastheft,- the First Division of this Corps, confining of Two thousand Two-hundred Eighty-two Men, in l’uch Manner that this" First'Division shall arrive, towards the 25 th of February, - at the Place of Embarkation to be agreed upon between the respective ' Ministers: As’ to the' Second 'Division- of the said

Body of Troops, amounting to Twothovtfand Eighteen Men, His Most Serene -Highness will cause them 'to begin their March in the last Week of the -Month of March at farthest. These Two Corps shall pals in Review, at the Place of their Embarkation before His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary; and, -in order to prevent Desertion.in their March, His Britannick Majesty will caiile the most precise Orders to ibe* given in his Electoral Dominions, that all necefl’aiy Measures be taken to Hop every Deserter from this Body of Troops, and to convey them without Delay to the Place of Embarkation, there to join their Regiments. His Britannick Majesty will cause Directions to be given to the Governors or Comhaaftdants of-Places, Bailiffs, and others, to execute these Orders with the same Exadtnels as is observed -with regard to His Majesty’s Electoral Troops.

Art. 4.

This Body of Infantry and of Light Cavalry shall be composed Of Five Regiufents and of Two . Battalions, according to the Lifts annexed to the present Treaty. The Officers -Servants on the said Lifts shall be fumished with /Arms and every necessary Equipment as Soldiers; they shall do Service like them, if Occasion requires it, and shall be paid as such.

Art.9.

The Most Serene - Duke engages to furnish: the .’Recruits that may be annually necessary. for this Corps. These Recruits shall be delivered, after a.previous. Notice of Four Months, to His Britannick' Majesty’s Commiflhiy, disciplined-arid - equipped. The - said. Recruits shall arrive at -the: Place of their Embarkation 1 at: the ‘Time that -shall bo agreed- upon before the Opening of each Campaign.

Art.- 6.

The King’s Service, and the Preservation‘.of the Troops, requiring equally that the Commanding Officers and Subalterns should be expert Persons, His Most Serene Highnest will take proper XJare in‘ the.Choice of them.

.'Art. 7.

The Most Serene Duke engages to put this Corps on the best Footing possible; and none shall be admitted mtoifr triir Persons' proper for' Campaign "Service, and acknowledged as such by His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary.

Art. 8.

This Corps shall be. fumished with Tents and all necessary Equipage.

Art 9.

The King grants to this Corps the -ordinary and extraordinary Pay,- as.weH as- all Advantages in Forage, Provision, &c.- &c. enjoyed by.: the Royal Troops: ’Arid the-Most Serene Duke engages to - Let this Corps enjoy all the Emoluments of Pay that His nick Majesty allows them. The Sick and Wounded of the said Corps shall be taken Care of in the Ilof-pitals,-and- at the Expence of the King, as i’ the 'Troops- of His Britannick Majesty. The-Wounded, not in a Condition to serve, shall be transported into Europe at the Expence of the King, and landed jn a Port on the Elbe or the Weser. As to what regards the Body of Light Cavalry, they shall be put on the Foot of the British Light Cavalry, when they are dif-mounted; but they shall have the same Pay, as well Ordinary as Extraordinary, as the Light Horse of His Majesty; from the Day that they shall serve on Horse-back.

Art. 10.

There shall be paid to His Most Serene Highness, under the Title of Levy Money, for each Foot Soldier or Trooper- not mounted,. Thirty Crowns Banco, the Crown reckoned at Fifty-three Sols Holland, and reckoned at'' Font Shillings Nine Pence Three Farthings. One Third of this Levy Money shall be paid

a Month

16 GeO. III. 190 Febfuarii.

a Month after the Signature of the Treaty, and the Two other Thirds shall he paid Two Months after the Signature. The Payment of this Levy Money shall be made nevertheless prt Condition that Thirty Crowns Banco shall be retained for each Soldier of the said Corps, who, without Cause of Sickness, shall be abl'ent on the Day when they pals in Review before His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary, which Thirty Crowns Banco shall however be paid as soon as the 'blent Soldiers shall join their respective Corps.

Art. 11.

According to Custom, Three wounded Men shall be reckoned as One killed. A Man killed shall be paid for at the Rate of Levy Money. If it shall happen that any of the Regiments, Battalions, or Companies of this Corps should fufler a Lois altogether extraordinary, either in a Battle, a Siege, or by an uncommon contagious Malady, or by the I^ols of any Transport Vessel in the Voyage to America, His Britannick Majesty will make good, in the moll equitable Manner, the Loss of the Officer or Soldier, and will be at the Expence of the necessary Recruits to re-establish the Corps that shall have suffered this extraordinary Loss.

Art. 12.

The Most Serene Duke reserves to himselfthe Nomination to the vacant Employments, as also the Administration of Justice. Moreover His Britannick Majesty will cause Orders to be given to the Commander of the Army in which this Corps shall serve, not to exact of this Corps any extraordinary Services, or such as are beyond their Proportion with the rest of the Army. This Corps shall take the Oath of Fidelity to His Britannick Majesty, without Prejudice to the Oath which they have taken to their Sovereign.

Art. 13.

Towards defraying the extraordinary Expences the hasty Equipment of this Body of Troops occasions. His Britannick Majesty grants Two Months Pay previous Jo the March of the said Troops. And from the Time the Troops shall have quitted their Quarters, in order to repair to the Place of their Dedination, all the Expences of their March and Transport shall be at the Charge of His JBritam Majesty.

Art. 14.

His Britannick Majesty grants to His Most Serene Highness an Annual Subsidy, which shall be regulated in the following IVfanner: It shall commence from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty, and shall be Angle, that is to say, of the Amount of Sixty-four thousand Five hundred German Crowns, as long as these Troops shall enjoy the Pay. From the Time the Pay shall cease, the Subsidy shall be double, that is to say, of One hundred Twenty-nine thousand German Crowns. This double Subsidy shall be continued during Two T ears after the Return of the said Troops into His Most Serene Highness’s Dominions.

Art. 15.

This Treaty shall be ratified by the High Con-trafting Parties; and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged as soon as possible.

Thus concluded and signed. by the Minister Plenipotentiary of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on one Part, and by the Minister Plenipotentiary of His Most Serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick and"

Lunenburgh on the other Part.

Done at Brunswick, this 9th January 1776.

William Faucitt. (L. S.) B. Feronce. (L. S.)

NOTE.

It is to be observed, That, by the Fourth Article of the Treaty, it is agreed, that the Officers Servants mentioned in the Establishment should receive Soldiers Pay; because they are equipped on the same Footing in order to serve in same of Neceftity. This Arrangement is made to prevent the Abuse which frequently takes place by Means of the Officers taking Soldiers of the Corps to serve them.

N O T E,

Concerning the Levy Money.

By the State annexed to the present Note, it is manifest, that the Total of the Heads for which Levy Money is paid, amounts to Four thousand Eighty-four. By the 10th Article, of the Treaty, it is agreed, That Thirty Crowns Banco, of Fifty-three Sols of Holland, shall be paid; the Crown Banco is valued at 4s. 9id. which makes for the Whole £.29,481. 7 s. 6 d. By the same 10th Article, it is agreed, That One Third Part of this Sum shall be paid One Month, and the Two other Third Parts Two Months after the Signature; consequently His Britannick Majesty will be pleased to order it to be paid on the 9th of February next, to the Banker properly authorized; the Third Part of the Levy Money making £.9,827. 2S.‘ 6 d. The Two other Third Parts shall be paid on the 9th of March next, the Amount of which is £. 19,654. 5 s. o d.

Done and Signed at Brunswick this 9th January 1776.

between His Majesty the King of Great Britain and His Mod Serene Highness the Landgrave of CaJJell, their Successors, and H<yr$, a drift Friendftup,. and a sincere firm and constant Union, inso much that the one shall consider the Interests of the other as his own, and shall apply himself with good Faith, to advance them to the utmost, and to prevent and avert mutually all Trouble and Loss. . '

2.

To this End it is agreed, That all former Treaties, principally of Guaranty, be deemed to be renewed and confirmed by the present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses, and shall be of the same Force as if they were herein inserted Word for Word, so far as is not derogated from them by the present Treaty.

3-

This Body of Twelve thousand Men of the Troops of HeJJe, which is to be employed in His Majesty’s Service, shall consist of Four Battalions of Grenadiers, of Four Companies each. Fifteen Battalions of Infantry, of Five Companies each, and Two Companies of Chasseurs, the Whole provided with General and other necessary Officers.

This Corps shall be completely equipped and provided with Tents and all Accoutrements, of which it may (land in need; in a Word, shall be put on the best Footing possible, and none shall be admitted into it but Men fit for Service, and acknowledged for such by His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary. Formerly the Signature of the Treaties has usually preceded, by some Time, the Requisition for the March of the Troops, but, as in the present Circumstances, there is no Ti me to be loft, the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty is deemed also to be the Term of the Requisition, and Three Battalions of Grenadiers, Six Battalions of Infantry, with One Company of Chasseurs, shall be in a Condition to pass in Review before His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary on the 14th of February, and shall begin to march on the Day following, the 15th of Februaryfor the Place, of Embarkation. The rest shall be ready in Four Weeks after, if possible, and march in- like Manner.

This Body of Troops shall not be separated, unless Reasons of War require- it, but shall remain under the Orders of the General, to whom His Mod Serene Highness has intruded the Command; and the Second Division shall be conducted to the same Places only, where the First shall actually be, if not contrary to the Plan of Operations.

.4*

Each Battalion of this Body_ of Troops shall be provided with Two Pieces of Field Artillery, with the Officers, Gunners, and other Persons, and the Train thereunto belonging, if His Majesty is desirous of it.

Years is stipulated for their Duration; but, in the present. His Britannick Majesty, choosing. rather not to engage Himself for any, longer Time than He shall have Occasion for these Troops, consents, instead thereof, that the Subsidy shall be double, from the Day of the Signature of this Treaty to its Expiration; that is to say. That it shall amount for this Body of Twelve thousand Men to the Sum of Four hundred and Fifty thousand Crowns Banco per , the Crown reckoned at Fifty-three Sols of , or

at Four Shillings and Nine Pence Three Farthings

English Money, and that the Subsidy shall continue upon this Foot during all the Time that this Body of Troops shall remain in B Pay. His Britannick Majesty engages also to give Notice to the Mod Serene Landgrave of its Determination, Twelve Months, or a whole Year, before it shall take Place, which Notice shall not even be given before this Body of Troops is returned, and actually arrived in the Dominions of the said Prince, namely, in , properly so called: His Majesty shall continue equally to this Corps the Pay and other Emoluments for the Remainder of the Month in which it shall repats the Frontiers of HeJJe, and his Mod Serene Highness reserves to him-

self, on his Side, the Liberty of recalling his Troops at the End of Four Years, if they are not sent back before, or to agree with His Britannick Majesty at the End of that Time for another Term.

7-

With regard to the Pay and Treatment, as well Ordinary as Extraordinary, of the said Troops, they shall be put)on the same Foot in all Respects with the National British Troops, and His Majesty’s Department of War shall deliver, without Delay, to that of his Mod Serene Highnefe, an exact and faithful State of the Pay and Treatment enjoyed by those Troops; which Pay and Treatment, in Consideration that His Mod Serene Highness could not put this Corps in a Condition to march in so short a Time, without extraordinary Expences, shall commence for the First Division on the first of February, and for the Second Seven Days ..Before it shall begin to march, and shall be paid into the Military Chest of without any

Abatement or Deduction, to be distributed according to the Arrangements which shall be made for that Purpose; and the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds Sterling shall be advanced immediately on Account of the said Pay.

8.

If it should happen, unfortunately, that any Regiment or Company of the said Corps, should be ruined or destroyed,.either-by Accidents on the Sea, or otherwise, in the Whole, or in Part, or that the Pieces of Artillery, or other Effects, with which they shall be provided, should be taken by the Enemy, or loft on the Sea, His Majesty, the King of Great , shall cause to be paid the Expences of the necessary Recruits,

as well as the Price of the said Field Pieces and Effects, in order forthwith to re-instate the Artillery,’and the said Regiments or Companies; and the said Recruits shall be settled likewise, on the Foot' of ‘ those which were furniftieti to the Hejpan Officers, by, virtue, of the Treaty of 1702, (Article 5th) to the End' that the Corps may be always preserved and sent back in as good.i State as it was delivered, in The Recruits an-- nually necessary shall be sent tb the Commissary,

disciplined arid completely equipped, at the Place of Embarkation,'at such Time as Hh Britannick Majesty shall appoint. . *
