In Europit His Majesty shall make use <?f this'Eody #of Troops by Land, wherever He shall judge proper; 'but North America is the only Country of the other Parts of the Globe where this Body of Troops shall be employed' ' They‘shall not serve on the Sea;

and they shall enjoy, in all Things, without any Restriction whatsoever, the same Pay and Emoluments as are enjoyed by the English Troops.

10.

In case the Mod Serene Landgrave should be attacked or disturbed in the Possession of his Dominions, His Britannick Majesty promises and engages to give him all the Succour that it shall be in his Power to afford, which Succour shall be continued to him until he shall have obtained an entire Security and just Indemnification: As the Most Serene Landgrave promises likewise, on his Part, that in case His Majesty, the King of Great B, is attacked or disturbed in His Kingdoms, Dominions, Lands, Provinces, or Towns, he will give Him in like Manner all the Succour that it shall be in his Power to afford, which Succour shall likewise be continued to Him until he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace.

1 r.

In order to render this Alliance and Union the more perfect, and to leave no doubt with the Parties about the Certainty of the Succour, which they have to expert by Virtue of this Treaty, it is expressly agreed, That to judge for the future, whether the same of this Alliance, and the stipulated Succour, exists, or not, it shall suffice, that either of the Parties is actually attacked by Force of Arms, without his having first used open Force against Him who attacks Him.

12.

The Sick of the Hejfian Corps shall remain under the Care of their Physicians, Surgeons, and other

Persons, appointed for that F*urpose, under the Orders of the General commanding the Corps of that Nation, and every Thing shall be allowed them that His Majesty allows to His own Troops.

1 3-

All the Hessian Deserters shall be faithfully given up, wherever they shall be discovered, in the Places dependant on His Britannick Majesty, and above all, as far as it is possible, no Person whatever of that Nation shall be permitted toestablish himself in America without the Consent of his Sovereign.

14-

All the Transports for the Troops, as well for the Men as for the Effects, shall be at the Expence of His Britannick Majesty; and none belonging to the said Corps shall pay any Pottage of Letters in Consideration of the Distance of the Places.

15-

The Treaty shall be ratified by the High contracting Parties, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged as soon as possible.

In Witness whereof. We, the undersigned, fumished with the full Powers of His Majesty the King of Great Britain on one Part, and-of His Most Serene Highness the Reigning Landgrave of Hejfe on

the other Part, have signed the present Treaty, and have caused the Seals of our Arms to be put thereon. Done at CaJJell, the 15th of January, in the Year 1776.

(L. S.) William Faucitt. (L. S.) M. Schlieffen

Translation of a Treaty between His Majesty and the Hereditary Prince of HeJJe Cajfell, Reigning Count of Hanau, &c. Signed at Hanau the 5 th February 1776.

Be it known to all whom it may concern. That His Majesty the King of Great Britain having judged proper to accept a Body of Infen try of the Troops of His Mott Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince of Hejfe Cajfell, Reigning Count of Hanau, i3c. to be employed in the Service of Great Britain, the High Contracting Parties have given Orders for this Purpose to their respective Ministers; that is to say. His Britannick Majesty to Col* William Faucitt, Captain of the Guards, and the Most Serene Hereditary Prince of HeJJ'e CaJJell to His Minister and Privy Counsellor Frederick de Maljbourg, who, after the Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Art. 1.

The feid Most Serene Prince yields to His Britannick Majesty a Body of Infantry of Six hundred Sixty-eight Men, which shall be at the entire Disposition of the King of Great Britain.

Art. 2.

The Most Serene Prince engages to equip copi-pleatly this Corps; and that it shall be ready to march the 20th of the Month of March next at fertheft. The said Corps shall pass in Review; before His Britannick Majesty’s ComUissary at Hanau, if that can be done, or at some other Place as Opportunity shall offer.

Art. 3.

The Most Serene Prince engages to furnish the Recruits annually necessary. These Reeruits shall be delivered to His Britannick Majesty’s Commissary, dif-ciplined and compleatly equipcd, His Most Serene

Vol. 35.

Highness will do His utmost that the Whole may arrive at the Place of their Embarkation at the Time His Majesty shall fix upon.

Art. 4.

The Service of His Britannick Majesty, and the Preservation of the Troops, requiring equally that the Commanding :OfEcers and Subalterns should be perfectly accquainted with the Service, His Most Serene Highness will, take proper Care in the Choice of them.

Art. 5.

The Most Serene Prince engages to put this Corps on the best Footing poftiblej and none shall be admitted into it, but Persons proper for Campaign Service, and acknowledged as such by His Britannick Majesty’s Commiftary.

Art. 6.

This Corps shall be furnished with'Tents, and all necessary Equipage.

Art. 7.

The King grants to thisJCorps*the Ordinary and Extraordinary Pay, as well as all the Advantages in Forage, Provisions, Winter Quarters, and Retrefh-ments, &c. &c. enjoyed by lihei Royal Troops: And the Most Serene Prince engages toulpbthis? Corps enjoy all the Emoluments of Pay that His {Britannick Majesty allows them. The Sick and ' Wounded of the said Corps shall be taken Care of ^in t>the King’s Hospitals, and shall be treated in this Respect as His Britannick Majesty’s Troops: andj the Wounded not in a Condition to serve, shall be transported-into Europe, and sent back into their own Country, at the Expence of the King.

Art. 8.

There shall be paid to His Most Serene Highness, under the Title of Levy Money, for each Foot Soldier Thirty Crowns Banco, the Crown reckoned at Fifty-

three

Treaties

for

Subsidiary

TVoops.

i90 Februariu

- As* 1776.;

three Sols of Holland: One Half of this Levy Money shall be paid Six Weeks after the Signature of the Treaty; and the other Half Three Months and an Half after the Signature.

Art. 9.

According to Custom, Three wounded Men shall be reckoned as One killed: A Man killed shall be paid for at the Rate of the Levy Money. If it shall happen that any Company of this Corps should be entirely ruined or destroyed, the King will pay the Expence of the necessary Recruits to re-establish this Corps.

Art. 10.

The Most Serene Prince reserves to Himself the Nomination to the vacant Employments, as also the Administration of Justice; moreover, His Britannick Majesty will cause Orders to be given to the Commander of the Army in which this Corps shall serve, not to exact of this Corps any extraordinary Services, or such as are beyond their Proportion with the rest of the Army; and when they shall serve with the English Troops, or with other Auxiliaries, the Officers shall command (as the Military Service requires of itself) according to their Military Rank, and the Seniority of their Commissions, without making any Dif-tindion of what Corps the Troops may be with which they may serve. This Corps shall take the Oath of Fidelity to His Britannick Majesty, without Prejudice to that they have taken to their Sovereign.

Art. 11.

Their Pay shall commence Fifteen Days before the

March ,of this Body of Trpops; and from the Time the Troops shall have qbitted their Quarters in order to repair to the Place of their Destination, all the Expences of March and Transport, as well as of the Future Return of the Troops into their own Country, shall be at the Charge of His Britannick Majesty.

Art. 12.

His Britannick Majesty will grant to the Mofl Serene Prince, during all the Time that this Body of Troops shall be in the Pay of His Majesty, an Annual Subsidy of Twenty-five thousand and Fifty Crowns Banco. His Majesty shall cause Notice of the Cessation of the aforesaid Subsidy to be given a whole Year before it shall ceaie to be paid; provided that this Notice shall not be given till after the Return of the Troops into the Dominions of His Mofl Serene Highness.

This Treaty shall be ratified by the High Con-trading Parties, and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged as soon as possible. In Witness whereof We the underlined, in virtue of our full Powers, have signed the pretent Treaty, and have thereto put the Seals of our Arms.

Done at Hanau the 5th of February 1776.

(L. S.) William Faucitt.

(L. S.) Frederick Bn de Mal/bourg.

Chatham Sir Charles IVhltworth reported from the Committee, Street*. to whom the Petition of the Commissioners for putting in Execution an Act made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King George the Third, for the better paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets and Lanes in the Town and Parish of Chatham, in the County of Kent, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House: and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vim.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act was read; and,

Mr. George Taylor, being examined, said, That, the Commissioners appointed to put the said Act in Execution had caused the greatest Part of the Street, and the Lanes communicating the rewith, to be paved and repaired.

That a certain Part of the High Street of the said Town is situated in the Parish of St. Margaret, next the City of Rochester, and another Part thereof in the Parish of Gillingham, in the said County of Kent, by reason whereof Doubts have arisen, whether the said former Act empowers the Commissioners to pave, cleanse, light, and watch such Parts of the said High Street, and Lanes adjoining, as lie out of the Parish of Chatham: And that the said Act has been found in several other Respects defective.

That it will be a great Advantage and public Convenience to the Inhabitants of that Part or the Parish of Saint Margaret's, commencing at a Boundary Stone, next a Plate called The Chapel Steps, in the Parish of Chatham, Kid extending along the South Side of Chatham High Street and Saint Margaret's Bank to a House called The Flying Horse, in the Parish of Saint Nicholas, within the City of Rochester, and also that Part of the Parish of Gillingham which adjoins the High Street of the Town of Chatham, and the several Lanes respectively adjoining, if the Paving thereof was put under the Management »id Direction of the Commissioners appointed by the said former Act.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to explain and amend an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of His present Majesty, for paving, cleansing, lighting, and watching the Streets and Lanes, in the Town and Parish of Chatham in the County of Kent, and for removing and preventing Nuisances and Annoyances therein; and to extend the Provisions of the said Act to such Parts of the Street in Chatham as are

situate in the Parishes of Saint Margaret and Gillingham, and to other Places adjoining or contiguous to the said Town: And that Sir Charles Whitworth and Mr. Whitworth do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Edward Foley reported from the Committee, to Du Hey whom the Petition of several Persons, whole Names are Caual* thereunto subscribed, residing in and near the Town of Dudley, in the County of Worcester, and concerned or interested in Lands, Mines, Trade, and Manufactures there, was referred; That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, relative to Navigation Bills, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to rejxirt the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the lie-port in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Yeomans, an Engineer, being examined, laid, he had surveyed the greatest Part of the Lands through which the Canal is meant to be made, and that it may be easily executed agreeable to the Plan annexed.

Mr. Robert Whitworth, being examined, confirmed Mr. Yeomans' Evidence: And,

Mr. Thomas Hately, being examined, laid, he had surveyed such Part of the lands through which the Canal is intended to be made, as had not been surveyed by Mr. Yeomans: That the Canal may be easily made through the Part lb by him surveyed, according to the Plan annexed to the Petition: That the Canal will open into several large Collieries, and bring Coals to Market, and Goods to and from the down of Dudley, which is a great manufacturing Town, and be of great public Utility.

Mr. Richard Mee, being examined, laid. That a Canal, as described in the Plan, would be of general Advantage to the adjacent Country, and of public Utility, particularly by reducing the Price of Coals.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for making and maintaining a Navigable Cut, or Caaal, from certain Lands belonging to Thomas Talbot Foley,

Butohen The Lord Mayor of London reported from the Com-Company. mittee, to whom the Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Alfillants, of the Art or Mystery of Butchers of the City of London, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; a State whereof they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his *5

Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table.

Ordered, That the Lord Mayor of London have Leave to make a Motion, it being near Eight of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly.

And the said Report was read j and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition is as follows:

It appeared to your Committee, that his late Majesty King George the Second did, by his Royal Letters Patent, under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing Date the 10th Day of October, in the Twenty-third Year of his Reign, incorporate the Freemen of the Society of the Art or Mystery of Butchers, within the City of London, and all Persons who then did, or thereafter should use or exercise the said Art or Mystery, within the said City, the Liberties and Suburbs thereof, and within the Space of Two Miles of the said City, with Power for the said Corporation to overlook, inr speft, and govern all Persons exercising or using the said Art or Mystery, and to inspect all Flesh Meat exposed for Sale within the Limits* aforesaid; and with full Power and Authority to make Bye-Laws, for the better and more effectual carrying the Intent of the said Letters Patent into Execution; and that, by virtue of the Powers granted to the said Company by their Charter, they did make and establish divers Bye-Laws, Rules, and Regulations, for the better governing the Members of the said Corporation, by which every Member thereof is to pay the Sum of Four Shillings annually, to be applied for carrying the Purposes of the said Charter into Execution; which laid Bye-Laws, Rules, and Regulations were approved of and signed by the late Earl of Hardwick, then Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, the Right honourable Sir William Lee, Chief Justice of the Court of King’s Bench, and the Right honourable Sir John Chief Justice

of the Court of Common Pleas.

And it appeared to your Committee, by the Examination of several Witnesses, that the said Company had frequently detested Persons exposing unwholesome Flesh Meat to Sale, and had caused such Meat to be publicly burnt; and that in case they could allow competent Salaries to a proper Number of Persons to attend and inspect all Markets, and other Places, within the Limits of their Charter, where Flesh Meat is fold, the pernicious Practice of exposing to Sale unwholesome Meat might in a great Measure be prevented; but that the employing a sufficient Number of Persons for that Purpose will be attended with a great Expence.

And it further appeared to your Committee, that all the Members of the said Corporation who are free of the Company, pay Four Shillings annually towards defraying the Expences of the said Corporation but Doubts have arisen whether such Members of the said Corporation as are not free of the said Company, can be compelled to contribute towards defraying the Expences of the said Corporation; and that, unless all such Members can be compelled to pay the like annual Sum as the Freemen of the said Company now pay, and some further Powers granted to the said Company, they cannot put a Stop to the pernicious Practice of exposing to Sale unwholesome Flesh Meat within the Limits of their Charter.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for better enabling the Company of Butchers of the City of London to prevent exposing unwholesome Flesh Meat to Sale within the Limits of their Charter: And that the Lord Mayor of London and Mr. Skipwith do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

And then Hie House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Ten of the Clock,

Mr. Thomas Cofway, Master Attendant at Deptford Tpd, being examined, informed; your Committee, That the Blocks that ..have beefi under his Inspection, and made by Mr. Taylor y are of greater Utility than any Blocks heaver law; and that by the Use of the said Blocks a great Saving accrues to Government, as well as to Trade in general, at least One Fourth Part being saved in the Expfence; and that they are much quicker of Use, add to Purchase, and contribute more to the Expedition in working a Ship, than any other Blocks, so that Two Men will perform as much with these as Three Men can with Blocks upon the old Construction.

Then a Member present informed your Committee, That he was well acquainted with the Utility of the said Blocks, having been at the Works; and that they are superior to any other Blocks.

Another Member present informed your Committee, That he Was a Commissioner of the Admiralty when these Blocks were examined and compared with those which had been before in Use; and that by the unanimous Opinion of the Board of Admiralty, they were recommended to the NavyiBoard. And,

iC " Navy Office, 5th August 1762.

" In Obedience to the Directions of the Right honbl° " the Lords Commissioners of 'the Admiralty, we have " taken into Cdnsideration tl>£ Proposal of Mr. Walter " Taylor, for erecting Engines in His Majesty’s Yards for making Blocks for the Navy, after a better " Method than is now practised; and having examined " the Patterns Mr, Taylor had provided, we directed " an Experiment to be made of their; Utility in His Majesty’s Yard at Deptford, at which tome of the " Members of this Board were present. In the course " of the Trial we were fully satisfied of the Advan-H tages that would be obtained by the Use of thfcfe " Blocks; as by their being cut with greater Accuracy " than those with which the Navy is at present supplied, the Friction is considerably reduced, and the " Purchase CQnfeque&tly increased: We are therefore " of Opinion this Improvement will be of great Benefit " to His Majesty’s Service, hoping that a considerable " Saving will be made by the L'fe of them, in the Wear " S>{ the Blocks and Rigging of the Fleet.

Then several Blocks of the Invention of Mr. Taylm, And Blocks upon the old Construction, were produced to your Committee; and it appeared upon Inspection and Comparrfon of the said Blocks, that the former were much stronger, and attended with a much less Degree of Friction; and that they were wrought with a wonderful Degree of Accuracy.

Mr. John Gofnell being examined, said. That he re-, membered very near the first Construction of those Blocks; that Mr. Taylor had been at a very great Expence in erecting the Engines, and injured his Health very much by his great Application to them.; that the Profit arising therefrom was not adequate to the Labour; and the Witness knew that Mr. Taylor was a great Loser by them — That Mr. Walter Taylor, the present Patentee, has been at great Expence in making Improvements, and by the Methods now taken by him, and the Expence of a Water-Mill, very considerable Improvements have been made. And,

Mr. John Lowe informed your Committee, That he had teen the said Water-Mill, and that he was a Judge of it, and knew it must have cost Mr. Taylor more than £.1,000. Then,

Mr. James Sheene informed your Committee, That, he knew the deceased Mr. Taylor, and was well acquainted with him; and that from the Trouble and Expence of prosecuting this Invention, he not only injured his Health, but almost ruined his Family; that the Witness believes it cost him 12 or £. 14,000; and that unless the Term of the said Letters Patent is pro~ longed, Mr. Taylor cannot be paid the Expences he has been at.

Upon the whole your Committee have come to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a reasonable Compensation for their Trouble and Expences, ought to be made to Pfersons who shall be summoned by an Order of the.House, to attend this House, to be examined as f Witnesses in any Inquiry into Matters of Public Concern, and also to such Persons as may be necessarily employed in the Course of such Inquiry.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Mr. Speaker be desired to take upon himself the Trouble of settling such reasonable Compensation.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleated to give Directions for the Payment of such reasonable Compensation, as from time to time shall be settled by Mr. Speaker; and to allure His Majesty, that this House wijl make good the lame. \

Mr. Darner reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town of in the County of Dorset, whole Names are thereunto fubi'cribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and after* wards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the tame was read; and is as followeth; 'viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Templeman, being examined, said. That the Streets,

Lanes, and other Public Passages, within the said Town, are in general very ill cleansed, lighted, and watched, and the Paths and Passages thereof greatly obstructed by Nuitances and Annoyances; and the Footways (many Parts of which are Turnpike, are very inconvenient for walking on, and particularly those of the Turnpike, cannot be remedied by the Trustees on account of the Insufficiency of the Revenues; and both the Horse and Foot Ways of such Parts as are not Turnpike are in a very ruinous Condition.

That On the 11 th Day of July last, a sudden Fire broke out in the Raft Street of the said Town, and by reason of the many thatched Houses in that Part of the Town, in a very short Time, consumed several Dwelling Houses and Outhouses; and the whole Town was in great Danger of being destroyed.

That it would tend greatly to the Health, Safety, and Advantage of the Inhabitants of the said Town, and be of public Utility, if the said Streets, Lanes, Alleys, and other public Passages, were properly cleansed, lighted, and watched, and the Nuisances, Obstructions, and Annoyances removed; and the Foot Ways of such Parts thereof as are Turnpike were rendered more convenient; and allb if the Horse, and Foot Ways of such Parts thereof as are not Turnpike were better repaired; and it would conduce to the preventing future Dangers by Fire, if thatched Houses ant! Buildings were prohibited in the said Town.

Mr. Robert Stickland confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Templeman i and added, that Twenty-two Dwelling Houses were destroyed by - the Fire which happened in the said Town on the nth of July last, exclusive of several Outhouses and other Buildings.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for better cleansing, lighting, and watching, the Streets, l anes, and other public Passages, within the Borough of

Dorchester, in the County of Dorset, and in the Tithing of Colliton Row, in the Town of Dorchester aforesaid; for

paving the Footways of such Parts thereof as are Turnpike; and for paving the Footways, and repairing the Horseways of such Parts thereof as are not Turnpike; for removing Nuisances, Annoyances, and Obstructions therein; and for preventing Houses or Buildings, hereafter to be erected in the said Borough and Ty thing from being thatched: And that Mr. Darner, Mr. Ewer, and Mr. Bond, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Mr. St. John reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Liardet, of Great Street, in

the Parish of St. Martin's in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex, Clerk, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fad: contained in the said Petition, a State whereof they had directed him to-re-port to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame-was read; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as follows:

letters Patent, dated the 3d Day of April, in the 13th Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, granting to the Petitioner an exclusive Privilege of making, using, and vending, a Composition or Cement for all the Branches concerning Buildings to which the same is applicable, with a certain Grease therein mentioned, for the Term of Fourteen Years, were produced to your Committee, and read.

Then a Specification executed by the Petitioner and inrolled in the Court of Chancery, within the Time limited by the said Letters Patent, describing the Nature of the said Invention, and in what Manner it was to be performed, was also produced, and read: And,

Mr. John Kennedy informed your Committee, That he was acquainted with every Branch of Building, and knew that the Composition used in Mr. s In-

vention was different from all others, and more useful; that, to the bell of his Remembrance, it began to be used last May was a Twelvemonth; that Mr. Liardet has from time to time made many Experiments, which, on Account of the Dearness of the Materials, and their being often loft in the Experiment, have been attended with great Expences; that the Materials used in the said Invention are Thirty Times more expensive than Materials generally used in that Sort of Work; that Mr. Liardet has made several Improvements in the said Invention, since the Commencement of the Letters Patent, both in the Application and Composition; and that the said Invention will be of great Use to the Public in the Building Way, nothing more so.

That there is a great Difficulty in teaching Workmen the Use of the said Materials, it being a new Thing to them; and when first employed, they destroy both Time and Materials, but when they are acquainted with the Use of them, they may easily counterfeit the Invention, as they are privy to the whole Process.

That tire Use of the said invention is not generally known, and the Public are apt to doubt of its Utility at first; Builders in general are backward of trying it, and'a longer Time is required than the Term of the Patent, before the Public in general can be acquainted With the Usefulness of the said Invention.

>4

And the Witness further said. That the said Invention is of such Utility, that it well delcrve? some public Encouragement. Then,

Mr. Andrew Thoruthwaite, being examined, confirmed the Whole of Mr. Kennedy's Evidence; and added. That he is well acquainted with Buildings, and had leen this Composition used in a great Number'of In (lances; and that he had frequently executed it himself.

That many other Inventions have been tried for covering the ©utiides of Buildings, but none are so useful as this, no other Materials being equal to those; and when the Invention is more known, it will be more useful than any other Composition; and that it is of equal Hardness with Portland Stone, or any other.

And the Witness further said, That it must be a considerable Time before the Inventor can derive an adequate Compensation for his Time, Trouble, and Expence, because of the Shyness of Builders to use, and the Time it will require to establish the Character of it, must run away with a considerable Part of the remaining Time the Patent has to run.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for vesting in John Liardet, Clerk, his Executors, Administrators, and Assigns, the sole Use and Property of a certain Composition or Cement, of his Invention, throughout His Majesty’s Kingdom of Great Britain, and in the Colonies and Plantations abroad, for a Time to be limited: And that Mr. St. John, Mr. Adam, and Sir Charles Whitworth, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

A Petition of the Commissioners for building W minster Bridge, being offered to be presented to the House;

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having ‘been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are, by virtue of several Acts of Parliament, palfed in the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, constituted, appointed, and continued Commissioners for building a Bridge crols the River Thames, from The Woolfiaple, or thereabouts, in the City of to the opposite

Shore, in the County of Surrey, and for maintaining, preserving, and supporting the lame, when built; and are allb, amongst other Things, empowered to delign, assign, and lay out, such Ways, Streets, and Passages, as they should think proper to be'opened and made on each Side of the River Thames, leading to and from the said Bridge, the Courts of Justice, and both Houses of Parliament, and the Parts adjacent, and to agree for and purchase such Houses and Ground, within certain Limits by the said Acts prescribed, as they should think proper to be possessed of; and that the Petitioners, in pursuance of the Powers vested in them by the said Acts, have, with the utmost Care, caused the said Bridge to be built, which has been passable many Years; and that the Petitioners have likewise, from time to time, proceeded with the greatest Caution and Frugality, in carrying into Execution the other Trulls reposed in them by the said Acts, which, as they apprehend, may appear by such States of their Proceedings and their Treasurer’s Accounts as have been annually laid before the House; but the Petitioners find that they cannot make an effectual and conllant Provision for the maintaining, supporting, cleansing, watching, lighting, paving, and gravelling the said Bridge, and preserving the feme from Annoyances and other Damages, unless Monies be granted to the Petitioners for those Purposes: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant them such Sums of Money as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

African A Petition of the Committee of the Company of Company. ^Merchants trading to A, being offered to be presented to the House j

The Lord North, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty, having been , informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recom-

4 mends it to the Confederation of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners have laid before the louse an Account of the Money granted for the ear 1774, examined and parted by the Cursitor Baron of the Exchequer, as required by an Act of the 23d of George the Second, intituled, "An Act for extending and improving the Trade to Africa and that they have inverted the Money granted in ;1775 for the Support and Maintenance of the Forts ‘ and Settlements on the said Coast; and that the said Forts and Settlements having been delivered to the Petitioners in a very bad State by the Royal; African Company, and the Sums annually granted

by Parliament being nearly expended in the Civil and Military Establishments, leaving very little for the Repairs of the said Forts, several of them Hill remain in a very ruinous Condition; and that the House, in the Year 1772, granted the Sum of £. 2,400 to finish the Repairs of Cape Coast ,but that the Walls of that Fort were found in lb very decayed a State, and many new Defects discovered in the Progress of the Works, which could not be foreseen, that the Petitioners have been unavoidably led into the Expence of a much larger Sum of Money than was granted by Parliament for that Service, and the Repairs of the said Fort still remain unfinished; and that the Petitioners being sensible of the great Regard shewn by the House for the British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Sum, for the necessary Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, and likewise for the Repairs Hill wanted, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That in order to prevent Mischiefs that niight happen by Fire, it will be necessary that Goods, under certain Circumstances, should be prohibited from being landed on the present Quays, and the Merchants who generally import those Sorts of Goods have had Two Meetings with the Committee of the Society, to consult what Proportions of the Cargoes of Lumber and enumerated Naval Stores should be prohibited from being landed on the present Quays; and it was then agreed, that -when Two Third Parts of a Cargo consisted of the above Articles, those Ships should not be allowed to discharge the Naval Stores or Lumber, at the present Quays, but be compelled to discharge them at the intended Quays of the New Dock; and the Rates to be paid for the same, and for Housing and Storing such Goods, were settled between the Merchants Importers and the Committee, whenever the intended New Quays should be established:

That, in order to effect the several Purposes aforesaid, it will be necessary for the Society to purchase feme Land in the said Parish of Clifton for the Purpose of enlarging the said Dock, building Quays, Warehousesi, and Sheds, and making other Conveniences as aforesaid; and as the Bull nets transaded there will be chiefly by Persons who are concerned in the Trade of the City of Bristol, it would be of great Benefit and Convenience to have the Jurisdiction of the said City extended to such Part of the said Parish of where the Business

mud be transaded, for the Trial of all Offences, and settling all Disputes and Differences that may arise or happen there.

The Witness further laid, That great Frauds and Abuses are committed by Persons loading Lighters for supplying Ships in the said Port with Ballast:; and it is necessary that they should be put under fotne Regulations, for at present Ships frequently go to Sea with not more than Two Thirds of the Ballast they pay for, and in Gales of Wind are greatly endangered thereby.

Mr. Samuel Worrull (Clerk to the said Society), being examined, said, That he has attended the Society upwards of Thirty Years, and knows the Port of Bristol; That great Inconveniences have attended the present Manner of landing Pitch, Tar, and Turpentine, Deals, and other Lumber; and it is the general Sense of the Merchants and Inhabitants of the City of , that the Danger by Fire to the Ships in the said Port, and to the Houses and Warehouses within that Part of the said City, which adjoins the Quays, from such Goods being suffered to remain upon the Quays, is very great, and the Landing them at the new-intended Quays, very de-firable, and will be a Convenience to Trade:

That the Society are possessed of a considerable Estate, which, in general, they apply for the Benefit of Trade, and are now considerably in Debt, having expended, within the last Thirty Years, near £. 60,000. £.10,000 whereof, or thereabouts, was, a few Years since, expended in building a Quay Wall; and near £ 15,000 in the Purchase and Completion of the Docks in the said Parish of Clifton.

That, in order to extend the Quay on the Western Side of the Floating Dock, as well as to enlarge the Dock itself, it will be necessary to purchase Four Sixth Parts of about Nine Acres of Ground, of which the Society are seised of the other Two Sixth Parts; and that a Minor is interested in such Four Sixth Parts.

And the Witness confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Jones, as to the Benefits which would accrue to the Parties concerned in the Trade of the City of Bristol, if the Jurisdiction of the said City was extended over certain Parts, of the said Parish of Clifton, for trying Offences, and settling Disputes happening the re.

Mr, ‘Thomas Hayes, (a Merchant of Bristol, but not a

Member of the said Society,) informed your Committee, That he is very largely concerned in the Importation of Naval Stores, and was One of the Merchants who met a Committee oi the said Society, to adjust the Establishing of a legal Quay, in the Parish of , for the Purposes-

aforesaid, and settling the Rates payable for the fame, and to restrain the Landing the several enumerated Articles, in certain Proportions, upon the present Quays, within the said City; and it was the unanimous Opinion' of all the Merchants who attended that Meeting, that the Regulations proposed by the said Society would be particularly beneficial to the Trade of the City of Bristol, and would be a Benefit to Trade in general; and that extending the Jurisdiction of the City of Bristol to the said Docks and Places before-mentioned would be of Benefit to the Merchants and all Persons concerned in the Trade of the said Port.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, to remove the Danger of Fire amongst- the Ships in the Port of Bristol, by preventing the Landing large Quantities of Timber, Deals, Staves, Tar, Pitch, Turpentine, and other Lumber, on the present Quays, and for providing a convenient Quay, and proper Places in the Parish of Clifton, in the County of for

[Standing Orders of the House, of 25th April 1774, relating to Navigations, read.]

Mr. George White Junior (Agent for the Petition).

I am not prepared to prove the Allegations of the Petition — the Witnesses not being yet tome up.

Have you any Plan of the Harbour, or the proposed Improvements?

No — and if I had had one, I should not have annexed it to the Petition, believing that it does not come within the Meaning of the Standing Orders relating to Navigations.

Has any Notice been given in the Papers ?

No — I conceive the House has determined that Point, by referring it to a Committee.

Have you a Copy of the intended Bill ?

No — I never law one.

In high Spring Tides near 20 Feet — and in Neap Has more Water come through that Passage within Tides not above 7 Feet sometimes. the last Three Years than before ?

What at low Water ?

About a Foot and an Half — it deepens upon the River by the Freshes — lad Winter I, could walk from Stone to Stone, without being over my Ancles, at the Time of the lad Frod — In Summer Time it is the lame.

For what Purpose was the Pile on the North Side erected ?

For the Preservation of the Ground, and to prevent the Works being washed away that were already erected there — it was erected at the Expence of Trustees appointed by the Ship Owners and Mailers.

Was it at any Rate erected for the Purpose of making the Darwent navigable ?

To affid the Navigation of the River Darwent.

Is it a navigable River ?

Only when the Tide is in the Ebbs from the Works not Ids than a Quarter of a Mile.

Don’t you under and it is navigable by the Influx of the Sea ?

Yes.

How far do Ships lay up that Part of the Ifarbour called the South Gut ?

Near John Smith's House — they discharge Timber there frequently.

Do you know the Limits of the Harbour?

I know what are reported the Limits — I can describe it by Nothing but the Notice at the Exchequer.

Whether those Piles were drove in for the Preservation of the Harbour, or to penn the Water for better assisting the Navigation of the River Darwent ?

For the Preservation of the Harbour only.

Have you not heard from old People, that the Harbour extended up as high as Cloddy Hole in the River

Darwent, and as high up the Mill Race as Margaret Miller's House ?

I have heard it so reported.

Was not the Limits so marked in the Plan you was present at the taking of ?

Yes.

Do you know how that Line came to be erafed in the Plan?

No.

What Persons ship Coals within the Limits of the Harbour ?

Sir James Lowther, Mr. Curwen. and Mr. Bacon.

In what Proportions ?

I can’t answer — nor make any Calculation.

Have any considerable Sums of Money been raised for supporting the Harbour ?

Since I have had the Collection, about £.9,000. has been raised by a voluntary Contribution of the Owners and Maders of Shipping, ascertained by the Quantity of Coals faken in, in the Name of Tonnage.

For what Purpose has it been applied ?

For the Preservation of the Harbour — deepening, enlarging, and preferring it, by the Direction of the Trustees appointed by the Maders and Owners of Shipping.

By the Tncrcafe of the Trade, the Harbour is too final!, and liable to be incommoded by Land Floods and high Tides.

>7

The Breach in the Pile Work was fir'd begun in October 1773.

Did you ever know Ships fail across that Point of Land called the Low Cloffack, from the North Side of the Harbour to the South ?

I do remember Two, in a high Tide, about Twenty Years ago, failed quite across; and anchored in the Race — the River Darwent run that Way about Sixty-five Years ago, as I have heard People lay, who are living.

Are there not large Overflowings of the River Darwent in the Old Channel, at high Tides and Land Floods ?

The common Spring Tides cover all the Low Ground.

Same Question ?

Yes — through the Old Coccafioned by its being deepened by a great Flood in 1773, which threw a Quantity of Stuff in the South Gut, and has since been washed deeper by succeeding Floods — before that Period that Old River Course was filled up in a good Measure with Ballad.

What are the Improvements that are proposed in the Harbour ?

They are to extend the Work on the Beach or Strand, on the North Side towards the Sea, as it may be found convenient and necessary for the Safety of the Harbour.

How far do you think it necessary to extend it ?

I think it will be necessary to extend it further than appears by the Plan.

Do you mean to shut up the Channel of the River wholly ?

To dig anew Channel for the River, and then to shut up the North Channel of the River.

What do you propose to do with the Bank thrown up by the Sea ?

The lower Bank is occasioned by the Land Floods — the upper Bank is thrown in by the Sea — I can hardly call the lower one a Bank — It is a flat Beach of Sand and Gravel, which we mean to cut through.

What other Alterations do you propose to make ?

A Cut upon the Rectory Ground at the lower End.

What other ?

To continue the South Key as far up as John Smith's House.

Do you propose to cut, widen, and deepen the Mill Race ?

Yes — in a Line 20 Yards from the North Corner of John Smith’s House, in a Line from the upper End of the present South Key.

Sir Thomas Clavering reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and Freeholders, residing in the County of Northumberland, whose Names are thereitftto subscribed, was referred That the Committee had examined how far the Standing Orders of the House, of the 25th of April 1774, have been complied with, and had dhrested him to report the Evidence thereupon to the House; and that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House $ and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Mr. Edward Hedley being examined, laid, That he law a Notice of the Intention of applying to Parliament for the Purpose mentioned in the Petition, affixed upon the Door of the Sessions House at Alnwick, in the County of Northumberland, upon the Twelfth Day of, Oticber last, being the Time of the last Michaelmas Quarter Sessions: And he produced to your Committee a Copy of the said Notice.

And being further examined, he said, That with an Intention to comply with the Standing Orders of the House, the Promoters of die Bill had also advertised such Notice in the Newcajle Courant, upon the 30th of September, and the 7th and 14th of October last: And he produced the Papers wherein the said Notice was inserted, to your Committee. And he also produced to your Committee, an Estimate of the Expence of making the Road mentioned in the Petition; which is hereunto annexed; and also a List of the Subscribers to the said Road, hereunto also annexed: Whereby it appears that the Expence of making and completing the said Road will amount to the Sum of £.1,800 $ and that the Money subscribed for that Purpose amounts to the Sum of £. 1,420. Then,

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Witness being further examined, laid, That be knows the Road deforibed in the Petition; that it is in very bad Condition at all Times, and particularly so in Winter Time, when it is impafiable for Carriages, and dangerous for Horses; and that he thinks the Stature Work liable to be done upon the said Road is not sufficient to keep the same in proper Repair; and that the said Road cannot be amended, altered, and kept in good Repair, by the ordinary Methods provided by Law. — And the Witness further said, That the present Road crosses the River Reed in many Places, and cannot be effectually made without some Alterations in the Course thereof; and that the making and completing the said Road will be very useful, not only to the Inhabitants on the Borders of England, but also to the Inhabitants on the Borders of Scotland, and of great public Utility.

Mr. Frankland reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Persons belonging to the Theatre Royal, Covent , whole Names are

thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the rest of the said Company, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the feme, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Joseph Booth, being examined, informed your Committee, That in the Year 1765 a Contribution was set on foot for the Purpose of establishing a Fund for the Support of such Performers belonging to the said Company, as by Age, Infirmity, or Accident, should want Assistance, or be under a Necessity of retiring from the Stage, and for the Relief and Support of Widows and Children of deceased Performers, by which Contribution, and other Means, the said Fund has increased to the Sum of £. 4,300, which is placed in the Public Funds in the Names of Trustees, and a considerable Number of proper Objects of Charity have, from time to time, been supported and relieved out of the feme j that the present annual Outgoings are £. 200, and upwards that the Committee for managing the said Fund, to whom he acts as Se* cretary, and the other Persons interested therein, are desirous that Provision should be made for the effectual Security, proper Management, and due Application, of the said Fund, and the Income thereof which, as

it has improved every Year since its Institution, they have reason to hope will be greatly increased.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for feeding a Fund, belonging to certain Persons of the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, applicable to charitable Uses j and for other Purposes: And that Mr. Frankland and Sir Charles Whitworth do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

Me of Wight :«5ir Richard Worfiey reported from the Committee, *>oor* to whom the Petition of the Guardians of the Poor within the Ifie of Wight, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act, made in the Eleventh Year of His present Majesty, for establishing a House or Houses of Industry in the Ifie of Wight, for the Reception, Maintenance, and Employment of the Poor, belonging to the several Parishes and Places within the said Island, was read; And,

Mr. Richard Clarke, Secretary to the Corporation, being examined, said, That the Guardians have proceeded to put the said Act in Execution, to the great Benefit and Advantage of the Inhabitants of the said Bland; but that, by reason of the Insufficiency of the Sum of Money they are authorized to borrow for the Purposes of the said Act, and on account of some Defects therein, with respect to the Regulations authorized thereby, they cannot completely execute the Trusts reposed in them, without the further Aid of Parliament.

And the Witness produced to your Committee, the Treasurer’s Account of Receipts and Disbursements; whereby it appeared, that the whole Money authorized to be borrowed, has been raised; and that there is now in his Hands a Balance of £. 378.

And he also produced to your Committee, their Carpenters and Bricklayers Accounts, as settled by the Corporation; whereby it appeared, that the Sum of £. 1,590. 6s. 7 %d.is now due to them on Balance for Work done in the Execution of the said Act.

And the Witness further said, That many Gentlemen in the Bland have given their own personal Security for the borrowing of more Money, in order that the Object of the said Act might not be flopped: And he thinks, that if the said Act was to be repealed, and the Whole of the Powers included in a new Act, it would be more convenient to the Inhabitants of the said Bland.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to continue the Corporation of the Guardians of the Poor within the Ifie of Wight, and to confirm the Powers and Authorities now vested in the said Corporation, and to provide new Powers and Regulations for the Members of the fame; and to repeal an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Ileign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for establishing a House " or Houses of Industry in the Ifie of Wight, for the " Reception, Maintenance, and Employment, of the " Poor belonging to the several Parishes and Places " within the said Bland And that Sir Worfiey,

Mr. Sloane, and Mr. Stanley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Adam Drummond reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Fish Curers, and other Inhabitants, in the Borough of Saint Ives, concerned in the Pilchard Fishery carried on in the Bay of Saint Ives, in the County of Cornwall, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. William Stephens, being examined, said. That there hath been for many Years pall a considerable Pilchard Fishery carried on in the Bay of; and that

the Fishermen and Fish Curers belonging to the said Fishery, have hitherto carried on the same conformable to certain Customs, or Constitutions, which have been, from time to time, deviled by them for their Government, and which, in general, have been complied with; but that in some Instances they have not been submitted to, whereby great Loss hath happened to the Fishery.

That of late Years the Adventurers in the said Fishery, and the Craft employed therein, are greatly increased, by means whereof the said Customs and Constitutions are more frequently infringed.

And the Witness further laid. That if some Alterations were made in the aforesaid Customs or Constitutions, and some new Regulations made, the said Fishery would be greatly improved and increased.

Mr. John Anthony confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for the Encouragement and Improvement of the Pilchard Fishery within the Bay of Ives, in the County of Cornwall: And that Mr. Adam Drummond, Mr. Eliot, and Sir William Lemon, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Weymouth A Petition of several Inhabitants of the Borough and Streets. Town of Weymouth and Melcombe Regis, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That a Bill is depending, for lighting and watching the Streets and other Places within the said Borough and Town, and for other Purposes; and that there are, within the said Borough and Town, many Houses and other Buildings covered entirely with Straw or Thatch, and that, if a Fire should happen amongst those Houses the said Borough and Town would, in all Probability, be entirely destroyed; and that it would be a great Security to the Property of the Petitioners, if all Persons wi re to be restrained from using Straw or Thatch for ccve ing their Houses and other Buildings, within the said Borough and Town, for the future: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant the Petitioners such Relief as shall be thought proper.

A Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Corporation of Trinity House of Deptford Stroud, was presented to the House, and read: Setting forth. That, by an Acfl passed in the 8th Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, the said Corporation were at all Times thereafter impowered to ereefl and maintain such and so many Beacons, Marks, and Signs for the Sea, in such Places of the Sea Shores and Uplands near the Sea Coasts or Fore-lands of the Sea only, for Sea Marks, whereby Dangers might be avoided, and Ships the better come into their Ports without Peril; and that, by Letters Patent granted by the said Queen, the Office of Beaconage and Buoyage

was granted to the said Corporation and their Successors for ever; and under which Grant the Petitioners are solely entitled to exercise that Office, and to the cretfl-ing and maintaining of all Light Houses, Beacons, Buoys, and other Marks and Signs for the Sea, in all Places in or upon the Sea, Places navigable, and Channels for passing into or out of Havens or Rivers, or Sea Coasts near the Sea, Uplands, or Forelands, or other Places near unto the Sea, as they shall think necessary or convenient; and that, by virtue of the said Letters Patent, the Petitioners are entitled to all Fees, Advantages, Salaries, Profits, and Rights, payable or appertaining to the said Office; and that, upon a Reference from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, the Petitioners lately considered of the Utility of a Light House on the Point of Air, in Flint shire, for the Security of Navigation between Dublin and Chester, as well as Liverpool, and represented to their Lordships, that such Light House would be of public Utility, and that they would carry' the same into Execution, in the usual Way, according to the Powers and Authorities vested in them; and that the Petitioners have been lately informed, by the Votes, that a Bill hath been brought into the House, by which it is proposed, that certain Trustees shall be impowered to erect Two Light Houses, the one at the said Point of Air, and the other at a Place called in Flint*

shire, and to erect Land Marks and place Buoys at certain Places near the Port of Chester, and to take certain Duties from Shipping for defraying the Expences attending the lame; and the Petitioners apprehend, that, if the said Bill should pals, the same will very materially affetfl their Rights, and that they are ready and willing to exercise their laid Right and Power in the Erection of the said Light Houses and other Marks for the Sea, and placing Buoys, as intended by the said Bill, they having a due Compensation in respect thereof by Duties on Shipping: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by themselves, and their Counsel, against lb much of the said Bill as empowers the erecting of Light Houses or other Marks or Signs for the Sea, or the Placing of Buoys, without the Petitioners License and Consent; and that the said Bill, as the same now Hands, may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee, to whom the Bill for erecting Light Houses and Land Marks in or near the Port of Chester, and for placing Buoys upon the Banks and Shoals leading into and in the said Port; and for regulating of Pilots and Persons towing or tracking of Vessels to and from the City of Chester, and for fixing the Rates payable for the same respectively, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by themselves or Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruiflion to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

A Petition of Eduard Richardson, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That, in the Y'car 1756, Admiral Cotes, before the breaking out of the late War, took Four French Ships, which were lent 16

1776.

by him to Jamaica, and condemned as lawful Prizes; and that Edward Manning, of Jamaica, Esquire, deceased, was at that Time Prize-Agent to the Crown, and, upon the Condemnation of the said Ships, took Possession of them, which, together with their Cor-goes, were valued at £.22,200, and upwards, which Sum he never accounted for to the Crown; and that, in the latter End of the Year 1756, the said Edward Manning died, possessed of a real and personal Estate worth £. 120,coo, and his Executors took Possession of his said Estates, Part of which consisted of the said £.22,200, and prevailed upon the Lieutenant Governor of Jamaica to certify to the Lords of the Treasury that he died insolvent; and that the Petitioner, being an Officer of His Majesty’s Customs, about Eleven Years after the Death of the said Edward Manning, made a Discovery to the Lords of the Treasury, that the said Certificate was fraudulently obtained, and that the Estate and Effects of the said Edward Manning would amount to £. 70,000, and upwards, after Payment of his Debts and Legacies; in consideration whereof, the Petitioner received Assurances from the Lords of the Treasury, that he should be paid his Portion of the said £.22,200, as the same should, from time to time, be returned into the Exchequer, for making the said Discovery, and was requested to persevere in the said Investigation, and to spare no Pains and Expence in the Course of it; and that, in order to come at a true State of the Estate and Effects of the said Edward Planning, the Petitioner filed a Bill in Chancery against his Exccu-> tors, which he was expressly directed to do by one of the Secretaries of the Treasury; and the Petitioner, confiding in the said Assurances, did prosecute the said Bill with uncommon Zeal, and was put to great Trouble and Expence in obtaining a Decree in the said Suit, and an Examination of the said Decree, whereby the Existence of the said Estate and Effedcs, to the Amount aforesaid, hath been established; and that the Petitioner acquainted the then Lords of the Treasury with the Account of the said Estate and Eff'edls, and in Consequence thereof their Lordships sent over Orders to Jamaica, and his Majesty’s Officers there took Possession of the said Estate and Effects, and have ever since been in Possession thereof; and that, in the Year 1775, divers Quantities of Silver, amounting to £. 10,000, and upwards, raised from the said Estate and Effects, arrived in,

in Part of the said £. 22,200, subject to tire Directions of the Lords of the Treasury; and upon the Arrival thereof, the Petitioner attended their Lordships, and made divers Applications to them for his Portion promised him, but was always so unfortunate as not to meet with due Encouragement; and that the Petitioner in the last Session of Parliament, prevailed with their Lordships to permit him to present a Petition to the House, upon Condition he w'ould submit such Petition to their Lordships Correction; and accordingly the Petitioner prepared a Petition, and laid it before their Lordships for their Approbation, who expunged from it the material Parts that stated the Petitioner’s Merit, and informed him, by One of their Secretaries, tint if he did not like it in that Shape, he would never get any Thing; and that, on the 2d of May 1775, the said Petition was presented to the House, when the House was pleased to resolve, that £. 550 should be paid to the Petitioner, in Reward and full Satisfaction for his Information and Assistance; and that the Petitioner hath received by Instalments 475 in Part < f the said £.550, but the Residue hath been withheld from him under Pretence that it was due for Fees and Perquisites; and that the Petitioner hath expended, in prosecuting the said Suit in Chancery £. 300, and upwards, for the Costs of that Suit, and ^.300 more incurred in the Course of tracing out the said Estate and EffeCls, anJ for Eight Years pall hath bellowed the

A Petition of the Merchants and Insurers of the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read;

taking Notice of the said Bill; and representing to the House, That the Petitioners, having sustained great LolTes from the Inefficacy of the Laws in being, conceive, that if Persons were encouraged by Rewards, or otherwise it was made the Interest of those, who, by their local Situation, are best enabled to render A Alliance, that then such would warmly exert themselves, as well to preserve the Lives of our brave Seamen, and protest and save Property under such distressful Circumstances, as to prosecute and bring to condign Punishment those who have dared to offend 5 and the Petitioners, having experienced the happy Effects of the Laws adopted by feme other European Powers, when Vessels have been unfortunately wrecked on their Coasts, cannot but think some Regulation to be exceedingly necessary for the Protection of Commerce, and Preservation of our Seamens Lives, from which, our national

And therefore praying, That such a Bill may pass into a Law.

A Petition of several Gentlemen, Farmers, and Turnpike, others. Occupiers of Lands in the West Riding of the ftRoJds:-County of York, in Behalf of themselves and others, \vh*c)s° was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth.

That, by an Act, made in the 13th Year of His present Majesty, to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the General laws now in being for regulating the Turnpike Roads in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for other Purposes, it is Enacted, That, from and after the 29th of September , 1776, all Waggons, and other Carriages, having the Fellies of the Wheels thereof of leis Breadth or Gauge than Six Inches, shall pay double Tolls for passing through any Turnpike Gate or Bar, where Tolls shall be payable by virtue <5f any Act of Parliament; and that the Tire of the Wheels of all Waggons, and other Carriages, to be used upon any Turnpike Road,

.shall be counterfunk, lb (hat the Nails shall not rife above the Surface; and the Owner of every Carriage offending therein, shall forfeit 40 s. and the Driver, not being the Owner, 20 s.for every Offence; and that many Farmers, and others, residing at a considerable Distance from any Turnpike Road, and being obliged to drive through narrow La. ties, and over Moors, several Miles before they come to the Turnpike Road, which Lanes and Moors are, aac3, from the Nature of the Soil, and Want of proper Materials for repairing such Roads, mull for ever be in such Condition as to be impradicable to be used with Wheels of the Breadth of Six Inches, it will be cjuite impossible for the Petitioners, and many others in the like Situation, to get to any Market Town with the Produce of their Lands, or for carrying on their other Concerns, except with Narrow Wheeled Carts and Waggons; and that the additional heavy Toll, laid by the said Act upon Narrow-wheeled Carriages, is so excessive, that the Petitioners, and others, the Occupiers of Lands in the like Situation with them, will be thereby drove to the greateffc Distress; and that the additional Expence, which the Petitioners and others must necessanly be put unto, in getting the Tire of the Wheels of their several Carriages countersink, will be such as several of the "Petitioners are not well able to bear, unless they have further Time allowed them for the wearing out the Tire, which now and heretofore hath been used: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Confi.deration, and to grant such Relief therein as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Mr. Grenville do make the Report Aneicfev from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Re- Co; p;r >.;.,'.es. verend Edward Hughes, Clerk, in Behalf of himself and other Owners and Proprietors of Copper Mines in the Isle of Anglesey, was referred.

Mr. Grenville accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; a State whereof they bad directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was lead; and is as followeth; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fast contained in the said

Petition is as follows; viz.

It appeared by the Evidence of Mr. Thomas Williams,

That there are Two considerable Mines of Copper in the Isle of Anglesey the Ore of which is near the Sur-

face, and that about 30,000 Tons have been taken up within the last Two Years; that the Mines are discovered to a great Extent, and appear at present almost inexhaustible; but that there is no Coal, or other Fuel, in the Isle proper for the Purpose of smelting the Ores:

That Coals brought into the Isle pay a Duty of 5 s. per Chaldron, besides Custom House Fees, which amount to near 2 s.6 d.a Chaldron more, exclusive of Freight:

That no Ore is smelted in the Isle, but is obliged to be carried to Bristol, Swansea, Neath, Warrington, and Liverpooli and that near 10,000 Tons have been smelted. at the above Places, the Expence of which exceeded £ 3,000:

That the Freight of this Ore to Briflof. Swansea, and Neath, is ior. and los.bd. a Ton, and to the other Places about 5J.

That above 20,000 Tons remaih on the Banks of the Mines unfinelted; and that the Ore is of an Inferior Quality, and contains a great Quantity of Sulphur and Drols, which consequently increases the Expence of Carriage — That a much greater Quantity might be smelted on the Spot, if Coals could be had free from Duty, but that it would not be worth the Proprietor’s While to pay the Duty on Coals for smelting the Ore at the Mines; and that none has been smelted there, nor any Duty paid at the Custom House on Coals used for that Purpose.

The Witness further laid. That if a Drawback of the Duties was allowed on Coals used for smelting Ore in the Isle of Anglesey, great Quantities could be smelted there, which would be of Advantage to the Proprietors, contribute to the Employment of the Poor in Anglesey, and prove beneficial to the Public in>general.

A Petition of the Justices of Peace, Gentlemen* Clergy, Land-owners, and Land-holders, of the several Hundreds or Commotts of Carnawllan, and

Derlis, all situate on the Sea Coast of the County of Caermarthen, was presented to the House, and read; taking Notice of the said Bill; and setting forth. That the Petitioners conceive the Laws in being are sufficient to prevent the Evils complained of; and if proper Persons were appointed, to give immediate No- tlce to the Magistrates of Accidents happening by Shipwreck, the Mischiefs of Plundering might be prevented, and the necessary Relief afforded, under the Powers of an Act passed in the 26th of his late Majesty; and submitting to the House, whether some Means of Prevention might not be established, whereby the Purposes of Humanity would be better served,t han by providing Remedies for Evils when they have happened, either by amercing the Hundred, or punishing the Offenders; but that, by the Provisions of this Bill, if a Ship is plundered, the Hundred is to make good the Damage, although every possible Effort of the Magis-tracy has been exerted to prevent it: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may not pafsinto a Law.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, that the said Bill be now read a Second Time;

The House divided.

The Noes went forth.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The Lord North acquainted the House, that he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty, relying on the experienced Zeal and Affection of His faithful Commons, and considering, that, during the present Troubles in North,

Emergencies may arise, which may be of the utmost Importance, and be attended with the most dangerous Consequences, if proper Means should not be immediately applied to prevent or defeat them, is desirous that this House will enable Him to defray any extraordinary Expences incurred, or to be incurred, on account of Military Sen-ices, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred Seventy-six, and as the Exigency of Affairs may require.' And His Majesty, having judged it expedient so issue His Proclamation, in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fourteenth Year of His Reign, for calling in the Remainder of the deficient Gold Coin, doubts not but that His faithful Commons will enable Him to make good the Charges which shall be incurred in this Service, and which cannot at this Tune be ascertained.

R.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s , said most gracious Message be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the Merchants, Traders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town and County of Rooky was prefen ted to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, That Leave is given to bring in a Bill for preventing the inhuman Practice of Plundering Ships that are wrecked on the Coast of Great Britain, and for the further Relief of Ships in Distress on the said Coasts; and, being convinced of the great and repeated Losses, from the Inefficacy of the Laws in being, humbly suppose, that, if Persons were appointed, or if it was made the Interest of those who by their local Situation are belt enabled to render Assistance, that then such would warmly exert themselves, as well to preserve the Lives of our brave Seamen, and protest and fate Property under such distressful Circumstances, as to prosecute with Severity those who shall dare to of* fend; and the Petitioners, knowing the happy Effects of the Laws adopted by some other European Powers when Vessels have been unfortunatly wrecked on their Coast, cannot but think some Regulation to be exceedingly necessary, for the Protection of Commerce, and Preservation of our Seamfens Lives, from which our national Riches and Strength are derived, and which may prove an effectual Means of putting a Stop to a Practice which has long reflected a Pit gace on this Nation: And therefore praying. That such a Bill may pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners called Mr. Jo/htta Am, who being examined, informed your Committee, That he is a considerable Farmer in the West Riding of Yorkshire, and concerned in other Undertakings that employ Horses and Carriages.

And being asked, What further Inconveniences will arise to the Owners of narrow-wheeled Carriages, betides pajnng the double Tolls ? he said, those who live at a Distance from a Turnpike Road will And the Isle of broad Wheels very inconvenient, from the Nature of the Lanes and Roads they mull pals through, before they come to a Turnpike Road, and the Want of Materials in many Places to amend the Roads; and he instanced several Places within his Knowledge; and he added, that Carriages can go over Moors and Marshes better with narrow Wheels than with Broad, because they are lighter, and do not throw up the Soil (o much.

He further said, That, if the double Toll, which he esteems equal to a Prohibition, takes Place, it will be with the greatest Difficulty that little Farmers, who live at a Distance from Turpike Roads, can get to them; for the)- will be obliged to carry their Corn on I lories Backs, or elle in narrow-wheeled Carriages, to the Turnpike Road, and so be obliged to keep Two Sets of Carriages, which they never can afford.

And being asked, If he knows any Market Towns that the Roads leading to them are not Turnpike ? he said, lcarcely any in his County, though they have Bye-Roads likewise.

A Petition of the several Householders in the optional Streets within the Parish of Saint Paul, Covent Garden, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners have borrowed several Sums of Money on the Security of the Rates made by several Acts for paving, cleansing, and lighting the said Streets, and are very desirous to discharge the lame; and that, if Power was given to the Commissioners for paving, cleansing, and lighting the several Streets within the City , and Liberty of to

raise and levy upon each of the said optional Streets any Sum of Money, not exceeding Two Shillings in the Pound, the Petitioners would be thereby enabled to discharge the Monies so due on the said Rates: And therefore praying. That Provision may be made in the Bill now depending, for remedying feme Defects in the several Acts passed for paving, cleansing, lighting, and regulating the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and other Places, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Sir Charles Whitworth, Mr. Whitworth, Sec.: And they are to meet Tomorrow Morning, at Nine of the Clock, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records.
