Mr. Elutesreported from the Committee, who were appointed to insped the Progreis that has been made by the several Persons appointed by Mr. Speaker, to make a General Index to the Journals of this House, and to report the lame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the Iioule; That the Committee had inipccded the same accordingly; and had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Entries in the Journal of the House of the 23d of January 1766, " That a Committee be appointed to consider of a proper Plan for making a " General Index to the printed Journals of this House," and allb the Entry of the 12th of May 1766, of the Report from the said Committee and the Proceedings of the House thereupon, were read:

Your Committee then called Mr. Moore (one

of the Persons employed in framing a General Index to the Journals of this House) who being asked, How long, and when he was first employed in this Work ? he informed your Committee, That he had been employed Eleven Years, and was first appointed in May 1 765, when he was directed to prepare a Plan for a General Index, which he did, and laid it before a Committee of the House for their Approbation in 1766; that in A)ayfollowing lie was appointed to make the

Ger.eral Index, in Conjunction with Mr.; that he proceeded in the Work till about April 1770, when a Ditapprobation of the Plan was signified to him by the present Speaker, who informed him that Doctor Flex-wan had undertaken, and engaged to make a General Index upon a different Plan; that Mr. Speaker then appointed him (the Witness) to assist the Doctor by working under his Direction; that he did so till about Midsummer 1771, when the Doctor’s Work was laid aside; that the Reverend Mr. Fqfter and Mr. Cunningham were then called in to assist in forming a new Plan; that they, the other Gentlemen, and Mr. Moore, began de Novo, and met on the 25th of July 1771 to form a new Plan, and about November following agreed upon a Plan, which was approved of by Mr. Speaker, and the Gentlemen he consulted on the 7 th of January 7772; that then he (the Witness) was ordered to make an Index upon the new Plan to the Sixteen Volumes of the Journals, commencing with the 18th Volume, and ending with the 33d Volume both in-clulive, which is above Half the Work; that he has digested almost all the Matter in Fifteen of his Volumes upon the new approved Plan; that Part of the Matter cantained in the 33d Volume is collected, and that he means to collect the Matter of the 34th Volume, and incorporate it in his Index so as to make a complete General Index to Seventeen Volumes:

He likewise informed your Committee, That Mr. Style, who assisted him for some Years, having been obliged from his great Age and Infirmities to decline the Employ, he thought it his Duty to inform your Committee, that the late Speaker, Sir John Cujl, observing the declining State of Mr. Style’s Health, told him (the W itness) about Two Months before his (the late Speaker’s) Death, that the Work being too laborious for Mr. Style, he would endeavour to get him an Allowance 100 per Annum, during his Life (which he observed cop Id not be long, Mr. Style being near Eighty Years of, Age) apd to let him retire; that the Witness laid, he had mentioned this to the present Speaker, who said he would do something of the same Sort: ... -r.

1 And the Witness informed your Committee, That it appeared by his Accpunt of the Disposition of the £. 2,000 in Sir John , Cust'sTime; that Mr. Style received £. 758. is., and that to the Witness’s Knowledge, the present Speaker gave Mr. Style, the First Year he came to tfTe Chair £. 150, and since then the-

Witness believes, about £. 60 Annually, but he cannot speak positively to that, not having seen Mr. Style these Two Years.

And being asked. What Sums of Money he had received on account of his Labours during this Period' of Eleven Years ?

He produced an Account (which is hereunto annexed) of the Disposition of the £. 2,000 granted by Parliament in the Years 1766, 1767, 1768, and 1769, during the Speakership of Sir John Cujt, which he proved to the Satisfaction of your Committee; by which it appeared that he had received in the Five Years that Sir Jqhn Cujl was Speaker, as follows:

For his Labours in making the Plans and Specimens, and on account of the Work, and for all incidental Expences of an Office, Clerks, &c. 895 19 —

Allb that he had received of the present Speaker for his Labours under Doctor Flexman’s Direction - 150 — —

And since engaged in the new Plan

with Messrs. Foster, Stc. - - 500 -r- — *

So that he has received for his 1 r Years Labour, and for all his incidental Expences, for Assistants, Stationery, Office, &c. - - 1,545 19 —

Out of this Sum he has yet to pay the Fees of passing the Account of the £. 2,000 before the Auditor of the Exchequer, which will at least be £. 50 or £. 60.

And being asked, Whether in the Course of executing his Part of the Work he had from time to time compared what he had done with what had been done by any of the other Gentlemen employed in the said Work ? he answered. That during the Progreis of the Work they had no such Communication, but that within thele few Days, he and the Reverend Mr. Foster had shewn their Works to each other, and that it appeared to the Witness, that the Execution of their Work varied with regard to several Particulars; that however he thought it possible to incorporate them, but it would require so much Time and Trouble, that he himself would not wish to undertake it, but if the Committee should think it proper to divide the Index into Periods making one distinct and separate Index for the Part undertaken by the Witness, and another separate and distinct Index for the Part undertaken by Mr. Forjler, that the Gentlemen who consulted those Indexes would find no great Difficulty in the Transitions from the one to the other, especially if a proper Explanation by way of Preface was annexed to each.

And the Witness being asked, What Time it would still require to complete the Index for his Period to the End of the 34th Volume ? he answered, Three Years.

Then your Committee called the Reverend Roger Flexman, who being asked* At what Time he was first engaged in the Business of making a General Index to the Journals, by what Authority, and how he had proceeded in the said Work ? He informed your Committee, That he was sent for by the present Speaker, about the Middle of Afarch 1770, who proposed to him to undertake the framing of the General Index; that he had several Conventions upon that Subject, with the Speaker, and other Members to whom he was referred; that be stated his Age and other Infirmities as a Reifon for not undertaking it alone, and in June following he was appointed to undertake the Direction, and overlce the Execution of the Work, and that Mr. Mr.

Then Mr. Timothy Cunningham being called 5 and the Paper and Account delivered in by Mr. Speaker being read to him, he confirmed the lame.

And being asked. How he reconciled the Account in that Paper with his Evidence given at a former Committee, where he said, " he had as yet done but about " a Fourth Part of the Work, and that it would still " require Two Years longer to finish the Whole?" he answered. That he was of Opinion* that as the other Gentlemen had made an untrue Repreleotation to Mr, Speaker (which he then thought to be the Oafe, but is now sensible that he was under a Mistake') he had' as good a Right to make an untrue Representation as them, especially as he knew in Point- of InduftVy he was equal to any, perhaps to all of them; having this Idea of Completion or Finiftring, that it must be so prepared, and so ready, as to deliver it to the Printer* Without having any other Alteration than the Correction of the Press, which was not the Cafe.

Your Committee having carefully compared the above Evidence with the Report of the former Committee, which has been referred to their Consideration, and having also further examined the Four different Indexes, are inclined to agree in Opinion with your former Committee; That the best Method to complete the General Index, fq is not to lose the Benefit of the Work already done, will be to comprise the Whole unde?

Three Forms of Indexes, with a proper Explanation to fcach: And as Mr. Cunningham, who had undertaken the first Seven Volumes of the Journals, has informed your Committee, that lie has as yet finished only One Fourth of the said Work, your Committee are of Opinion, that it will be proper to dire ft him to difeon-tinue the present Form of Index on which he has been hitherto employed, and to adopt in its room the Reverend Roger Flexman's Form of Index, and to complete

his whole Period, confiding of the fird Seven Volumes of the Journals, agreeable to that Form.

Edward Moore, and Mr. Cunningham, to proceed in the

£. 127 to pay the Balance due upon the Account produced by Mr. Speaker i And,

£. 100 to be paid to Mr. Style; and the Remainder to pay Fees arid Contingences.

A Petition of the Honourable George Berkeley Glottcefcr

was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, Election. That an Election of a Member to lerve in Parliament for the County of Gloucester began on the 6th Day of May 1776, at which the Petitioner and William Bromley Chester, Esquire, were Candidates; and that Henry

Lippincott, Esquire, High Sheriff of the same County, shewed great and manifest Partiality in Favour of the said William Bromley Chester, and, in the Course and

Progress of the Poll, rejected great Numbers of Votes of Persons who had a Right by Law to vote, and who offered to vote, and demanded of the said Sheriff to be permitted to vote for the Petitioner; and at length# when a very finall Majority of Votes Appeared upon the Poll in Favour of the said William Bromley Chester, the said Sheriff, in an hasty and precipitate Manner, doled the Books, in Exclulion of the Votes of many Freeholders who were near the Hustings, and ready to have voted for the Petitioner; and that the said Henry Lippincott, the High Sheriff of the said County, did admit a great Number of Persons to vote for the said William Bromley Chester, who had no Right whatever to vote in the Election of a Knight of the Shire to represent the said County in Parliament, although the Petitioner remonstrated against the fame, and required the said Sheriff to reject the Votes of such Persons unqualified as aforesaid; and that the said William Bromley Chester, by the Threats, Promises, and other undue Influence, of his Friends and Agents, did prevail upon divers Persons, who otherwise intended to have voted for the Petitioner, to forbear from voting in the said Election; and in like Manner did attempt and endeavour to persuade divers other Persons from voting for the Petitioner, and, by Threats and Menaces, to intimidate and deter many other Freeholders of the said County from voting for the Petitioner; and that divers Persons, pretending to be Freeholders of the said County, in Right of certain supposed Freehold Leased granted to them by the said William Bromley , and other Persons, offered to vote at the said Election, and were admitted by the said Sheriff to vote for the said William Bromley Chester, although the said Persons had no Freehold Estate whatever in the said County, and notwithstanding the Petitioner and divers Freeholders of the said County did object to the fame, and did request the said Sheriff not to permit such Persons to vote in the said Election; and that, by these illegal Practices the said High Sheriff was induced to return, and did return, the said William Bromley Chester as duly elected, when the Petitioner of Right ought to have been returned duly elected, to represent the said County in Parliament; and that such Proceedings arc in Prejudice of the Rights of a Majority of the legal Eledors of the said County, in Violation and Defiance of the Laws requiring a fair and free Election, and to the manifest Injury of die Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to give the Petitioner such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into Confederation upon Friday the 21ft, Day of June next, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon.

be ignorantly or deflrudively applied by his Ministers; and as the Events of this anxious and important Year may probably be decisive to the future Union and Wellbeing of all His Majesty’s Dominions; and as the Advice of Parliament at the shorteft Notice may be of the utmost Importance to the Salvation of these Kingdoms j and as a continued Series of unsuccessful and unpro-mifed Events have attended the Execution of His Majesty’s Counsels for many Months past, from the Loss of Ticonderoga to the Retreat of His Majesty’s Forces from Boston, which seem to betray either Ignorance or

Gentlemen of the House of Cotnmons,

It was with real Regret and Concern, that I found Myself under the Necessity of asking of My faithful Commons any extraordinary Supplies: I thank you for the Readinels and Dispatch with which they have been granted; and they are the more acceptable to Me, as you have shewn, in the Manner of raising them, an equal Regard to the Exigences of the Service, and the Ease of My People; and you may be allured, that the Confidence you repose in Me shall be used with proper Frugality, and applied only to the Purposes for which it was intended.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

We are engaged in a great National Cause, the Prosecution of which mud inevitably be attended with many Difficulties, and much Expence: But when We consider that the essential Rights and Interests of the whole Empire are deeply concerned in the Issue of it, and can have no Safety or Security but in that Constitutional Subordination for which We are contending,

I am convinced that you will not think, any Price too high for the Preservation of such Objects.

I will Hill entertain a Hope, that My rebellious Subjects may be awakened to a Sense of their Errors; and that, by a voluntary Return to their Duty, they will justify Me in bringing about the favourite Wilh of My Heart, the Restoration of Harmony, and the Re-establishment of Order and Happiness in every Part of My Dominions. But if a due Submission should not be obtained from such Motives, and such Dispositions on their Part, I trull that I shall be able, under the Blelfing of Providence, to effectuate it by a full Exertion or the great Force with which you have intruded Me.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said,

My Ixtrds, and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the First Day of August fjext, to be then here held: And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the First Day ot August next.
